items.e: Sarcomas that frequently spread to lymph nodes are remembered by the SCARE mnemonic: Synovial sarcoma, Clear cell sarcoma, Angiosarcoma, Rhabdomyosarcoma, and Epithelioid sarcoma. Regional lymph node metastasis in Enneking staging is considered M1 (Stage III).

items.q: A 10-year-old boy presents with pain and swelling of the first metatarsal head three days after stepping on a nail while wearing sneakers. Which organism is the most likely cause of osteochondritis in this specific setting?
items.e: While S. aureus is the most common cause of osteomyelitis overall, Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the characteristic organism associated with puncture wounds through the rubber soles of shoes (sneakers).

items.q: Under the ACR 2020 gout guideline, which agent for an acute gout flare is reserved for patients in whom first-line anti-inflammatory therapy is ineffective, poorly tolerated or contraindicated?
items.e: ACR 2020 strongly recommends colchicine, NSAIDs or glucocorticoids (oral, intra-articular or intramuscular) as interchangeable first-line options for a flare. IL-1 inhibitors such as anakinra are conditionally recommended only when these are ineffective, poorly tolerated or contraindicated.

items.q: A 60-year-old man with suspected chronic tophaceous gout has a swelling over the Achilles tendon and aspiration is not feasible. Which imaging modality can specifically identify and quantify monosodium urate deposits non-invasively?
items.e: Dual-energy CT distinguishes urate from calcium by its attenuation at two energy levels, colour-coding and quantifying MSU deposits; it is included in the ACR/EULAR 2015 classification criteria. MRI shows tophi but is not specific for urate.

items.q: A 68-year-old man has deep femoral pain worse at night. Radiographs show an anterolaterally bowed femur with a sharply demarcated, V-shaped lucent front advancing along the diaphysis into normal bone ('blade of grass' appearance). This finding represents:
o: The advancing osteolytic front of active Paget disease
A healing stress fracture with periosteal callus
The nidus of an intracortical osteoid osteoma
Permeative destruction by a small round cell tumour
items.e: The 'blade of grass' or 'flame-shaped' lucency is the advancing edge of osteoclast-driven resorption in the lytic phase of Paget disease of a long bone, usually progressing from one end of the bone toward the diaphysis.

items.q: A 70-year-old woman with polyostotic Paget disease involving the skull reports gradually progressive bilateral hearing loss. What is the principal mechanism?
o: Pagetic remodelling of the petrous temporal bone involving the otic capsule and ossicles
items.e: Hearing loss (conductive, sensorineural or mixed) is the commonest complication of skull Paget disease and results mainly from involvement of the petrous temporal bone, cochlear (otic) capsule and ossicles; compression of CN VIII in the internal auditory canal is less common.

items.q: A 66-year-old man has pain and bowing of the left tibia. Alkaline phosphatase is elevated with normal calcium and phosphate, and radiographs show cortical thickening with coarse trabeculae. Renal function is normal. What is the first-line drug treatment?
o: Single intravenous infusion of zoledronic acid 5 mg
items.e: A single 5 mg infusion of zoledronic acid is the preferred first-line treatment for symptomatic Paget disease, giving higher and longer-lasting biochemical remission than oral bisphosphonates or calcitonin; adequate vitamin D and calcium should be ensured first to avoid hypocalcaemia.

items.q: When planning a surgical procedure on a patient with extensive Paget disease of the femur, which intraoperative complication is most feared?
o: Inadequate implant fixation due to poor bone quality
items.e: Pagetic bone is highly vascular with arteriovenous shunts, making uncontrolled intra‑operative bleeding a major risk.

items.q: Which skull radiograph appearance is characteristic of Paget disease?
items.e: Patchy, fluffy sclerotic foci in a thickened vault ('cotton-wool' skull) are typical of the mixed phase of Paget disease. Hair-on-end suggests thalassaemia, salt-and-pepper hyperparathyroidism, and punched-out lesions myeloma.

items.q: An 11‑year‑old girl with sickle cell disease presents with sudden onset groin pain. She has no history of trauma. Which factor is the most likely direct cause of her osteonecrosis?
o: Sickle‑cell sickling within femoral head vessels
items.e: In sickle cell disease, sickle‑cell sickling of marrow vessels causes intravascular occlusion and focal ischaemia of the femoral head.

items.q: A frog-leg lateral radiograph of a patient with femoral head osteonecrosis shows a subchondral crescent sign. What does this finding represent?
o: Early secondary osteoarthritis with joint-space narrowing
A subchondral fracture marking the onset of collapse (ARCO stage 3)
Reparative sclerosis at the margin of a pre-collapse lesion (ARCO stage 2)
Transient bone marrow oedema that will resolve spontaneously
items.e: The crescent sign is a subchondral fracture through the necrotic segment and places the hip in ARCO stage 3 (collapse); it signals that head-preserving procedures such as core decompression are unlikely to succeed.

items.q: A 40-year-old man on long-term corticosteroids has hip pain. Radiographs show patchy sclerosis without a crescent sign or collapse, and MRI shows a small anteromedial necrotic lesion (<30% of the head). What is the most appropriate treatment?
items.e: Pre-collapse (ARCO 1-2) osteonecrosis with a small or medium lesion is best treated with joint-preserving core decompression (with or without grafting or cell therapy). Arthroplasty is reserved for collapse with symptomatic arthritis.

items.q: Which mechanism is most widely accepted for corticosteroid-associated osteonecrosis of the femoral head?
o: Antibody-mediated vasculitis of the retinacular arteries
Marrow adipocyte hypertrophy and fat accumulation raising intraosseous pressure
Traumatic disruption of the lateral epiphyseal vessels
Red cell sickling within the subchondral sinusoids
items.e: Corticosteroids promote marrow adipogenesis and hypertrophy of fat cells, increasing pressure in the closed femoral head compartment and compromising venous outflow and arterial inflow; fat emboli and hypercoagulability also contribute.

items.q: A 9-year-old has a post-traumatic central physeal bar of the distal femur. Resection of the bar with interposition (Langenskiold) is generally considered when the bar involves less than what proportion of the physeal area, with at least 2 years of growth remaining?
items.e: Bar resection with fat or cement interposition is indicated for bars involving less than about 50% of the physis in a child with at least 2 years (or 2 cm) of remaining growth; larger bars are managed by completing the epiphysiodesis with contralateral epiphysiodesis or later lengthening/osteotomy.

items.q: Which bone formation marker is an osteoblast cell-membrane enzyme that hydrolyses pyrophosphate to permit mineralisation?
items.e: Bone-specific alkaline phosphatase is anchored to the osteoblast membrane and cleaves inorganic pyrophosphate, an inhibitor of mineralisation. Osteocalcin is a secreted formation marker, whereas TRAP and cathepsin K are osteoclast (resorption) products.

items.q: On histology of adult articular cartilage, the basophilic line separating the deep (radial) zone from the underlying calcified cartilage is the:
items.e: The tidemark marks the mineralisation front between uncalcified and calcified cartilage; the cement line lies deeper, between calcified cartilage and subchondral bone. Advancement or duplication of the tidemark is seen in osteoarthritis.

items.q: Which proteoglycan is predominantly responsible for the osmotic swelling pressure that gives articular cartilage its load‑bearing resistance?
items.e: Aggrecan carries large GAG chains (chondroitin and keratan sulfate) that attract water via the Donnan effect, producing compressive stiffness.

items.q: A 14-year-old has a diaphyseal femoral tumour composed of sheets of small round blue cells with membranous CD99 positivity. Which nuclear immunohistochemical marker is more specific than CD99 and supports the diagnosis of Ewing sarcoma?
items.e: NKX2.2 is a downstream target of EWSR1-FLI1 and is a sensitive nuclear marker that is considerably more specific than CD99 for Ewing sarcoma. Desmin and myogenin indicate rhabdomyosarcoma; STAT6 indicates solitary fibrous tumour.

items.q: In Ewing sarcoma, which factor present at diagnosis is the most powerful adverse prognostic indicator?
items.e: Metastasis at presentation is the strongest adverse prognostic factor in Ewing sarcoma (5-year survival roughly 20-30% versus about 70% for localised disease); after chemotherapy, poor histological response is the key additional factor.

items.q: A 15-year-old has a rapidly growing forearm mass. Biopsy shows small round cells in nests separated by fibrous septa, positive for desmin and myogenin, and cytogenetics show t(2;13)(q35;q14). What is the diagnosis?
items.e: Alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma carries PAX3-FOXO1 from t(2;13) (or PAX7-FOXO1 from t(1;13)), typically affects adolescents' extremities, and has a worse prognosis than the embryonal type.

items.q: A 25-year-old has a destructive rib lesion. Histology shows a biphasic tumour of undifferentiated small round blue cells with islands of well-differentiated hyaline cartilage. Which gene fusion is characteristic?
items.e: This is mesenchymal chondrosarcoma, defined molecularly by the HEY1-NCOA2 fusion. IDH1/2 mutations occur in conventional chondrosarcoma, EWSR1-NR4A3 in extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma and COL1A1-PDGFB in dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans.

items.q: What is the most common histological type of primary lymphoma of bone?
items.e: Over 80% of primary bone lymphomas are diffuse large B-cell lymphomas. They are treated with chemoimmunotherapy (R-CHOP) with or without radiotherapy, surgery being limited to fracture stabilisation.

items.q: A 40-year-old has a deep thigh mass diagnosed as myxoid liposarcoma with a FUS-DDIT3 fusion. Besides CT of the chest, which staging investigation is specifically recommended for this subtype?
items.e: Myxoid liposarcoma has a peculiar tendency to metastasise to extrapulmonary sites, especially the spine, retroperitoneum and soft tissues, which are often missed by chest CT and bone scan; whole-spine MRI is therefore recommended for staging.

items.q: A 28-year-old has a deep calf mass near the knee. Biopsy shows a monophasic spindle cell tumour. Which immunohistochemical marker most strongly supports synovial sarcoma?
items.e: Strong diffuse nuclear TLE1 supports synovial sarcoma, which is confirmed by the SS18-SSX fusion from t(X;18). MDM2 amplification indicates atypical lipomatous tumour, STAT6 solitary fibrous tumour and INI1 loss epithelioid sarcoma.

items.q: A large, deep, fatty thigh mass with thick septa is difficult to distinguish from a lipoma on histology. Which test best confirms atypical lipomatous tumour/well-differentiated liposarcoma?
items.e: Atypical lipomatous tumour/well-differentiated liposarcoma has supernumerary ring or giant chromosomes with amplification of 12q13-15 including MDM2 and CDK4, best shown by FISH; FUS-DDIT3 defines myxoid liposarcoma and S100 stains both benign and malignant fat.

items.q: A 2 cm subcutaneous forearm 'lipoma' was shelled out in a clinic and histology unexpectedly shows a high-grade sarcoma. After restaging, what is the standard management?
o: Re-excision of the tumour bed and scar with wide margins, with radiotherapy as indicated
items.e: After an unplanned ('whoops') excision, residual tumour is found in roughly half of cases, so the scar, tumour bed and any contaminated tissues are re-excised with wide margins at a sarcoma centre, with radiotherapy according to grade and margins.

items.q: In the NCIC SR2 trial (O'Sullivan, Lancet 2002) comparing preoperative with postoperative radiotherapy for extremity soft-tissue sarcoma, preoperative radiotherapy was associated with:
o: More late fibrosis and joint stiffness
A higher rate of major wound complications
items.e: Preoperative radiotherapy roughly doubled major wound complications (about 35% versus 17%), particularly in the thigh, but uses a lower dose and smaller field, causing less late fibrosis, oedema and joint stiffness; local control was similar.

items.q: A 24-year-old man has a slowly enlarging, ulcerating nodule on the volar forearm that was treated as a granuloma. Biopsy shows epithelioid cells with central necrosis, positive for cytokeratin and with loss of nuclear INI1 (SMARCB1). What is the diagnosis?
o: Giant cell tumour of tendon sheath
items.e: Epithelioid sarcoma is the commonest soft-tissue sarcoma of the hand and forearm in young adults, mimics granulomatous lesions, shows INI1 loss, and spreads to regional lymph nodes and along fascial planes.

items.q: A 30-year-old has a mass attached to the Achilles tendon. Histology shows nests of pale cells positive for S100 and HMB-45, and molecular testing shows an EWSR1-ATF1 fusion. What is the diagnosis?
items.e: Clear cell sarcoma ('melanoma of soft parts') arises from tendons and aponeuroses of the foot and ankle in young adults, expresses melanocytic markers, and is defined by EWSR1-ATF1 (or EWSR1-CREB1) fusion, distinguishing it from melanoma.

items.q: A 32-year-old woman has an asymptomatic 6 cm extra-abdominal desmoid tumour of the thigh with a CTNNB1 mutation and no functional deficit. What is the recommended initial management?
items.e: Current consensus recommends active surveillance as first-line for asymptomatic, non-threatening desmoid tumours, because many stabilise or regress spontaneously and surgery has high recurrence; treatment is reserved for progression or symptoms.

items.q: A 70-year-old has a lytic lesion in the peritrochanteric femur from breast carcinoma, with pain on walking, occupying 1/3 to 2/3 of the cortical width. What is the Mirels score and recommendation?
items.e: Mirels: peritrochanteric site 3, functional pain 3, lytic 3, size 1/3-2/3 = 2, giving 11. A score of 9 or more indicates high fracture risk (about 33% or more) and prophylactic fixation, followed by radiotherapy.

items.q: Before surgical fixation of an impending pathological fracture, preoperative angiographic embolisation is most strongly indicated for metastasis from which primary?
items.e: Renal cell (and thyroid) metastases are highly vascular and can bleed torrentially; embolisation within about 24-48 hours before surgery significantly reduces intraoperative blood loss.

items.q: A 65-year-old presents with a destructive bone lesion and no known primary. Using a systematic work-up (history, examination, labs, chest radiograph, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis and bone scan; Rougraff), which primary site is most commonly identified?
items.e: In Rougraff's series of skeletal metastases of unknown origin, lung carcinoma was the most common primary, followed by kidney; this protocol identified the primary in about 85% of patients before biopsy.

items.q: A 72-year-old with metastatic lung cancer sustains a displaced pathological fracture through a lytic lesion of the femoral neck. What is the preferred treatment?
o: Cemented hemiarthroplasty or total hip arthroplasty
items.e: Pathological femoral neck fractures rarely heal and fixation fails, so cemented arthroplasty (with a long stem if there is further femoral disease) is preferred to allow immediate weight-bearing.

items.q: After intramedullary nailing of a pathological femoral fracture from metastatic carcinoma, postoperative external beam radiotherapy to the whole operative field primarily serves to:
o: Reduce disease progression, implant failure and need for reoperation
items.e: Townsend and colleagues showed that postoperative radiotherapy after fixation of metastatic lesions improves function and reduces the rate of reoperation for local progression and loss of fixation; it is given once the wound has healed.

items.q: Under the NOMS framework, a patient with multiple myeloma has high-grade epidural spinal cord compression at T8, no neurological deficit, a mechanically stable spine and good systemic status. What is the recommended treatment?
o: Separation surgery followed by stereotactic radiosurgery
items.e: Myeloma, lymphoma and seminoma are radiosensitive, so conventional external beam radiotherapy is used even with high-grade ESCC in a stable spine. Separation surgery with SRS is for radioresistant tumours with high-grade compression.

items.q: Which spinal metastasis scoring system uses only three prognostic factors (growth rate of the primary tumour, visceral metastases and bone metastases) to guide the surgical strategy?
items.e: The Tomita score (2-10) combines primary tumour growth rate, visceral metastases and bone metastases to recommend wide/marginal excision, palliative surgery or supportive care. The revised Tokuhashi score uses six parameters including performance status and neurology.

items.q: In a patient with a suspected primary bone sarcoma, why should MRI of the lesion and whole bone be performed before the biopsy?
o: Biopsy-induced haemorrhage and oedema distort tumour extent on subsequent MRI
MRI after biopsy carries a risk of tumour seeding
Biopsy tracks cannot be seen on MRI
items.e: Staging imaging precedes biopsy because haemorrhage and oedema from the biopsy obscure the true tumour margins and intraosseous extent on MRI, compromising surgical planning.

items.q: In Enneking's classification of surgical margins, a resection whose plane of dissection passes through the reactive zone around a sarcoma is termed:
items.e: A marginal margin passes through the reactive zone and may leave satellite tumour cells; a wide margin passes through normal tissue beyond the reactive zone within the compartment, and a radical margin removes the entire compartment.

items.q: A 6-year-old with an irritable hip refuses to bear weight, has a temperature of 38.9 C and an ESR of 52 mm/h, but a WBC of 9,800/mm3. Using Kocher's criteria, the predicted probability of septic arthritis is approximately:
items.e: Kocher's four predictors are non-weight-bearing, fever >38.5 C, ESR >40 mm/h and WBC >12,000/mm3; the probability of septic arthritis is about 3%, 40%, 93% and 99.6% with one, two, three and four predictors respectively.

items.q: A 2-year-old has a mildly febrile septic knee with modest CRP rise; Gram stain and routine cultures of joint fluid are negative. Which organism is most likely, and how is it best identified?
o: Kingella kingae, by PCR of synovial fluid
Group B Streptococcus, by blood culture
Haemophilus influenzae type b, by latex agglutination
items.e: Kingella kingae is the commonest cause of osteoarticular infection between 6 months and 4 years; it is fastidious and often culture-negative, so specific PCR (or inoculation into blood-culture bottles) is used.

items.q: A 12-year-old has 6 weeks of tibial pain without systemic upset. MRI shows a metaphyseal abscess cavity lined by a rim of relatively high signal on T1-weighted images. What is this sign called and what does it indicate?
o: Fallen fragment sign; simple bone cyst
items.e: The penumbra sign is a T1-hyperintense layer of vascularised granulation tissue lining an abscess cavity, characteristic of subacute osteomyelitis and helpful in distinguishing it from tumours such as Ewing sarcoma.

items.q: A 22-year-old sexually active woman has migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis of the wrist extensors and a few painless pustules on her limbs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: The triad of tenosynovitis, dermatitis (pustules) and migratory polyarthralgia is characteristic of disseminated gonococcal infection; cultures of blood, joint fluid and genitourinary sites (or NAAT) should be taken and treated with ceftriaxone.

items.q: According to the 2018 International Consensus Meeting (ICM) definition of periprosthetic joint infection, which single finding is a major criterion that alone establishes infection?
o: Synovial fluid WBC count above 3,000 cells/uL
A single positive culture of a virulent organism
A sinus tract communicating with the prosthesis
items.e: The two ICM 2018 major criteria are a sinus tract communicating with the joint or visualisation of the prosthesis, and two positive cultures of the same organism; serum and synovial markers and a single positive culture are minor criteria scored together.

items.q: In uncomplicated acute haematogenous osteomyelitis in a child who is improving clinically with a falling CRP, current evidence supports which antibiotic strategy?
o: Short intravenous course of a few days followed by oral antibiotics, total about 3-4 weeks
Oral antibiotics only after surgical drainage in all cases
items.e: Randomised data (Peltola and colleagues) show that a short intravenous course of about 2-4 days followed by oral therapy for a total of about 3-4 weeks is as effective as prolonged intravenous treatment in uncomplicated cases.

items.q: In the Masquelet induced-membrane technique for a segmental bone defect after debridement of infected nonunion, when is the cement spacer usually removed and the defect grafted?
items.e: The PMMA spacer induces a vascularised membrane that secretes growth factors (VEGF, TGF-beta, BMP-2); this activity peaks at around 4-8 weeks, when the second stage is performed by filling the membrane with cancellous autograft.

items.q: In children with sickle cell disease, which organism causes osteomyelitis disproportionately often compared with the general population?
items.e: Bowel infarction allows Salmonella to enter the circulation and seed infarcted bone, so Salmonella osteomyelitis is far more frequent in sickle cell disease, although Staphylococcus aureus remains common; empirical cover should include both.

items.q: Which pattern of vertebral involvement is the most common in spinal tuberculosis?
items.e: Paradiscal involvement, with destruction of adjacent endplates and narrowing of the intervening disc, is the commonest pattern; central lesions cause vertebra plana and may mimic tumour.

items.q: Compared with early-onset Pott paraplegia (active disease), late-onset paraplegia occurring years after healed spinal tuberculosis is characterised by:
o: Better prognosis and good response to ATT alone
Compression by cold abscess and granulation tissue
Worse prognosis, often from an internal gibbus or stretched cord over a severe kyphosis
Usually involvement of the lumbar spine below the conus
items.e: Late-onset paraplegia results from mechanical factors such as an internal bony ridge, fibrosis or a cord stretched over a rigid kyphus, and has a poorer prognosis than early-onset paraplegia, which is due to abscess, granulation tissue or sequestra.

items.q: In a child with dorsal spinal tuberculosis, which radiographic finding is one of Rajasekaran's 'spine-at-risk' signs predicting progression of kyphosis?
o: Toppling of the upper vertebra over the lower
items.e: Rajasekaran's four spine-at-risk signs are separation of the facet joints, posterior retropulsion, lateral translation and toppling; two or more predict severe progressive kyphosis and indicate early surgical correction.

items.q: The Xpert MTB/RIF (GeneXpert) assay detects rifampicin resistance by identifying mutations in which gene?
items.e: Xpert MTB/RIF is a cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test that detects M. tuberculosis DNA and mutations in the 81-bp rifampicin resistance-determining region of rpoB within about 2 hours; katG and inhA confer isoniazid resistance.

items.q: A 2-year-old has rickets with hypocalcaemia, raised PTH, normal 25-hydroxyvitamin D and low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. Which treatment is required?
items.e: This is vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1A, caused by CYP27B1 (1-alpha-hydroxylase) deficiency; the patient cannot activate vitamin D and needs physiological doses of calcitriol (or alfacalcidol).

items.q: Burosumab, used in X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets, is a monoclonal antibody directed against:
items.e: In XLH, PHEX mutations raise FGF23, causing renal phosphate wasting and low calcitriol. Burosumab neutralises FGF23, normalising phosphate reabsorption and improving rickets better than conventional phosphate and calcitriol.

items.q: A 50-year-old has progressive bone pain, proximal weakness and multiple insufficiency fractures. Serum phosphate is low with renal phosphate wasting, calcitriol is low-normal and FGF23 is markedly elevated. What is the most likely cause and its definitive treatment?
o: Tumour-induced osteomalacia; excision of a phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour
items.e: Adult-onset FGF23-mediated hypophosphataemic osteomalacia suggests tumour-induced osteomalacia from a small phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour (often FN1-FGFR1 fusion), located by Ga-68 DOTATATE PET-CT; complete excision is curative.

items.q: The lateral spine radiograph of a patient on long-term haemodialysis shows alternating dense sclerotic bands at the vertebral endplates with lucent centres. This 'rugger jersey' spine is caused by:
items.e: Rugger jersey spine reflects subendplate osteosclerosis from secondary hyperparathyroidism in chronic kidney disease; osteopetrosis produces 'sandwich' vertebrae with sharper, denser endplates.

items.q: Romosozumab, used for severe postmenopausal osteoporosis, carries a boxed warning for which adverse effect?
o: Myocardial infarction, stroke and cardiovascular death
items.e: Romosozumab, an anti-sclerostin antibody with dual anabolic and antiresorptive effects, showed an excess of serious cardiovascular events versus alendronate in ARCH, so it should not be started within a year of MI or stroke.

items.q: A 68-year-old woman stops denosumab after 4 years without further treatment and 10 months later sustains several spontaneous vertebral fractures. What is the mechanism and how should this be prevented?
o: Rebound increase in bone turnover; follow denosumab with a bisphosphonate
Atypical femoral fracture pathway; give teriparatide
items.e: Denosumab's effect wears off rapidly, with a rebound surge of osteoclast activity and multiple vertebral fractures; denosumab should not be stopped without transition to a bisphosphonate such as zoledronic acid.

items.q: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates such as alendronate and zoledronic acid inhibit osteoclast function by inhibiting which enzyme?
items.e: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway, preventing prenylation of small GTPases needed for the osteoclast ruffled border and causing apoptosis; non-nitrogen bisphosphonates form toxic ATP analogues.

items.q: According to the ASBMR 2013 task force, which is a MAJOR feature of an atypical femoral fracture?
o: Generalised increase in femoral cortical thickness
Localised periosteal or endosteal thickening of the lateral cortex at the fracture site
items.e: Major features are minimal or no trauma, a fracture line originating at the lateral cortex that is substantially transverse, a medial spike in complete fractures, minimal comminution and localised lateral cortical 'beaking'; generalised cortical thickening, prodromal pain and bilaterality are minor features.

items.q: Before starting allopurinol, ACR 2020 recommends testing for which HLA allele in patients of Southeast Asian (e.g. Han Chinese, Korean, Thai) or African American descent?
items.e: HLA-B*58:01 strongly predicts allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (including SJS/TEN) and is common in these populations. HLA-B*57:01 predicts abacavir hypersensitivity.

items.q: In a patient with tophaceous gout on urate-lowering therapy, what serum urate target is recommended by ACR 2020?
items.e: ACR 2020 recommends a treat-to-target approach with serum urate below 6 mg/dL for all patients on urate-lowering therapy; EULAR suggests below 5 mg/dL for severe tophaceous disease to speed tophus dissolution.

items.q: An 80-year-old woman has a large, cool, blood-stained shoulder effusion with destruction of the humeral head and a massive rotator cuff tear (Milwaukee shoulder). Which crystal is implicated?
items.e: Milwaukee shoulder is a destructive arthropathy associated with basic calcium phosphate crystals, which are not birefringent and are seen with alizarin red staining or electron microscopy; synovial fluid is typically non-inflammatory.

items.q: In the CARES trial in gout patients with established cardiovascular disease, febuxostat compared with allopurinol was associated with:
o: Lower rates of gout flares and mortality
items.e: CARES met non-inferiority for the composite cardiovascular endpoint but showed higher cardiovascular and all-cause death with febuxostat, prompting an FDA boxed warning; ACR 2020 prefers allopurinol as first-line urate-lowering therapy.

items.q: Mutations in which gene, encoding a protein in the RANK-NF-kB signalling pathway, are the most common genetic cause of familial Paget disease of bone?
items.e: SQSTM1, encoding sequestosome-1 (p62), is mutated in a substantial proportion of familial and some sporadic Paget disease and enhances osteoclast activity via NF-kB signalling.

items.q: What is the most common malignant tumour arising in pagetic bone?
items.e: Secondary (Paget) sarcoma occurs in under 1% of patients, most often in the pelvis, femur and humerus; it is usually osteosarcoma and has a very poor prognosis. A new, increasing pain in a pagetic bone should raise suspicion.

items.q: Autosomal dominant osteopetrosis type II (Albers-Schonberg disease), with 'sandwich' vertebrae and 'bone-in-bone' appearance, is most commonly caused by mutation of which gene?
items.e: ADO II results from CLCN7 mutations affecting the osteoclast chloride channel, impairing acidification of the resorption lacuna. TCIRG1 causes infantile malignant (autosomal recessive) osteopetrosis and CTSK pycnodysostosis.

items.q: Under the 2019 ARCO classification of femoral head osteonecrosis, a hip with a subchondral fracture and femoral head depression greater than 2 mm is staged as:
items.e: ARCO 2019: stage 1 MRI-positive with normal radiographs, stage 2 radiographic changes without collapse, stage 3 subchondral fracture or collapse (3A head depression 2 mm or less, 3B more than 2 mm), and stage 4 osteoarthritis.

items.q: A 72-year-old woman has sudden severe medial knee pain without trauma. MRI shows a subchondral fracture line with extensive marrow oedema in the medial femoral condyle and an associated medial meniscal root tear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Subchondral insufficiency fracture of the knee (formerly SONK)
items.e: Spontaneous osteonecrosis of the knee in elderly women is now regarded as a subchondral insufficiency fracture, typically of the medial femoral condyle and often linked to a medial meniscal root tear; small lesions are managed with protected weight-bearing.

items.q: Sclerostin, the target of romosozumab, is secreted mainly by which cell and acts by which mechanism?
o: Osteoblasts; activating RANK on osteoclast precursors
Osteocytes; binding LRP5/6 and inhibiting Wnt signalling
items.e: Sclerostin (SOST) from osteocytes binds LRP5/6 co-receptors and inhibits canonical Wnt/beta-catenin signalling, suppressing bone formation; mechanical loading reduces sclerostin, and its absence causes sclerosteosis and van Buchem disease.

items.q: According to Perren's interfragmentary strain theory, lamellar bone can form directly across a fracture gap only when the strain is below approximately:
items.e: Granulation tissue tolerates up to about 100% strain, cartilage about 10% and bone less than 2%; direct (primary) bone healing therefore needs absolute stability, while relative stability with higher strain produces callus.

items.q: Which collagen type is a marker of hypertrophic chondrocytes and is found in the calcified cartilage layer of articular cartilage?
items.e: Type X collagen is produced by hypertrophic chondrocytes in the growth plate and in the calcified zone of articular cartilage, where it aids mineralisation; type II is the main collagen of hyaline cartilage and type VI is pericellular.

items.q: Lubricin (proteoglycan 4), the main boundary lubricant of the joint, is secreted by type B synoviocytes and which other cells?
o: Chondrocytes of the superficial zone of articular cartilage
Hypertrophic chondrocytes of the calcified zone
items.e: Lubricin (PRG4) is made by fibroblast-like type B synoviocytes and superficial-zone chondrocytes; it provides boundary lubrication of the articular surface, whereas type A synoviocytes are phagocytic macrophage-like cells.

items.q: Which change in articular cartilage distinguishes early osteoarthritis from normal ageing?
items.e: In early osteoarthritis water content rises because collagen network disruption allows proteoglycans to swell, and modulus falls; with ageing, water content decreases and keratan sulphate increases relative to chondroitin sulphate.

items.q: Microfracture of a full-thickness chondral defect typically produces repair tissue composed predominantly of which collagen type?
items.e: Marrow stimulation brings mesenchymal cells into the defect, forming fibrocartilage rich in type I collagen, which is mechanically inferior to hyaline (type II) cartilage and may deteriorate over time.

items.q: Which matrix metalloproteinase is considered the principal enzyme degrading type II collagen in osteoarthritic cartilage?
items.e: MMP-13 cleaves type II collagen most efficiently and is upregulated by IL-1 and TNF-alpha in osteoarthritis, while ADAMTS-4 and -5 (aggrecanases) degrade aggrecan.

items.q: Which implant material has an elastic modulus closest to that of cortical bone?
items.e: Cortical bone has a modulus of about 15-20 GPa; titanium alloy is about 110 GPa, stainless steel about 200 GPa, cobalt-chromium about 210-230 GPa and alumina about 380 GPa. The lower modulus of titanium reduces stress shielding.

items.q: Highly cross-linking ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene by irradiation reduces adhesive and abrasive wear, but at the cost of:
o: Reduced fracture toughness and fatigue resistance
items.e: Cross-linking improves wear resistance but lowers ductility, fracture toughness and fatigue strength; residual free radicals are reduced by remelting (which further lowers strength) or annealing, or stabilised with vitamin E.

items.q: In bridge plating of a comminuted diaphyseal fracture, increasing the plate working length (the distance between the screws nearest the fracture on either side) will:
o: Decrease construct stiffness and spread strain over a longer segment of plate
Have no effect on construct stiffness
Increase the risk of compression at the fracture
items.e: A longer working length makes the construct more flexible, allowing relative stability for callus and distributing bending stress over a greater length of plate, reducing the risk of fatigue failure at a single screw hole.

items.q: Which screw property contributes most to its pull-out strength in bone?
items.e: Pull-out strength is mainly determined by outer diameter (and thread depth, the difference between outer and core diameters) together with bone density; core diameter governs bending and torsional strength.

items.q: When a constant load is applied to a ligament and it continues to elongate over time, this viscoelastic property is called:
items.e: Creep is continued deformation under constant load; stress relaxation is decreasing stress under constant deformation, and hysteresis is the energy lost between loading and unloading curves.

items.q: Corrosion at the modular head-neck taper of a total hip arthroplasty ('trunnionosis'), causing metallosis and adverse local tissue reaction, is best described as:
items.e: Micromotion at the taper disrupts the passive oxide layer while the confined crevice becomes acidic and oxygen-depleted, leading to fretting-crevice (mechanically assisted crevice) corrosion with cobalt and chromium release.

items.q: Before awl perforation in microfracture of a full-thickness femoral condyle chondral defect, the surgeon curettes away the layer of calcified cartilage at the base of the lesion while preserving the subchondral plate. What is the purpose?
o: It improves the amount and attachment of the repair tissue
It reduces the risk of postoperative infection
It allows a thicker cartilage graft to be inserted
items.e: Experimental work (Frisbie, Steadman) showed that removing the calcified cartilage layer increases the amount and improves the attachment of the fibrocartilaginous repair tissue; the subchondral plate is preserved and perforated to release marrow elements.

items.q: A skier sustains a tibial shaft fracture from a twisting fall with the foot fixed in the binding. Which fracture pattern is expected from this pure torsional load?
o: Short oblique with a butterfly fragment
items.e: Torsion produces maximal tensile stress on planes at 45 degrees to the long axis, so the fracture propagates as a spiral; bending gives transverse or butterfly patterns, and axial compression gives oblique or impaction fractures.

items.q: Which statement about fatigue failure of orthopaedic implants is correct?
o: Fatigue failure occurs only when the ultimate tensile strength is exceeded
The endurance limit is the stress below which the material can withstand an infinite number of loading cycles
Titanium alloys are insensitive to notches and scratches
A scratch on a stainless-steel plate does not alter its fatigue life
items.e: Fatigue failure occurs with cyclic loading below the ultimate strength; below the endurance limit the material survives infinite cycles. Titanium is particularly notch sensitive, and surface scratches act as stress risers that shorten fatigue life.

items.q: A long-bone fracture with a transverse component and a triangular butterfly fragment is most characteristic of which loading mode?
items.e: Bending places one cortex in tension, where a transverse fracture begins, and the other in compression; combined bending and compression produces a butterfly fragment on the compression side.

items.q: Which of the following has the lowest elastic (Young's) modulus?
items.e: In descending order of modulus: ceramics, cobalt-chromium, stainless steel, titanium, cortical bone (about 15-20 GPa), PMMA (about 2-3 GPa), polyethylene (about 1 GPa), cancellous bone, tendon/ligament and articular cartilage (MPa range).

items.q: A long longitudinal cortical window (open-section defect) is cut in a femoral diaphysis to remove a cement mantle. By approximately how much does this reduce the bone's torsional strength?
items.e: An open-section defect prevents the tube from resisting shear around its circumference and reduces torsional strength (energy-storage capacity) by up to about 90%, far more than a single drill-hole stress riser.

items.q: Bone loaded at a higher strain rate becomes stiffer and stronger and absorbs more energy before failure. This behaviour is explained by bone being:
items.e: Viscoelastic materials have rate-dependent mechanical properties; bone is stiffer and stores more energy at high loading rates, which is why high-energy injuries cause greater comminution. Bone is also anisotropic.

items.q: Which of the following is the most characteristic immunohistochemical marker for a primary lymphoma of bone?
items.e: Diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma shows strong CD45 and CD20 expression; CD99 is typical of Ewing, CD138 for myeloma, and synaptophysin for neuroendocrine tumours.

items.q: A 55-year-old has an 8 cm deep thigh mass. Which MRI feature most suggests an atypical lipomatous tumour rather than a high-grade sarcoma?
o: A predominantly fat-signal mass containing thickened septa
Central necrosis with peripheral contrast enhancement
An infiltrative margin into surrounding muscle
items.e: A mostly fatty mass with thick (over 2 mm) or nodular septa suggests atypical lipomatous tumour/well-differentiated liposarcoma; necrosis, peritumoural oedema and infiltrative margins favour high-grade sarcoma.

items.q: A 16-year-old with neurofibromatosis type 1 notices that a long-standing plexiform neurofibroma in the forearm has become painful and is enlarging rapidly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: NF1 carries a lifetime MPNST risk of about 8-13%, typically arising in plexiform neurofibromas; new pain or rapid growth warrants MRI and FDG-PET with biopsy of the most avid area.

items.q: What is the preferred biopsy technique for a suspected deep extremity soft-tissue sarcoma?
o: Image-guided core-needle biopsy after MRI, at the treating sarcoma centre
Open incisional biopsy at the referring hospital
items.e: Multiple-core image-guided needle biopsy after local imaging gives tissue for grading and molecular tests with low contamination, and should be planned by the treating team so the track can be excised.

items.q: Under the AJCC 8th edition for soft-tissue sarcoma of the trunk and extremities, a 12 cm grade 1 tumour with no nodal or distant spread is stage:
items.e: T3 is over 10 cm and up to 15 cm. Grade 1 tumours are stage IA if T1 and IB if T2-T4; grade 2-3 tumours are II (T1), IIIA (T2) or IIIB (T3-T4); N1 or M1 is stage IV.

items.q: A 62-year-old with metastatic breast cancer is confused and dehydrated with a corrected serum calcium of 14.2 mg/dL. What is the first step in management?
items.e: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy causes volume depletion, so aggressive isotonic saline is the first step, followed by an intravenous bisphosphonate (or denosumab) and calcitonin for rapid effect; loop diuretics are used only after volume repletion.

items.q: A 15-year-old has 6 weeks of night pain around the knee and a firm swelling over the distal femur. What is the first investigation?
o: Plain radiographs of the femur and knee in two planes
items.e: Plain radiographs in two planes are the first investigation for suspected bone tumours and often suggest the diagnosis; MRI of the whole bone and systemic staging follow before biopsy.

items.q: A 65‑year‑old woman with a long‑standing sinus tract over the mid‑tibial bone is suspected of having chronic osteomyelitis. Which pathological finding on debridement would confirm the diagnosis of chronic disease?
o: Dense new bone surrounding the lesion
A sharply marginated dead bone fragment (sequestrum)
Diffuse marrow infiltration by inflammatory cells
items.e: Chronic osteomyelitis is defined by the presence of a dead bone (sequestrum) within the infected area.

items.q: A 25‑year‑old man from a high‑TB‑burden area presents with insidious right hip pain, restricted motion and a minimal effusion. Radiographs show juxta‑articular osteoporosis with marginal erosions but preserved joint space. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: The classic Phemister triad—juxta‑articular osteopenia and marginal erosions with a preserved joint space—points to tubercular arthritis.

items.q: In Indian osteoarticular TB, why are AFB smears often negative?
o: The disease is paucibacillary with few organisms in tissue
The sample is usually contaminated with debris
items.e: Osteoarticular TB is paucibacillary; hence smears have low sensitivity compared with culture or molecular tests.

items.q: Which laboratory finding is most useful for monitoring disease activity in osteoarticular TB?
items.e: ESR, though non‑specific, rises with active TB and falls with treatment response.

items.q: An 8-year-old girl has short stature and progressive genu varum; her father had similar bowed legs. Genetic testing shows a PHEX mutation. Which biochemical pattern is expected?
o: High calcium, low phosphate, low ALP
High phosphate, low calcium, high PTH
Low phosphate, normal calcium, raised ALP
Low calcium, high phosphate, low ALP
items.e: X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets (X-linked dominant) has raised FGF23 causing renal phosphate wasting: low serum phosphate, normal calcium, raised ALP, normal or mildly raised PTH and inappropriately low-normal calcitriol.

items.q: Which instruction is correct for taking weekly oral alendronate?
o: Take with food to reduce gastric irritation
Take with a calcium supplement to improve absorption
Take on an empty stomach with plain water and remain upright for at least 30 minutes before eating
items.e: Oral bisphosphonate absorption is under 1% and is abolished by food, calcium or other drinks, and reflux can cause oesophagitis; they are taken fasting with plain water, staying upright for 30 minutes before food or other medicines.

items.q: A 72-year-old woman with a lumbar T-score of -3.2 and a recent vertebral fragility fracture is started on a monthly injectable agent that both stimulates bone formation and reduces bone resorption. Which drug is it?
items.e: Romosozumab, a monoclonal antibody to sclerostin, has a dual effect, increasing formation and decreasing resorption; it is given monthly for 12 months and followed by an antiresorptive. Teriparatide is anabolic only.

items.q: A 65‑year‑old postmenopausal woman has been on oral alendronate for 5 years without fracture. Her latest DXA shows a femoral neck T‑score of −2.4. Which strategy is most appropriate regarding her anti‑resorptive therapy?
o: Start a drug holiday for 2 years
items.e: After 5 years of oral bisphosphonate and no high‑risk features, a 2‑year drug holiday is reasonable per ASBMR guidelines.

items.q: Which laboratory value is most useful to confirm that a patient can safely receive IV zoledronate for osteoporosis?
items.e: IV bisphosphonates are contraindicated in CK < 35 mL/min to avoid renal toxicity.

items.q: A 60-year-old man on a thiazide diuretic has an acutely red, hot first MTP joint. Aspiration shows needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent crystals. When should the serum urate be measured to guide long-term management?
o: Two to four weeks after the flare has settled
Never, as crystal identification is sufficient
Only after one year of urate-lowering therapy
items.e: Serum urate may be falsely normal during a flare, so it is rechecked about 2-4 weeks after resolution to establish the baseline and then monitored to keep it below 6 mg/dL on urate-lowering therapy.

items.q: A 14-year-old has hip pain. Radiographs show a well-defined lytic lesion with a thin sclerotic rim and stippled calcification confined to the femoral head epiphysis, with marked surrounding marrow oedema on MRI. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Chondroblastoma is an epiphyseal tumour of skeletally immature patients with a sclerotic rim, chondroid calcification and striking surrounding oedema; giant cell tumour occurs after physeal closure and simple bone cysts are metaphyseal.

items.q: During osteoblast differentiation, which transcription factor acts as the master switch, and its loss of function leads to cleidocranial dysplasia?
items.e: RUNX2 drives osteoblast lineage commitment; mutations cause cleidocranial dysplasia.

items.q: Which serum marker is recommended by the IOF and IFCC as the reference marker of bone formation for monitoring osteoporosis therapy?
o: C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (CTX)
items.e: P1NP, released during type I collagen synthesis, is the reference formation marker and serum CTX the reference resorption marker; TRAP 5b and deoxypyridinoline are resorption markers.

items.q: Among patients with localised Ewing sarcoma, which primary site carries the poorest prognosis?
items.e: Axial, especially pelvic, Ewing sarcoma presents with large volume, is difficult to resect with clear margins and has worse survival than distal extremity tumours.

items.q: A 5-year-old with vertebra plana has a biopsy showing cells with grooved nuclei that are CD1a and langerin (CD207) positive. Which somatic mutation is found in about half of these lesions?
items.e: Langerhans cell histiocytosis is a myeloid neoplasm driven by MAPK pathway activation, with BRAF V600E in about 50%; GNAS occurs in fibrous dysplasia and H3F3A G34W in giant cell tumour of bone.

items.q: A 25-year-old has a deep, slowly growing mass near the knee. Radiographs show a soft-tissue mass containing spotty calcification. Which sarcoma is most likely?
items.e: Synovial sarcoma typically affects young adults near large joints (especially the knee) and shows calcification on radiographs in about a third of cases; slow growth and small size may falsely suggest a benign lesion.

items.q: In the Patchell randomised trial (Lancet 2005) of metastatic epidural spinal cord compression, direct decompressive surgery followed by radiotherapy, compared with radiotherapy alone, resulted in:
o: More patients walking after treatment and for longer
Better outcomes only in radiosensitive tumours such as lymphoma
items.e: Surgery plus radiotherapy allowed significantly more patients to walk (84% vs 57%) and to retain ambulation longer, and more non-ambulatory patients regained walking; radiosensitive tumours were excluded.

items.q: Why is a technetium-99m bone scan unreliable for skeletal staging in multiple myeloma?
o: Myeloma lesions are purely lytic with little osteoblastic response, so they are often 'cold'
Myeloma cells excrete the tracer through the kidneys
Bone scan cannot detect lesions under 5 cm
items.e: Bone scintigraphy depends on osteoblastic activity, which myeloma suppresses, so lesions are frequently missed; whole-body low-dose CT (or PET-CT/MRI) is the preferred imaging.

items.q: When planning a needle biopsy of a large heterogeneous bone tumour with a necrotic centre, where should the sample be taken?
o: From the solid, enhancing component identified on MRI or PET
From the reactive periosteal new bone
items.e: Biopsy should target the viable, enhancing or most FDG-avid solid part of the tumour, which reflects the highest grade; necrosis and reactive tissue give non-diagnostic samples and risk under-grading.

items.q: In the Cierny-Mader classification of osteomyelitis, a lesion with full-thickness cortical sequestration that can be excised without destabilising the bone is anatomical type:
items.e: Type I is medullary, type II superficial (outer cortex), type III localised full-thickness but stable after debridement, and type IV diffuse with instability before or after debridement.

items.q: A 10-year-old girl has recurrent episodes of clavicular and distal tibial metaphyseal pain over 18 months with sterile bone biopsies showing chronic inflammation. What is the first-line treatment?
items.e: Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis (chronic non-bacterial osteomyelitis) is an autoinflammatory disorder favouring the clavicle and metaphyses; NSAIDs are first-line, with bisphosphonates or TNF inhibitors for refractory or spinal disease.

items.q: The LRINEC score for necrotising soft-tissue infection uses CRP, white cell count, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine and glucose. A score of at least what value is generally taken to raise suspicion of necrotising fasciitis?
items.e: A LRINEC score of 6 or more raises suspicion and 8 or more is strongly predictive; however, the score has limited sensitivity, so clinical suspicion still mandates urgent surgical exploration.

items.q: Under Tuli's 'middle-path' regimen for spinal tuberculosis with neurological deficit, which is an indication for surgical decompression?
o: No neurological recovery after 3-4 weeks of ATT and rest
Disc space narrowing at a single level
items.e: The middle-path regimen starts ATT and rest, reserving surgery for failure of neurological recovery after about 3-4 weeks, worsening deficit, recurrence, severe or rapidly progressive paraplegia, or diagnostic doubt.

items.q: A 30-year-old on treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis develops a symmetrical, non-erosive polyarthritis of the knees and ankles; joint aspirates are sterile with no AFB. What is this condition?
items.e: Poncet disease is a reactive polyarthritis in active tuberculosis without direct joint infection; it resolves with antituberculous treatment without joint destruction.

items.q: In a child with nutritional (vitamin D deficiency) rickets, which laboratory abnormality is the most consistent?
items.e: Alkaline phosphatase is almost always elevated and falls with healing. Calcium is low or normal, phosphate low, PTH raised and 25-hydroxyvitamin D low.

items.q: In an adult with hypophosphatasia (low serum ALP, raised pyridoxal-5-phosphate) and metatarsal stress fractures, which osteoporosis treatment is contraindicated?
o: Calcium and vitamin D at normal dietary levels
items.e: Hypophosphatasia (ALPL mutation) results in accumulation of pyrophosphate, which inhibits mineralisation; bisphosphonates are pyrophosphate analogues that worsen this and can cause atypical femoral fractures. Asfotase alfa is enzyme replacement.

items.q: Teriparatide should be avoided in which patient because of a theoretical risk of osteosarcoma?
o: A 70-year-old woman with prior vertebral fractures
A patient with Paget disease of bone or prior skeletal radiotherapy
A man with osteoporosis and low testosterone
items.e: Rat studies showed osteosarcoma with high-dose teriparatide, so it is avoided in patients at increased baseline risk: Paget disease, unexplained raised ALP, open epiphyses, prior skeletal irradiation or bone malignancy.

items.q: FRAX estimates which outcome?
o: 10-year probability of hip fracture and of a major osteoporotic fracture
items.e: FRAX combines clinical risk factors with or without femoral neck BMD to give the 10-year probability of hip fracture and of major osteoporotic fracture (hip, clinical spine, forearm, humerus), used for treatment thresholds.

items.q: In calcific tendinitis of the rotator cuff, which phase is associated with the most severe acute pain?
items.e: In Uhthoff's cycle, the resorptive phase involves vascular invasion and phagocytosis of the toothpaste-like hydroxyapatite deposit, causing intense pain; radiographs then show a fluffy, ill-defined deposit.

items.q: Which bone is most commonly involved in Paget disease?
items.e: The pelvis is the commonest site, followed by the lumbar spine, femur, skull and tibia; disease is polyostotic in most patients but rarely spreads to new bones after diagnosis.

items.q: A 20-year-old with hepatosplenomegaly has an Erlenmeyer flask deformity of the distal femora and osteonecrosis of the femoral head. Deficiency of which enzyme is responsible?
items.e: Gaucher disease results from glucocerebrosidase deficiency, with lipid-laden macrophages infiltrating marrow and causing Erlenmeyer flask deformity, bone crises and osteonecrosis; it is treated with enzyme replacement (imiglucerase).

items.q: Which integrin mediates attachment of the osteoclast to bone matrix at the sealing zone?
items.e: Integrin alpha-v-beta3 binds RGD sequences in osteopontin and bone sialoprotein to form the sealing zone, isolating the resorption lacuna into which protons and cathepsin K are secreted through the ruffled border.

items.q: In the BESTT trial, rhBMP-2 on an absorbable collagen sponge applied at definitive wound closure in open tibial fractures treated with nailing was shown to:
o: Eliminate the need for wound debridement
Reduce secondary interventions for delayed union and accelerate healing
Replace the need for intramedullary nailing
items.e: BESTT showed that rhBMP-2 (1.5 mg/mL) reduced secondary interventions and the infection rate in Gustilo III fractures and accelerated fracture and wound healing compared with standard care.

items.q: The circumferentially arranged collagen fibres of the meniscus, which convert axial load into hoop stress, are predominantly of which type?
items.e: Meniscal fibrocartilage is mainly type I collagen arranged circumferentially, with radial tie fibres; a radial tear or root avulsion disrupts the hoop fibres and functionally equals a meniscectomy.

items.q: In total hip arthroplasty, which change reduces the hip joint reaction force?
o: Lateralising the acetabular centre of rotation
Carrying a heavy bag in the hand opposite the operated hip
items.e: Increasing femoral offset lengthens the abductor lever arm, so less abductor force is needed; medialising the cup shortens the body-weight lever arm. Lateralising the cup, reducing offset or carrying a load in the contralateral hand increase the joint reaction force.

items.q: Zirconia-toughened alumina ('Delta') ceramic used for modern THA bearings has a lower fracture risk than pure alumina mainly because:
o: It is a metal alloy coated with ceramic
Zirconia particles undergo transformation toughening that resists crack propagation
It is less hard and therefore wears in
items.e: In zirconia-toughened alumina, metastable zirconia grains change from tetragonal to monoclinic phase at a crack tip, expanding and closing the crack, and platelet-like strontium aluminate deflects cracks, so head fracture is much rarer than with earlier alumina.

items.q: Polyethylene wear particles most likely to cause macrophage-mediated periprosthetic osteolysis are approximately what size?
items.e: Submicron particles (about 0.1-1 um) are phagocytosed by macrophages, which release TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6 and RANKL, activating osteoclasts and causing osteolysis and aseptic loosening.

items.q: During mechanical loading of knee articular cartilage, the fluid phase initially supports the majority of the applied load. What is the approximate percentage of load carried by fluid pressurisation?
items.e: A biphasic cartilage model shows that over 90 % of the load is transiently borne by interstitial fluid pressurisation, protecting the solid matrix from immediate damage.

items.q: Why does a slotted (open-section) intramedullary nail have much lower torsional stiffness than a closed-section nail of the same diameter and material?
o: Its open cross-section cannot resist shear around the circumference
Its lower number of locking screws
items.e: Torsional rigidity depends on the polar moment of inertia of a closed tube; a longitudinal slot creates an open section that twists easily, reducing torsional stiffness many-fold, which is why modern nails are closed-section.

items.q: A 4-year-old has night-time limb pain, a limp and low-grade fever. Radiographs show transverse lucent metaphyseal bands, and the blood count shows mild anaemia and thrombocytopenia with a normal white cell count. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Musculoskeletal pain is a presenting feature in up to a third of children with ALL; night pain, cytopenias and metaphyseal lucent ('leukaemic') lines should prompt a blood film and marrow examination before steroids are given for presumed JIA.

items.q: Osteosarcoma has a bimodal age distribution. The second peak in older adults is mostly associated with:
o: Paget disease of bone and prior irradiation
items.e: The first peak is in adolescence during the growth spurt; the second, after about 60 years, consists largely of secondary osteosarcomas arising in pagetic or irradiated bone, which have a poorer prognosis.

items.q: What is the most common histological type of radiation-associated sarcoma arising in bone?
items.e: Post-radiation sarcomas of bone arise within the field after a latency of years (Cahan criteria); osteosarcoma is the commonest type, followed by undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, and prognosis is worse than for primary tumours.

items.q: A 60‑year‑old woman with advanced breast cancer has a vertebral lesion that is purely sclerotic on X‑ray. Which cytokine is most likely responsible for the osteoblastic activity?
items.e: Endothelin‑1, secreted by breast tumour cells, stimulates osteoblasts and leads to sclerotic metastases.

items.q: A 22‑year‑old male presents with a painful, enlarging diaphyseal mass of the tibia. Plain radiographs show a permeative lytic lesion; MRI reveals marrow and soft‑tissue involvement but no skip lesions. Which imaging test is most appropriate to rule out pulmonary metastasis before considering biopsy?
items.e: Chest CT is the investigation of choice for systemic staging of bone sarcomas; it detects small pulmonary nodules that plain film would miss.

items.q: In the Cierny-Mader host classification for osteomyelitis, which factor is a LOCAL (Bl) compromise?
items.e: Local factors include chronic lymphoedema, venous stasis, major vessel disease, arteritis, extensive scarring and radiation fibrosis; diabetes, renal or hepatic failure, malnutrition, immunosuppression and extremes of age are systemic (Bs) factors.

items.q: A 60-year-old has had a discharging sinus from chronic tibial osteomyelitis for 30 years. The sinus has recently become painful, foul-smelling and bleeds easily, with an everted edge. What is the most likely malignant complication?
items.e: Long-standing sinus tracts can undergo malignant change to squamous cell carcinoma after decades; biopsy confirms it, and treatment is usually wide excision or amputation.

items.q: A Staphylococcus aureus fracture-related infection is treated with debridement while retaining a stable intramedullary nail. Which antibiotic principle is most important against the biofilm on the implant?
o: A rifampicin-containing combination started once the wound is dry and bacterial load reduced
items.e: Rifampicin is active against staphylococci in biofilm but rapidly selects resistance if used alone, so it is always combined with another active agent (e.g. a beta-lactam or fluoroquinolone) for implant-retention strategies.

items.q: A 6‑year‑old boy with rickets receives oral vitamin D and calcium supplements. After 3 months, his 25(OH)D rises to 40 ng/mL but serum phosphate remains low and his bone pain persists. Which investigation should be pursued next?
items.e: Persistently low phosphate despite adequate vitamin D suggests phosphaturic disease; measuring FGF23 distinguishes XLH, tumour‑induced osteomalacia, etc.

items.q: Which of the following statements about denosumab is correct?
o: It permanently binds to bone and can be stopped with no rebound effect
It requires renal dose adjustment if eGFR is <45 mL/min
A single annual infusion is the usual schedule
It is contraindicated in patients with hypocalcaemia
items.e: Denosumab’s effect reverses after stopping; patients need calcium and vitamin D to prevent hypocalcaemia, and the drug is given every 6 months.

items.q: When aspirating a joint for suspected septic arthritis, which handling of synovial fluid improves culture yield, especially for fastidious organisms?
o: Inoculating it directly into blood culture bottles
Sending a dry swab dipped in the fluid
items.e: Inoculating synovial fluid into aerobic and anaerobic blood culture bottles at the bedside increases the yield, particularly for Kingella kingae and other fastidious organisms; a fresh sample is also sent for Gram stain, cell count and crystals.

items.q: According to ACR 2020, how should allopurinol be started in a patient with gout and stage 3 chronic kidney disease?
o: It should be avoided in CKD
Start at 100 mg/day or less and titrate gradually to reach the serum urate target
items.e: ACR 2020 recommends starting allopurinol at 100 mg/day or less (50 mg/day or less in CKD stage 4 or worse) and titrating to a serum urate below 6 mg/dL, with 3-6 months of anti-inflammatory flare prophylaxis; it may be started during a flare.

items.q: Which imaging modality is recommended for mapping the extent of polyostotic Paget disease at diagnosis?
o: Plain radiographs of all affected bones
items.e: A whole‑body bone scan with 99mTc‑MDP shows intense uptake in all affected bones and is the gold standard for extent mapping.

items.q: After a traumatic posterior dislocation of the hip in a young adult, which factor most increases the risk of osteonecrosis of the femoral head?
o: Use of skeletal traction after reduction
items.e: The risk of osteonecrosis rises markedly when reduction is delayed beyond about 6 hours because of prolonged kinking and tearing of the retinacular vessels, so dislocation is reduced as an emergency.

items.q: In mature cortical bone, type I collagen constitutes approximately what proportion of the organic matrix?
items.e: Type I collagen accounts for ~90 % of the organic (osteoid) matrix.

items.q: The degradation products of collagen cross‑links pyridinoline and deoxypyridinoline are best used as markers of which bone process?
items.e: They are released during collagen breakdown, reflecting bone resorption.

items.q: In normal adult bone, the mineralisation lag time between deposition of osteoid and its mineralisation is approximately:
items.e: Osteoid normally begins to mineralise after a lag of roughly 10-15 days; in osteomalacia the lag is greatly prolonged (often over 100 days) with widened osteoid seams on tetracycline-labelled biopsy.

items.q: Loss-of-function mutations in LRP5, a Wnt co-receptor, cause which condition?
items.e: Loss of LRP5 function causes osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome (severe juvenile osteoporosis and blindness), whereas gain-of-function LRP5 mutations cause high bone mass; sclerosteosis results from SOST (sclerostin) loss.

items.q: Which cells are the principal source of RANKL driving osteoclastogenesis in normal bone remodelling?
items.e: RANKL is expressed by osteoblast-lineage cells, and osteocytes embedded in bone are now considered its main source in remodelling; it binds RANK on osteoclast precursors, opposed by the decoy receptor osteoprotegerin.

items.q: Which histological feature is characteristic of established osteoarthritic articular cartilage?
o: Chondrocyte clusters (cloning) with surface fibrillation and tidemark duplication
Inflammatory pannus eroding the cartilage margins
Diffuse neutrophil infiltration of the cartilage
Crystal deposits within the superficial zone
items.e: OA cartilage shows fibrillation and fissuring, proteoglycan loss, chondrocyte proliferation into clusters, and advancement or duplication of the tidemark; pannus is typical of rheumatoid arthritis.

items.q: In the posterior (Southern/Moore) approach to the hip, gluteus maximus is split in line with its fibres. Which nerve supplies the muscle being split?
items.e: Gluteus maximus is supplied by the inferior gluteal nerve; splitting it means the posterior approach has no true internervous plane. The superior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus medius, minimus and TFL.

items.q: During the posterior approach, the short external rotators are detached close to the femur and reflected posteriorly. Apart from exposing the capsule, this manoeuvre mainly serves to:
o: Protect the sciatic nerve by placing the muscle bellies between it and the operative field
Allow ligation of the ascending branch of the lateral femoral circumflex artery
Avoid injury to the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve
items.e: The reflected piriformis, gemelli and obturator internus act as a cushion over the sciatic nerve. The LFCA ascending branch and LFCN are concerns of the anterior approach.

items.q: In the direct lateral (Hardinge) approach, the superior gluteal nerve runs in which plane, where it is endangered by a proximal split?
o: Between gluteus maximus and gluteus medius
Between gluteus minimus and the hip capsule
Between gluteus medius and gluteus minimus
Within the substance of tensor fasciae latae only
items.e: The superior gluteal nerve and vessels course anteriorly between gluteus medius and minimus about 3-5 cm above the trochanter tip, so extending the medius split proximally endangers them.

items.q: In the Hardinge direct lateral approach, the anterior part of gluteus medius is elevated in continuity with which structure, using the tendinous attachment over the greater trochanter?
items.e: Hardinge elevated the anterior gluteus medius and anterior vastus lateralis as one sleeve (they are in continuity through the trochanteric periosteum/tendon), then repaired it back.

items.q: To reduce the risk of injury to the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve in a direct anterior THA, the fascia is usually entered:
o: Directly over the sartorius muscle belly
Over the tensor fasciae latae, lateral to the sartorius
Medial to the sartorius, over the femoral neurovascular bundle
Through the inguinal ligament at the ASIS
items.e: Opening the TFL sheath laterally and working medially beneath it keeps dissection away from the LFCN, which usually lies over or medial to sartorius near the ASIS.

items.q: A 70-year-old has a direct anterior THA. During femoral preparation, when the femur is extended, externally rotated and elevated, which intraoperative complication is characteristically more frequent with this approach?
items.e: Difficult femoral elevation and broaching through the anterior approach increases intraoperative femoral fractures (trochanteric and calcar), particularly during the learning curve.

items.q: After an anterolateral THA, a patient cannot lift the straight leg, has a weak knee extension and numbness of the anteromedial thigh. The most likely cause is:
o: Superior gluteal nerve injury from a proximal gluteus medius split
Sciatic nerve stretch from limb lengthening
Obturator nerve injury from a long acetabular screw
Femoral nerve injury from an anterior acetabular retractor placed too medially
items.e: A retractor levered over the anterior rim too medially compresses the femoral nerve (quadriceps weakness, anteromedial thigh numbness). Obturator injury causes adductor weakness and medial thigh sensory change.

items.q: Two days after THA, a patient on low-molecular-weight heparin develops severe increasing buttock pain, a tense swelling and a new, progressive foot drop. The best management is:
o: Urgent surgical evacuation of the haematoma to decompress the sciatic nerve
Observation and an ankle-foot orthosis, as most recover
Nerve conduction studies at 3 weeks before deciding
Shortening the femoral neck at revision
items.e: A progressive palsy with an expanding haematoma is a compressive emergency; early decompression improves the chance of recovery, unlike a static intraoperative stretch palsy.

items.q: Limb lengthening of more than about how much during THA is commonly quoted as markedly raising the risk of sciatic nerve palsy?
items.e: Sciatic (mainly peroneal) palsy is associated with lengthening beyond roughly 2.5-4 cm; lengthening under 1 cm is generally well tolerated.

items.q: Why is the peroneal division of the sciatic nerve injured more often than the tibial division during THA?
o: It lies anterior to the tibial division and against the acetabular rim
It has a separate, more fragile blood supply from the obturator artery
It is more tightly tethered (sciatic notch and fibular neck) and has larger fascicles with less protective connective tissue
It passes through the piriformis muscle in all patients
items.e: The lateral (peroneal) division is fixed at two points and has fewer, larger fascicles with less epineurial padding, so it tolerates stretch and pressure less well.

items.q: A screw placed in the anteroinferior quadrant of the acetabulum (Wasielewski) is most likely to injure the:
items.e: The obturator neurovascular bundle lies on the quadrilateral plate in the anteroinferior quadrant; the external iliac vessels are related to the anterosuperior quadrant.

items.q: In the Wasielewski acetabular quadrant system, the first reference line is drawn from the:
o: Pubic symphysis through the ischial tuberosity
Anterior superior iliac spine through the centre of the acetabulum
Teardrop to the tip of the greater trochanter
Posterior inferior iliac spine through the obturator foramen
items.e: A line from the ASIS through the acetabular centre and a perpendicular line through the centre divide the acetabulum into four quadrants; posterosuperior is the safest for screws.

items.q: A long screw in the posteroinferior acetabular quadrant can injure the:
o: Sciatic nerve and the inferior gluteal and internal pudendal vessels
items.e: The posteroinferior quadrant is 'relatively safe' but long screws can exit through the ischium near the sciatic nerve and inferior gluteal/internal pudendal vessels.

items.q: After THA, a patient has recurrent posterior dislocations when rising from a low chair. CT shows the acetabular component in 5 degrees of retroversion. The best management is:
o: A hip abduction brace for 3 months
Isolated exchange to a larger femoral head
Revision of the acetabular component to correct its version
items.e: Recurrent instability from a malpositioned component is corrected by revising that component; braces or bigger heads alone do not fix a retroverted cup.

items.q: An anterior dislocation after THA typically occurs with the hip in:
items.e: Anterior dislocation follows extension and external rotation (often with excessive anteversion); posterior dislocation follows flexion, adduction and internal rotation.

items.q: Excessive anteversion of the acetabular component predisposes mainly to which complication?
items.e: Too much cup anteversion leaves the head uncovered anteriorly in extension-external rotation; retroversion predisposes to posterior dislocation.

items.q: Using a long 'skirted' femoral head (with a collar extending over the taper) increases the risk of dislocation after THA mainly because it:
o: Reduces the head-neck ratio and so the range of motion before impingement
items.e: The skirt thickens the neck, lowering the head-neck ratio so the neck impinges on the cup earlier and levers the head out.

items.q: Larger femoral heads reduce dislocation after THA mainly by:
o: Lowering frictional torque at the bearing
Increasing the jump distance and the impingement-free range of motion
items.e: Jump distance (how far the head must translate to dislocate) and head-neck ratio both rise with head size, improving stability.

items.q: Four weeks after a posterior-approach THA, a patient sustains a first dislocation while bending to tie shoelaces. Radiographs show well-positioned components. The best management is:
o: Closed reduction followed by precautions or a brace
Immediate revision to a constrained liner
items.e: Most early first-time dislocations with well-positioned components are treated by closed reduction; about two-thirds do not recur.

items.q: Ten years after a conventional polyethylene THA, a patient has his first dislocation. Components were well positioned at surgery. Which mechanism most commonly underlies such late dislocation?
o: Polyethylene wear with soft-tissue (pseudocapsule and abductor) laxity
Cup retroversion due to positioning error
items.e: Late dislocation is usually due to liner wear allowing eccentric head position and progressive soft-tissue laxity; revision often includes liner exchange and stability measures.

items.q: Compared with THA for osteoarthritis, THA for a displaced femoral neck fracture carries a higher risk of:
items.e: Patients with fracture have normal, compliant soft tissues and often cognitive impairment, so dislocation rates are higher than after THA for arthritis.

items.q: After Charnley's transtrochanteric approach, which complication is characteristic of the osteotomy itself?
o: Trochanteric non-union or migration with abductor weakness
items.e: Trochanteric osteotomy gives wide exposure but risks non-union, proximal escape, wire breakage and bursitis, leading to limp and instability.

items.q: A Vancouver type A_G periprosthetic fracture of the greater trochanter that is minimally displaced and stable is usually managed by:
o: Non-operative treatment with protected weight-bearing and avoidance of active abduction
Plate fixation spanning the whole femur
items.e: Undisplaced greater trochanter fractures with a well-fixed stem are treated non-operatively; displaced fragments (about 2.5 cm or more) affecting abductor function may need fixation.

items.q: An 86-year-old with poor bone stock has a periprosthetic femoral fracture around a loose stem with severe proximal comminution (Vancouver B3). The usual treatment is:
o: Locking plate and cables leaving the stem
Revision to a proximal femoral replacement (megaprosthesis)
items.e: B3 means a loose stem with poor proximal bone stock; in elderly patients a proximal femoral replacement allows early mobilisation, while young patients may need an allograft-prosthesis composite.

items.q: When revising a loose stem for a Vancouver B2 fracture, the new long stem should bypass the most distal fracture line by at least:
o: The full length of the femur
items.e: Bypassing the fracture by about two cortical diameters (or more) reduces the stress riser and secures distal fixation in intact diaphysis.

items.q: A periprosthetic femoral fracture was classified as Vancouver B1 on radiographs. At surgery the stem is found to be loose. The correct management is:
o: Proceed with plate and cable fixation as planned
Remove the stem and leave a Girdlestone
Treat as B2: revise to a long stem that bypasses the fracture
items.e: Many apparent B1 fractures are actually loose; stem stability must be tested intraoperatively and a loose stem requires revision, since ORIF around it fails.

items.q: In the Unified Classification System for periprosthetic fractures, a femoral fracture lying between an ipsilateral THA stem and a TKA femoral component is type:
items.e: UCS type D = dividing (between) two implants in the same bone; B is around the implant bed and C is clear of the implant.

items.q: In patients over about 75 years, registry data comparing cemented and uncemented femoral stems in THA show uncemented stems have a higher:
o: Rate of aseptic loosening at 20 years
Rate of early periprosthetic femoral fracture and revision
Rate of bone cement implantation syndrome
items.e: Press-fit stems in osteoporotic bone cause more intraoperative and early postoperative periprosthetic fractures, so cemented stems are favoured in the elderly.

items.q: On radiographs after THA, heterotopic ossification shows bone spurs arising from the pelvis or proximal femur with a gap of more than 1 cm between opposing surfaces. This is Brooker grade:
items.e: Brooker I is islands of bone; II spurs with over 1 cm between them; III spurs with under 1 cm gap; IV apparent ankylosis.

items.q: Which patient is at the highest risk of clinically significant heterotopic ossification after THA?
o: A 55-year-old woman with osteonecrosis on bisphosphonates
A 60-year-old man who developed Brooker IV ossification after his contralateral THA
items.e: Previous HO is the strongest risk factor; others are male sex, ankylosing spondylitis, DISH and hypertrophic OA. Rheumatoid arthritis is not a classic risk factor.

items.q: The usual pharmacological prophylaxis against heterotopic ossification after THA in a high-risk patient is:
items.e: Indomethacin (an NSAID) inhibits mesenchymal differentiation into osteoblasts. Etidronate only delays mineralisation and ossification rebounds when it is stopped.

items.q: A patient has painful Brooker IV heterotopic ossification after THA. Excision is best timed when:
o: Within 2 weeks of diagnosis, before it matures
The ossification is mature: normal alkaline phosphatase and a quiescent bone scan, usually 6-12 months after surgery
As soon as serum alkaline phosphatase peaks
items.e: Excising immature HO leads to recurrence; wait until it matures, then excise with prophylaxis (indomethacin or radiotherapy).

items.q: After elective THA, extended pharmacological VTE prophylaxis is generally recommended for about:
items.e: Guidelines (for example NICE) advise extended prophylaxis for about 28-35 days after THA (versus about 10-14 days after TKA), with mechanical methods and early mobilisation.

items.q: In the Donaldson grading of bone cement implantation syndrome, grade 3 is defined by:
o: Fall in systolic pressure of more than 20%
Transient rash at the cementing site
