items.e: Chrisman-Snook uses half the peroneus brevis through the fibula to the calcaneus; Evans tenodeses the whole tendon to the fibula alone.

items.q: The first syndesmotic ligament to fail in an external-rotation high ankle sprain is the:
items.e: External rotation of the talus first tears the AITFL, then the interosseous membrane/ligament and finally the posterior structures.

items.q: Compared with a lateral ankle sprain of similar severity, a stable syndesmotic (high ankle) sprain usually:
o: Heals faster because the ligaments are extracapsular
Takes about twice as long to return to sport
items.e: High ankle sprains have prolonged recovery, roughly double that of lateral sprains.

items.q: Compressing the fibula against the tibia at mid-calf reproduces pain at the distal tibiofibular joint. This test is the:
items.e: The squeeze test indicates syndesmotic injury; Kleiger is the external rotation test and Thompson tests the Achilles tendon.

items.q: At ankle arthroscopy, syndesmotic instability is confirmed when probing shows tibiofibular diastasis of more than about:
items.e: Arthroscopy is the gold standard; diastasis over 2 mm on probing indicates instability.

items.q: A transsyndesmotic screw is ideally inserted:
o: Straight in the coronal plane of the leg, perpendicular to the fibula's lateral surface
From posterolateral fibula to anteromedial tibia, angled 20-30° anteriorly, parallel to the plafond about 2-5 cm above it
Obliquely upward from the fibular tip through the plafond
items.e: The fibula lies posterior to the tibia in the incisura, so the screw is aimed 20-30° anteriorly from posterolateral.

items.q: Compared with a syndesmotic screw, a suture-button device for an unstable syndesmosis is associated with:
o: Lower rates of malreduction and of implant removal
A routine need for removal at 12 weeks
items.e: Dynamic suture-button fixation allows the fibula to settle in the incisura, with fewer malreductions and removals.

items.q: After fixation of a syndesmotic injury, the factor most strongly linked to a poor functional outcome is:
o: Malreduction of the fibula in the tibial incisura
Use of a 3.5 mm rather than a 4.5 mm screw
Engaging three rather than four cortices
Removal of the screw at 12 weeks
items.e: Anatomic reduction of the fibula is the key; direct visualisation or CT is recommended because malreduction is common.

items.q: The superficial deltoid ligament (tibionavicular, tibiospring and tibiocalcaneal bands) chiefly resists:
items.e: The superficial deltoid resists hindfoot eversion; the deep deltoid is the primary restraint to lateral talar shift and external rotation.

items.q: On a gravity stress radiograph after a Weber B fibular fracture, deep deltoid insufficiency is suggested when the medial clear space:
o: Is more than 1 mm wider than the superior clear space (or over 4-5 mm)
Narrows by 1 mm compared with the unstressed view
items.e: Widening of the medial clear space beyond the superior clear space (or above 4-5 mm) indicates deep deltoid incompetence.

items.q: A 60-year-old with long-standing flatfoot has valgus tilt of the talus within the ankle mortise due to deltoid insufficiency. In the Myerson modification of the Johnson-Strom classification this is stage:
items.e: Stage IV adds deltoid failure and valgus talar tilt to the hindfoot deformity of earlier stages.

items.q: Stress radiographs used to evaluate subtalar instability, which often coexists with lateral ankle instability, are:
items.e: Brodén views show the posterior facet of the subtalar joint; Canale views are for the talar neck and Saltzman for hindfoot alignment.

items.q: The average thickness of tibiotalar articular cartilage is about:
items.e: Ankle cartilage is thin (about 1-1.7 mm) but stiffer and richer in proteoglycan than knee cartilage, making it resistant to primary OA.

items.q: SF-36 studies of patients awaiting surgery show that end-stage ankle arthritis causes disability comparable to:
items.e: Glazebrook and colleagues showed mental and physical impairment similar to end-stage hip arthritis and heart failure.

items.q: Which radiograph measures calcaneal alignment relative to the tibial axis when planning surgery for ankle arthritis?
items.e: The Saltzman view (beam angled 20° caudally, posteroanterior) shows the calcaneal position relative to the tibial shaft.

items.q: In the Takakura classification of varus ankle osteoarthritis, stage 3B means:
o: Joint-space obliteration extending from the medial gutter to the roof of the talar dome
Obliteration of the medial gutter only
Joint-space obliteration across the whole joint
Subchondral sclerosis and osteophytes without narrowing
items.e: 3A is medial gutter obliteration; 3B extends to the talar dome roof; 4 involves the whole joint.

items.q: Which shoe modification reduces pain in ankle arthritis by substituting for lost sagittal motion?
o: Rocker-bottom sole with a solid-ankle cushioned heel (SACH)
items.e: A rocker sole with a SACH heel allows roll-over and cushions heel strike without needing ankle motion.

items.q: When performing a medial opening-wedge supramalleolar osteotomy for varus ankle osteoarthritis, the aim is to:
o: Slightly overcorrect into about 2-4° of valgus
Correct exactly to the native varus angle
items.e: Slight overcorrection shifts load onto the preserved lateral joint, as in high tibial osteotomy.

items.q: For asymmetric valgus ankle osteoarthritis with a preserved medial joint, the supramalleolar osteotomy of choice is:
items.e: Valgus OA needs varus correction, achieved by a medial closing (or lateral opening) wedge; medial opening and lateral closing wedges correct varus.

items.q: Which is a contraindication to supramalleolar osteotomy for ankle arthritis?
o: Post-traumatic varus OA with a preserved lateral joint
items.e: SMOT relies on healthy cartilage elsewhere in the joint; inflammatory arthritis, neuropathy and end-stage panarthritis are contraindications.

items.q: Ankle joint distraction arthroplasty for a young patient with post-traumatic arthritis involves:
o: A unilateral fixator distracting 1 cm for 2 weeks
A hinged fixator distracting 2 mm for 12 months
A bulk fresh osteochondral allograft of tibia and talus
A circular frame distracting the joint about 5 mm for about 3 months
items.e: Distraction of about 5 mm for roughly 3 months unloads the cartilage and allows some repair; results are variable.

items.q: Compared with open ankle arthrodesis, arthroscopic arthrodesis in a mildly deformed ankle has been associated with:
o: Faster union, less blood loss and fewer complications
items.e: Arthroscopic arthrodesis unites faster (about 8-12 weeks) with less morbidity, but is limited to deformity under about 10-15°.

items.q: In screw fixation for ankle arthrodesis, the 'home-run' screw passes:
o: From the lateral talar body into the tibia
From the posterior malleolus obliquely into the talar neck and head
Across the subtalar joint into the calcaneus
From the medial malleolus into the fibula
items.e: The home-run screw runs from the posterior tibia into the talar neck and head, compressing and resisting dorsiflexion.

items.q: The strongest modifiable risk factor for non-union after ankle arthrodesis is:
o: Use of three rather than two screws
items.e: Smoking markedly increases non-union; other risks are diabetes, talar AVN, infection and open approaches.

items.q: An ankle arthrodesis fused in excessive plantarflexion typically produces:
items.e: Equinus forces the knee into hyperextension during stance; varus malposition causes lateral foot overload.

items.q: A tibiotalar arthrodesis fused in hindfoot varus most often leads to:
items.e: Varus locks the transverse tarsal joint and overloads the lateral column; about 5° of hindfoot valgus is the target.

items.q: Which total ankle replacement is a three-component mobile-bearing design?
items.e: HINTEGRA (like European STAR) has a mobile polyethylene bearing; INBONE, Infinity and Salto Talaris are fixed-bearing.

items.q: The UK TARVA randomised trial (2022) comparing total ankle replacement with ankle arthrodesis found:
o: No significant difference in the primary patient-reported outcome at 12 months
Clear superiority of replacement for all outcomes
Clear superiority of arthrodesis with fewer reoperations
Early termination because of replacement failures
items.e: TARVA showed similar MOXFQ walking/standing scores at 12 months; some secondary outcomes favoured TAR.

items.q: The commonest intraoperative fracture during total ankle replacement involves the:
items.e: The thin medial malleolus can fracture during tibial cuts or trial insertion; it is often prophylactically pinned.

items.q: In total ankle replacement, aseptic loosening and subsidence most commonly affect the:
items.e: The talar component, with its small bony footprint and vulnerable blood supply, is the commoner site of subsidence.

items.q: A failed total ankle replacement with massive talar bone loss is salvaged with:
o: Tibiotalocalcaneal nail arthrodesis with bulk femoral head allograft
Revision of the polyethylene liner only
items.e: Salvage arthrodesis bridges the void with structural allograft; union rates are lower (about 80%) than in primary fusion.

items.q: During total ankle replacement in a varus ankle, a tight medial side preventing balance of the components is addressed by:
items.e: In varus ankles the medial structures are contracted, so deltoid release (with lateral ligament reconstruction if lax) balances the joint.

items.q: A 64-year-old has end-stage ankle osteoarthritis and an existing ipsilateral subtalar and talonavicular arthrodesis. Which treatment best protects the remaining joints?
items.e: Fusing the ankle next to a triple fusion creates a rigid foot that overloads the midfoot and knee; TAR preserves motion.

items.q: Arthroscopic debridement and bone marrow stimulation for an osteochondral lesion of the talus gives the best results when the lesion is smaller than about:
items.e: Larger or cystic lesions do worse with microfracture and are considered for osteochondral grafting or ACI/MACI.

items.q: Perpendicular access for osteochondral autograft transfer to a posteromedial talar dome lesion usually requires:
items.e: A medial malleolar osteotomy exposes posteromedial lesions; its risks include malunion and non-union.

items.q: Which classification of osteochondral lesions of the talus is based on CT?
items.e: Ferkel is CT-based, Hepple MRI-based and Berndt-Harty radiographic; Outerbridge grades cartilage at arthroscopy.

items.q: Osteoarticular tuberculosis accounts for approximately what proportion of all cases of tuberculosis?
items.e: Bone and joint TB forms about 1-3% of all TB and about 10-15% of extrapulmonary TB; the spine accounts for about half of osteoarticular cases.

items.q: Excluding the spine, the most commonly affected joint in osteoarticular tuberculosis is the:
items.e: The order of frequency is spine (about 50%), then hip, then knee; shoulder involvement is uncommon.

items.q: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is slow-growing, with a doubling time of approximately:
items.e: M. tuberculosis divides about every 15-20 hours, which explains the weeks needed for culture; most pyogenic bacteria double in under an hour.

items.q: Osteoarticular tuberculosis due to Mycobacterium bovis is classically acquired by:
o: Inhalation of droplets from an infected household contact
items.e: M. bovis is transmitted mainly through unpasteurised cow's milk; aquarium exposure causes M. marinum, and post-surgical outbreaks are due to rapidly growing mycobacteria.

items.q: In a patient with tuberculosis of the knee, which statement about the pulmonary focus is correct?
o: Active pulmonary disease is present in nearly all patients
Active pulmonary disease is present in less than half of patients
Skeletal TB always follows direct spread from the lung
A normal chest radiograph excludes osteoarticular TB
items.e: Skeletal TB is always secondary to haematogenous spread from a primary focus that may be quiescent; active lung disease is found in under half, so a normal chest film does not exclude it.

items.q: The tissue reaction to Mycobacterium tuberculosis that produces caseating granulomas is which type of hypersensitivity?
items.e: Tuberculous granulomas with epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells and caseous necrosis result from a cell-mediated type IV hypersensitivity response.

items.q: A synovial biopsy of a chronically swollen knee shows epithelioid cell granulomas with central caseous necrosis and multinucleate giant cells with nuclei arranged in a horseshoe at the periphery. These giant cells are:
items.e: Langhans giant cells with peripheral horseshoe nuclei are characteristic of tuberculous granulomas; Touton cells are seen in xanthomatous lesions.

items.q: In synovial tuberculosis, the pannus first erodes which part of the articular surface?
o: The subchondral bone beneath the centre of the joint
The peripheral bare areas at the joint margins
items.e: Tuberculous granulation tissue spreads from the synovium over the cartilage margins and erodes the non-weight-bearing peripheral bare areas first, producing marginal erosions.

items.q: The strongest single risk factor for developing osteoarticular tuberculosis is:
items.e: HIV is the strongest risk factor; diabetes, alcohol, malnutrition, CKD and immunosuppression including anti-TNF therapy also increase risk.

items.q: Before starting infliximab for rheumatoid arthritis in a patient from an endemic area, screening for latent tuberculosis is mandatory because anti-TNF therapy:
o: Impairs granuloma maintenance and can reactivate latent TB
Interferes with the absorption of isoniazid
items.e: TNF-alpha is essential for forming and maintaining granulomas, so its blockade allows latent infection to reactivate; screening with IGRA or Mantoux and chest radiograph precedes biologics.

items.q: 'Night cries' in a child with tuberculosis of the hip are explained by:
o: Evening rise of temperature causing rigors
Raised intraosseous pressure from venous congestion at night
Relaxation of protective muscle spasm during sleep, allowing painful movement of the inflamed joint
items.e: Protective spasm splints the joint while awake; during sleep it relaxes, movement of the diseased joint causes pain and the child wakes crying.

items.q: In an immunocompetent adult, the Mantoux test (5 TU PPD) is read as positive when the induration measured at 48-72 hours is at least:
items.e: Induration of 10 mm or more at 48-72 hours is positive in the general population; a 5 mm cut-off is used in HIV and other immunosuppressed patients.

items.q: The advantage of an interferon-gamma release assay (QuantiFERON) over the tuberculin skin test is that it:
o: Is not affected by prior BCG vaccination
items.e: IGRAs use antigens (ESAT-6, CFP-10) absent from BCG and most environmental mycobacteria, so BCG does not cause false positives; like the Mantoux test they indicate infection, not active disease.

items.q: Culture of Mycobacterium tuberculosis on solid Lowenstein-Jensen medium typically takes about:
items.e: Growth on LJ medium takes about 4-8 weeks; liquid MGIT culture is faster at about 1-3 weeks. Culture is still needed for full drug susceptibility testing.

items.q: The gold standard for diagnosing tuberculous arthritis of the knee is:
o: Raised ESR with juxta-articular osteopenia on radiographs
Synovial biopsy with histology and microbiology (CBNAAT and culture) of the tissue
items.e: Tissue obtained by synovial or bone biopsy for histology plus CBNAAT and culture is the gold standard; smears are often negative because the disease is paucibacillary.

items.q: First-line line probe assay (LPA) on a tuberculous tissue isolate is used mainly to detect resistance to:
items.e: First-line LPA detects isoniazid (katG, inhA) and rifampicin (rpoB) resistance; second-line LPA detects fluoroquinolone and injectable resistance.

items.q: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) is defined as resistance to at least:
items.e: MDR-TB is resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampicin; rifampicin resistance on CBNAAT is used as a surrogate marker for MDR-TB.

items.q: According to the 2021 WHO definitions, MDR/rifampicin-resistant TB with additional resistance to any fluoroquinolone, but not to bedaquiline or linezolid, is termed:
items.e: Pre-XDR is MDR/RR-TB plus fluoroquinolone resistance; XDR additionally requires resistance to bedaquiline and/or linezolid.

items.q: The 6-month all-oral BPaLM regimen recommended by WHO (2022) for MDR/RR-TB consists of bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid and:
items.e: BPaLM = bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid and moxifloxacin; it replaced long injectable-containing regimens for many patients.

items.q: The imaging investigation of choice for early diagnosis and defining the extent of tuberculous arthritis is:
items.e: MRI shows synovial thickening, marrow oedema, early erosions and abscesses long before radiographic change; radiographs change late.

items.q: On contrast-enhanced MRI, a tuberculous cold abscess characteristically shows:
o: A thick, irregular nodular enhancing wall
Diffuse solid enhancement without a fluid centre
items.e: Tuberculous abscesses typically have thin smooth enhancing walls, whereas pyogenic abscesses tend to have thick irregular walls.

items.q: A 25-year-old has a chronically swollen knee with recurrent brown haemorrhagic effusions, preserved joint space, and low-signal synovium that 'blooms' on gradient-echo MRI. Compared with tuberculosis, this picture favours:
items.e: Haemorrhagic fluid and haemosiderin blooming on gradient echo are characteristic of PVNS; tuberculous synovial fluid is turbid with lymphocyte predominance.

items.q: The recommended daily dose of rifampicin in adult antitubercular therapy is approximately:
items.e: Rifampicin is given at about 10 mg/kg (8-12); isoniazid 5 mg/kg, pyrazinamide 25 mg/kg and ethambutol 15 mg/kg.

items.q: A patient on a streptomycin-containing regimen for osteoarticular TB develops giddiness and unsteadiness in the dark. The toxicity is:
items.e: Streptomycin causes vestibular (more than cochlear) ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity; optic neuritis is due to ethambutol and neuropathy to isoniazid.

items.q: Which first-line antitubercular drug is chiefly responsible for the 'sterilising' activity against semi-dormant bacilli that allows shorter regimens?
items.e: Rifampicin (with pyrazinamide for intracellular acid-pH organisms) kills semi-dormant bacilli and is the key sterilising drug; ethambutol is bacteriostatic and mainly prevents resistance.

items.q: Pyrazinamide is especially active against tubercle bacilli that are:
items.e: Pyrazinamide works in acid pH and targets intracellular bacilli within macrophages, contributing sterilising activity in the intensive phase.

items.q: The main role of ethambutol in first-line antitubercular therapy is:
o: Rapid bactericidal action on multiplying bacilli
Bacteriostatic cover to prevent emergence of resistance
items.e: Ethambutol is bacteriostatic and is included mainly to protect the other drugs against the emergence of resistance; isoniazid is the main early bactericidal drug.

items.q: A patient on antitubercular therapy develops a malar rash, arthralgia and positive antinuclear antibodies. The drug most likely responsible is:
items.e: Isoniazid can cause a drug-induced lupus-like syndrome, in addition to hepatitis and pyridoxine-preventable peripheral neuropathy.

items.q: A patient on ATT for knee tuberculosis notices orange-red discolouration of urine and tears. The responsible drug is:
items.e: Rifampicin colours body fluids orange-red (and can stain contact lenses); this is harmless but patients should be warned.

items.q: In a patient on first-line ATT, hepatotoxic drugs should be stopped when serum transaminases rise to more than:
o: 1.5 times normal in an asymptomatic patient
5 times the upper limit of normal, or 3 times with symptoms or jaundice
items.e: Drug-induced hepatitis warrants stopping hepatotoxic drugs when transaminases exceed 5 times normal, or 3 times with symptoms, or when bilirubin rises; mild rises are monitored.

items.q: After drug-induced hepatitis on ATT has resolved, first-line drugs are usually reintroduced:
o: Sequentially, starting with rifampicin, then isoniazid, with pyrazinamide often omitted
Starting with pyrazinamide as it is least hepatotoxic
Only after a mandatory 6-month drug-free interval
items.e: Drugs are reintroduced one at a time (rifampicin, then isoniazid) while monitoring liver function; pyrazinamide, the most hepatotoxic, is often left out and the regimen prolonged.

items.q: A patient with newly diagnosed tuberculosis of the hip is found to be HIV positive (not TB meningitis). Antiretroviral therapy should be started:
o: Before ATT, at least 3 months earlier
Within about 2 weeks of starting ATT
items.e: ATT is started first and ART within about 2 weeks (delayed in TB meningitis); clinicians must watch for IRIS and rifampicin interactions with protease inhibitors.

items.q: Which MRI finding indicates healing of osteoarticular tuberculosis during ATT?
o: Replacement of marrow oedema by fatty marrow signal
New marrow oedema in the adjacent bone
items.e: MRI healing signs include fatty marrow replacement, resolution of oedema and abscesses, and reduced enhancement; an enlarging abscess suggests a paradoxical reaction or failure.

items.q: Drug-resistant tuberculosis should be suspected in a compliant patient with osteoarticular TB who shows poor clinical response after about:
items.e: Failure to improve after about 3-5 months of compliant ATT should prompt repeat tissue sampling for culture and drug susceptibility testing.

items.q: Traditionally, total joint arthroplasty in a joint previously affected by tuberculosis was deferred until the disease had been quiescent for about:
items.e: The traditional rule was about 10 years of quiescence; current evidence supports arthroplasty earlier, even in active disease, with radical debridement and perioperative ATT cover.

items.q: Babcock's triangle, a site where tuberculous foci arise in the hip, is located in the:
items.e: Babcock's triangle is a relatively radiolucent region of the femoral neck metaphysis, one of the initial foci of hip TB along with the acetabular roof, epiphysis and synovium.

items.q: A 14-year-old with hip tuberculosis has a hip held in flexion, adduction and internal rotation with apparent shortening; radiographs show marginal erosions and reduced joint space without major destruction. The Tuli stage is:
items.e: Stage II early arthritis gives flexion-adduction-internal rotation with apparent shortening and marginal erosions; stage I is flexion-abduction-external rotation with apparent lengthening, and true shortening appears in stage III.

items.q: A 30-year-old with stage IV tuberculosis of the hip has a wandering acetabulum with pathological dislocation and a painful, unstable joint. Appropriate surgical options are:
o: Girdlestone excision arthroplasty or arthrodesis (or later THA when healed)
items.e: Stage IV disease with subluxation or dislocation is managed by excision arthroplasty or arthrodesis, with total hip arthroplasty possible in healed disease; synovectomy is for early disease.

items.q: The recommended position for knee arthrodesis after tuberculous destruction is approximately:
o: 0-15 degrees flexion, 5-8 degrees valgus and about 10 degrees external rotation
items.e: The knee is fused in slight flexion (0-15 degrees), 5-8 degrees valgus and slight external rotation for a functional gait.

items.q: Which technique of knee arthrodesis, using transfixing pins with external compression clamps, is classically used for a destroyed tuberculous knee?
o: Intramedullary nail arthrodesis with bone allograft
Plate arthrodesis with a dynamic hip screw
items.e: Charnley compression arthrodesis with transfixing Steinmann pins and compression clamps is the classic technique for TB knees in young labourers; it avoids permanent implants in an infected field.

items.q: In tuberculous dactylitis (spina ventosa), the bones most commonly affected are:
o: Proximal phalanges and metacarpals of the hand
items.e: Spina ventosa affects children under about 6 years and involves the short tubular bones of the hand (proximal phalanges, metacarpals) more than those of the foot.

items.q: In tuberculosis of the foot and ankle, the most commonly involved bones are the:
items.e: The calcaneus and talus are the commonest foot bones affected; sinuses are common and the lesions may mimic chronic pyogenic osteomyelitis or tumour.

items.q: A 22-year-old has unilateral buttock pain with a positive FABER test on one side. Imaging shows erosions and widening of one sacroiliac joint with an iliac fossa collection. The most likely diagnosis in an endemic area is:
items.e: Unilateral SI involvement with erosions, widening and a cold abscess in the buttock or iliac fossa suggests TB; ankylosing spondylitis is bilateral and symmetrical.

items.q: An outbreak of chronic discharging wound infections after laparoscopic or cosmetic procedures, not responding to standard antitubercular drugs, is typically due to:
o: Rapidly growing mycobacteria such as M. fortuitum, M. chelonae or M. abscessus
items.e: Rapidly growing non-tuberculous mycobacteria cause post-surgical and post-injection outbreaks; they are resistant to standard ATT and are treated with macrolides, amikacin and debridement.

items.q: A child has multiple well-defined lytic cyst-like lesions in several bones without surrounding sclerosis; biopsy shows caseating granulomas. This form of skeletal tuberculosis is called:
items.e: Cystic TB of bone produces multiple well-defined lytic lesions without sclerosis in children; differentials include Langerhans cell histiocytosis, sarcoid and fungal infection.

items.q: Under Tuli's 'middle path' for tuberculous arthritis of a joint, operative debridement or synovectomy is indicated when:
o: The diagnosis is confirmed by CBNAAT
There is no response after about 3-6 months of ATT and conservative care
The ESR is above 30 mm/h at presentation
items.e: The middle path uses ATT with rest, splintage and mobilisation, reserving surgery for specific indications such as diagnostic doubt, large abscesses or failure to respond after about 3-6 months.

items.q: A tuberculous osseous focus in the metaphysis close to the knee joint, with a sequestrum, is curetted early mainly to:
o: Provide bone graft for later arthrodesis
Remove the source of positive Mantoux reactivity
Prevent its rupture into the joint and intra-articular spread
items.e: Curettage and sequestrectomy of a juxta-articular osseous focus removes dead bone and caseous material and prevents the disease breaking into the joint.

items.q: A tuberculous knee with an open discharging sinus becomes secondarily infected with Staphylococcus aureus. If the joint heals, the expected outcome is more likely to be:
o: Fibrous ankylosis with a painful arc
items.e: Uncomplicated TB heals with fibrous ankylosis, whereas bony ankylosis is typical of pyogenic infection, including secondary infection of a tuberculous joint.

items.q: In a conventional metal-on-polyethylene total hip, the predominant wear mechanism, in which polymer transfers to the counterface and is pulled off, is:
items.e: Adhesive wear dominates the conforming hip articulation with polyethylene. Fatigue/delamination is the dominant mechanism in the low-conformity TKA, not the hip.

items.q: Years after THA, the femoral head has worn completely through the polyethylene liner and now articulates directly against the metal acetabular shell. In McKellop's classification this is wear mode:
items.e: Mode 2 is a primary bearing surface moving against a secondary surface it was never meant to touch (head on shell after liner wear-through). Mode 1 is the intended surfaces; mode 3 is third bodies trapped between primary surfaces.

items.q: Backside wear of a modular polyethylene acetabular liner rubbing against the inner surface of its metal shell is classified by McKellop as wear mode:
items.e: Mode 4 describes two secondary (non-bearing) surfaces rubbing together: liner backside against shell, neck against cup rim, or fretting at the trunnion.

items.q: Fragments of bone cement trapped between the femoral head and polyethylene liner, causing accelerated abrasive wear of the intended bearing surfaces, represent McKellop wear mode:
items.e: Mode 3 is the intended articulating surfaces separated by third-body particles (cement, bone, metal, ceramic debris).

items.q: In tribology, a lambda ratio (fluid-film thickness divided by the combined surface roughness) greater than 3 indicates:
o: Full fluid-film lubrication with the surfaces completely separated
items.e: Lambda above 3 means the fluid film is thick enough to separate the asperities completely (the ideal, seen with ceramic-on-ceramic and well-designed large MoM bearings). Lambda below 1 is boundary lubrication.

items.q: The lubrication regime that predominates in a metal-on-polyethylene hip bearing is:
items.e: In MoP bearings the surfaces remain in contact with adsorbed lubricant molecules (boundary lubrication). Full fluid-film separation is approached only by hard-on-hard bearings such as ceramic-on-ceramic.

items.q: Charnley chose a small (22.25 mm) femoral head for his low-friction arthroplasty principally to:
o: Increase range of motion before impingement
Minimise frictional torque and volumetric polyethylene wear
Minimise linear penetration of the head into the cup
items.e: A small head reduces the frictional torque at the cement-bone interface and the volumetric (swept-volume) wear. It actually increases linear penetration and reduces stability, the trade-offs of the design.

items.q: Wear particles stimulate periprosthetic macrophages and stromal cells to activate osteoclasts mainly through upregulation of:
o: RANKL (receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand)
items.e: Particle-activated macrophages release TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6 and PGE2, which upregulate RANKL on osteoblasts and stromal cells and drive osteoclastogenesis. Osteoprotegerin is the decoy receptor that inhibits RANKL.

items.q: Which pro-inflammatory cytokine released by macrophages after phagocytosis of polyethylene debris is central to periprosthetic osteolysis?
items.e: TNF-alpha (with IL-1, IL-6 and PGE2) is the key mediator of particle-induced osteoclastic bone resorption. IL-4 and IL-10 are anti-inflammatory cytokines.

items.q: Schmalzried's concept of the 'effective joint space' after arthroplasty refers to:
o: The radiographic gap between the femoral head and the liner
All periprosthetic regions that joint fluid and wear particles can reach, along the implant-bone interface
The capsular volume measured at arthrography
The space between the liner and the metal shell only
items.e: Joint fluid under pressure carries particles along any accessible implant-bone interface (screw holes, gaps), so osteolysis can appear far from the joint itself.

items.q: The most accurate imaging for estimating the size of acetabular (pelvic) osteolytic lesions around a THA is:
o: CT scan with metal artefact reduction
items.e: Plain radiographs consistently underestimate the size of pelvic osteolysis because of overlap with the shell; CT with artefact reduction defines the lesion for planning.

items.q: A 58-year-old has an asymptomatic but enlarging retroacetabular osteolytic lesion 12 years after an uncemented THA. The shell is well fixed and well positioned, the locking mechanism is intact and the liner is markedly worn. The usual treatment is:
o: Revision of both acetabular and femoral components
Exchange of the liner with debridement and bone grafting of the lesion, retaining the shell
items.e: With a well-fixed, well-positioned shell and competent locking mechanism, the wear generator (liner) is exchanged and the lesion grafted. Bisphosphonates have no proven role in established osteolysis.

items.q: The most frequent complication after isolated polyethylene liner exchange for wear and osteolysis in THA is:
items.e: Isolated liner exchange has a high dislocation rate (capsular excision, worn soft tissues); larger heads and capsular repair are used to reduce it.

items.q: A well-fixed, well-positioned acetabular shell has a damaged locking mechanism and no compatible liner is available. An accepted option is:
o: Leaving the old worn liner in place
Cementing a new polyethylene liner into the retained shell
Placing the femoral head directly into the metal shell
Impacting a ceramic liner into the damaged shell
items.e: Cementing a liner (with a roughened or scored backside and an adequate cement mantle of about 2 mm) into a well-fixed shell is a proven option. A ceramic liner needs a perfect taper seat and must never go into a damaged shell.

items.q: Highly cross-linked polyethylene for hip liners is typically produced using a total radiation dose of about:
items.e: Cross-linking doses are 5–10 Mrad, followed by thermal treatment. 2.5–4 Mrad is the conventional sterilisation dose, which produces only modest cross-linking.

items.q: Compared with conventional polyethylene, highly cross-linked polyethylene in THA reduces wear by approximately:
items.e: Clinical and RSA studies show HXLPE reduces femoral head penetration and wear by around 80–90%, with a marked fall in osteolysis and revision for wear.

items.q: A thin HXLPE liner coupled with a 40 mm head in a vertically placed cup fractures at its rim within a few years. The material property of HXLPE most responsible is:
o: Reduced fracture toughness and fatigue strength
items.e: Cross-linking (especially with remelting) lowers fatigue strength and toughness, so thin rims under edge loading or impingement can crack. Remelting removes free radicals and does not increase oxidation.

items.q: For tibial polyethylene inserts in TKA, which manufacturing method has historically shown the best resistance to fatigue wear?
o: Heat pressing of the articular surface after machining
items.e: Direct compression-moulded polyethylene has more uniform consolidation and better wear performance. Heat pressing of machined surfaces (e.g. PCA knee) produced subsurface delamination.

items.q: Hylamer, used in the 1990s for acetabular liners, is best described as:
o: A zirconia ceramic that underwent phase transformation
A titanium nitride coating for femoral heads
A modified high-crystallinity UHMWPE that showed high wear and early osteolysis
items.e: Hylamer was an extended-chain, high-crystallinity UHMWPE; when gamma-sterilised in air it oxidised and had high wear and osteolysis, and was abandoned.

items.q: Calcium stearate was eliminated from modern UHMWPE resins mainly because it was associated with:
o: Fusion defects that act as sites of fatigue crack initiation
Taper corrosion of the femoral head
items.e: Calcium stearate (a processing additive) was linked to incomplete consolidation (fusion defects) and oxidation, initiating cracks and delamination.

items.q: Backside wear of a modular tibial polyethylene insert, a cause of tibial osteolysis after TKA, results mainly from:
o: Adhesive wear at the patellofemoral joint
Micromotion between the undersurface of the insert and the tibial tray
Third-body cement debris in the femoral box
items.e: Inadequate locking allows micromotion of the insert on the tray, generating particles that migrate down screw holes and around the keel. Polished trays and better locking mechanisms reduce it.

items.q: Which tibial tray design feature reduces backside polyethylene wear in modular TKA?
o: Multiple unused screw holes in the tray
A highly polished cobalt-chromium tray surface with a secure peripheral locking mechanism
items.e: Polished cobalt-chromium trays with rigid capture mechanisms markedly reduce micromotion and backside wear compared with rough titanium trays.

items.q: The excellent lubrication of ceramic bearing surfaces is mainly attributed to their:
o: High wettability (hydrophilic surface) allowing a thin fluid film
items.e: Ceramics are extremely hydrophilic and can be polished very smooth, favouring fluid-film lubrication. They are the hardest, not the softest, bearing materials.

items.q: Which of the following bearing materials has the greatest hardness and scratch resistance?
items.e: Hardness decreases from ceramic to cobalt-chromium, stainless steel, titanium and polyethylene. Titanium is too soft and notch-sensitive to be used as a bearing surface.

items.q: The fracture rate of modern zirconia-toughened alumina (BIOLOX delta) femoral heads is approximately:
items.e: Fourth-generation delta heads fracture in only a few per 100,000 (about 0.002%); liner fractures are slightly more frequent but still very rare.

items.q: A localised band of wear ('stripe wear') on a ceramic femoral head in a ceramic-on-ceramic THA is caused by:
o: Edge loading from microseparation or cup malposition
items.e: Microseparation of the head from the liner during gait (swing phase) and edge loading against the rim produce stripe wear, which is linked to squeaking.

items.q: Chipping of a ceramic acetabular liner at the time of THA is most commonly due to:
o: Malseating (tilted insertion) of the liner in the shell
items.e: If the ceramic liner is not seated concentrically in the taper of the shell, the edge is loaded and chips during impaction or later; seating must be checked by palpation and visual inspection.

items.q: A ceramic femoral head fractures 5 years after THA; the trunnion has visible scratches. Which femoral head option is most appropriate at revision?
o: A new ceramic head mounted on a titanium adapter sleeve
A cobalt-chromium head placed directly on the trunnion
A ceramic head impacted directly onto the damaged trunnion
An oxidised zirconium head without synovectomy
items.e: Retained ceramic particles would destroy a metal head, so a ceramic head is used; on a damaged taper it must sit on a titanium sleeve to avoid a new fracture. A thorough synovectomy is also performed.

items.q: In a young patient receiving highly cross-linked polyethylene, choosing a ceramic rather than a cobalt-chromium femoral head principally:
o: Avoids taper corrosion at the head-neck junction and lowers polyethylene wear
Allows use of a smaller acetabular component
items.e: Ceramic heads are smoother and more wettable (less PE wear) and do not fret and corrode at the trunnion. Squeaking is a ceramic-on-ceramic phenomenon.

items.q: After a THA with an oxidised zirconium head on polyethylene dislocates and is closed-reduced, rapid wear may follow because:
o: Cobalt is released from the head
The thin oxide layer is breached against the cup rim, exposing the soft zirconium substrate
items.e: Dislocation and reduction over the metal shell rim can scratch through the thin oxide layer; the exposed soft alloy then wears rapidly and generates metal debris.

items.q: The 2001 recall of Prozyr yttria-stabilised zirconia femoral heads was due to:
o: Phase transformation of the ceramic causing a cluster of head fractures
items.e: A change in the sintering process caused accelerated tetragonal-to-monoclinic phase transformation, roughening and fracture of these zirconia heads.

items.q: Compared with polyethylene debris, particles generated by metal-on-metal bearings are:
o: Several microns in size and few in number
Nanometre-sized and produced in far greater numbers
items.e: Although volumetric wear is low, MoM bearings release enormous numbers of nanometre-scale particles and cobalt/chromium ions, which drive local and systemic reactions.

items.q: ALVAL (aseptic lymphocyte-dominated vasculitis-associated lesion) seen with metal-on-metal bearings represents which hypersensitivity reaction?
items.e: ALVAL is a T-lymphocyte-mediated delayed-type hypersensitivity with perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates, within the spectrum of adverse local tissue reactions.

items.q: A patient with a failed metal-on-metal THA has a blood cobalt level of several hundred µg/L. Which systemic manifestation of cobalt toxicity may occur?
items.e: Systemic cobaltism causes cardiomyopathy, hypothyroidism, peripheral neuropathy and visual and hearing loss.

items.q: Which patient with a metal-on-metal hip resurfacing is at greatest risk of an adverse reaction to metal debris?
o: A woman with a small (44 mm) component and a cup inclination of 60°
A man with a 54 mm component and a cup inclination of 40°
A man with a 50 mm component and a cup inclination of 45°
A woman with a 52 mm component and a cup inclination of 40°
items.e: Female sex, small component size and steep cup inclination (edge loading, loss of fluid-film lubrication) all increase metal wear and ALTR risk.

items.q: In 2010, a metal-on-metal hip system was recalled worldwide because of high early revision rates for adverse reactions to metal debris. This implant was the:
items.e: The ASR resurfacing and ASR XL THA had high failure rates (shallow cup with a small functional arc, edge loading). The Birmingham Hip Resurfacing has good results in men with large heads.

items.q: When revising a failed large-head metal-on-metal THA for a pseudotumour with a well-fixed stem, the preferred new bearing is:
o: A cobalt-chromium head on a cobalt-chromium liner of smaller size
A ceramic head with a titanium sleeve on a polyethylene liner
A hemiarthroplasty with a bipolar metal head
items.e: ALTR revisions avoid further metal bearings; a ceramic head (on a sleeve if the taper is used) with polyethylene or ceramic is standard. Outcomes after ALTR revision are worse than after other aseptic revisions.

items.q: The commonest cause of early failure after metal-on-metal hip resurfacing is:
items.e: Femoral neck fracture (associated with notching of the superior neck, varus positioning, cysts and poor bone) is the commonest early failure mode.

items.q: Which technical error during hip resurfacing most increases the risk of femoral neck fracture?
o: Notching of the superior femoral neck cortex while preparing the head
Valgus placement of the femoral component
items.e: Superior neck notching creates a stress riser; slight valgus positioning is recommended, and varus placement increases fracture risk.

items.q: Which finding most strongly argues against metal-on-metal hip resurfacing in a 50-year-old active man?
o: Primary osteoarthritis with a 54 mm femoral head
Large avascular necrosis lesion with collapse of the femoral head
items.e: Resurfacing needs good femoral head bone; large necrotic segments or cysts give poor support and high failure. A large head in an active man with OA is the ideal indication.

items.q: Which configuration most increases the risk of taper corrosion (trunnionosis) in a metal-on-polyethylene THA?
o: A 32 mm ceramic head with a short neck on a titanium stem
A 28 mm ceramic head on a cobalt-chromium stem
A 40 mm cobalt-chromium head with a long (+8 mm) neck on a titanium stem
A 32 mm cobalt-chromium head with a short neck on a cobalt-chromium monoblock stem
items.e: Large CoCr heads and long necks increase torque and micromotion at the taper, and mixed metals (CoCr on titanium) promote mechanically assisted crevice corrosion.

items.q: The 2012 recalls of certain femoral stems with dual-taper modular necks (e.g. Rejuvenate, ABG II) were due to:
o: Fretting and crevice corrosion at the neck-stem junction with adverse local tissue reaction
items.e: Cobalt-chromium modular necks in titanium stems corroded at the additional junction, releasing cobalt and causing ALTR, so these designs were withdrawn.

items.q: During THA, which step at head assembly best reduces the later risk of taper corrosion?
o: Cleaning and drying the trunnion and impacting the head firmly along the neck axis
Applying bone cement to the taper
Lubricating the taper with saline before assembly
Lightly seating the head with hand pressure only
items.e: Fluid, blood or debris on the taper and inadequate axial impaction reduce taper engagement and allow micromotion, the trigger for fretting corrosion.

items.q: A painful MoP THA with a well-fixed stem has blood cobalt raised much more than chromium and a fluid collection on MARS MRI. Besides debridement and liner exchange, the head should be:
o: Replaced with a new cobalt-chromium head of larger size
Replaced with a ceramic head on a titanium sleeve
Left in place and the stem revised only if pain persists
Replaced with a metal-on-metal large head
items.e: For taper corrosion with a usable trunnion, a ceramic head on a titanium sleeve removes the corroding CoCr-titanium interface; the stem is revised only if the trunnion is severely damaged.

items.q: In a metal-on-metal bearing, which design factor favours fluid-film lubrication and lower wear?
o: Small head diameter with high radial clearance
Large head diameter with low radial clearance
items.e: Larger diameters increase the sliding speed and entraining velocity, and low clearance improves conformity, both thickening the fluid film. Steep cups cause edge loading.

items.q: The wear pattern of a well-functioning metal-on-metal bearing over time is typically:
o: No measurable wear for the first 10 years
Constant high wear equal to metal-on-polyethylene
An early 'run-in' phase of higher wear followed by a low steady-state wear rate
items.e: MoM bearings show a bedding-in (run-in) period during the first year or about a million cycles, after which the surfaces become self-polished and wear falls to a low steady state.

items.q: Large-diameter metal-on-metal THAs had higher failure rates than resurfacings with similar bearings, partly because:
o: Additional metal debris was released by corrosion at the large-head taper junction
Their bearing surfaces were made of titanium
items.e: Large CoCr heads on a stem taper have a long moment arm, producing taper fretting and corrosion in addition to bearing wear, raising cobalt levels and ALTR rates.

items.q: Metal-on-metal bearings are relatively contraindicated in patients with which condition, because metal ions are excreted mainly by this organ?
items.e: Cobalt and chromium ions are cleared by the kidneys; renal impairment raises blood levels and the risk of systemic toxicity.

items.q: A motorcyclist has these Abbreviated Injury Scale (AIS) scores: head 4, chest 3, abdomen 2 and lower extremity 5. What is his Injury Severity Score (ISS)?
items.e: ISS is the sum of the squares of the highest AIS in the three most severely injured body regions: 5² + 4² + 3² = 25 + 16 + 9 = 50. Adding the fourth region (54) is wrong because only three regions count.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: A patient has two lower-extremity injuries scored AIS 4 and AIS 3, and a head injury scored AIS 2, with no other injuries. What is the New Injury Severity Score (NISS)?
items.e: NISS squares the three most severe injuries regardless of body region: 16 + 9 + 4 = 29. The conventional ISS would be only 20 (16 + 4) because it takes one injury per region.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: When any single injury in a trauma patient is coded AIS 6, the Injury Severity Score is assigned as:
items.e: An AIS 6 (currently untreatable/unsurvivable) injury automatically sets the ISS to its maximum of 75. The ISS range is therefore 1 to 75.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: A 70 kg man after a road traffic accident has a heart rate of 112/min, normal systolic blood pressure, a narrowed pulse pressure and is anxious. According to ATLS, his estimated blood loss is about:
items.e: Tachycardia with preserved systolic pressure but narrowed pulse pressure and anxiety is class II haemorrhage (15-30%, 750-1500 ml in a 70 kg adult). Systolic pressure does not consistently fall until class III.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: In the ATLS classification of haemorrhagic shock, the first class in which systolic blood pressure consistently falls is:
items.e: Hypotension appears in class III (30-40% loss), with tachycardia of about 120-140 and confusion. Class II maintains systolic pressure with only a narrowed pulse pressure.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: In the CRASH-2 trial of tranexamic acid in bleeding trauma patients, treatment started after what interval from injury was associated with an increased risk of death from bleeding?
items.e: Benefit was greatest within 1 hour and present up to 3 hours; starting TXA after 3 hours increased bleeding deaths. Hence the regimen of 1 g over 10 minutes then 1 g over 8 hours, given within 3 hours.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: For a polytrauma patient needing massive transfusion, current damage-control resuscitation targets a ratio of packed red cells : plasma : platelets of approximately:
items.e: Balanced (haemostatic) resuscitation uses roughly equal units of red cells, plasma and platelets to prevent and treat trauma-induced coagulopathy. Crystalloid-heavy or red-cell-dominant regimens worsen dilutional coagulopathy.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: A 24-year-old has a closed femoral shaft fracture awaiting fixation on skeletal traction. At 40 hours after injury he becomes tachypnoeic and hypoxic, then confused, and petechiae appear in the axillae and conjunctivae. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Respiratory insufficiency, cerebral involvement and a petechial rash 24-72 hours after a long-bone fracture fulfil Gurd's major criteria for fat embolism syndrome. The petechial rash is not a feature of pulmonary thromboembolism.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: Which measure has the best evidence for reducing the incidence of fat embolism syndrome after long-bone fractures?
items.e: Early fracture stabilisation reduces fat embolism and pulmonary complications; treatment of established FES is supportive (oxygen, ventilation). Prolonged delay in traction increases the risk rather than reducing it.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: Bone and colleagues' 1989 randomised trial of femoral shaft fractures showed that fixation within 24 hours, compared with delayed fixation, mainly reduced:
o: Pulmonary complications such as ARDS, fat embolism and pneumonia
items.e: Early stabilisation of femoral fractures reduced pulmonary complications, length of ICU stay and cost, which underpins early total care in stable patients. Union and infection rates were not the main differences.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: In the 'two-hit' model of post-traumatic organ failure, the 'second hit' that damage-control orthopaedics aims to avoid is:
o: The initial tissue injury and haemorrhage
Major surgery such as prolonged femoral reaming and blood loss on an already primed inflammatory system
Exposure and hypothermia at the scene of the accident
items.e: The injury itself is the first hit that primes the immune system (SIRS); a large early operation adds a second hit that can tip the patient into ARDS and multiple organ failure. DCO therefore uses brief temporary fixation.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: After damage-control external fixation in polytrauma, conversion to definitive fixation is usually avoided on days 2-4 because during this period:
o: Coagulation factors have not yet been synthesised
The systemic inflammatory response and tissue oedema are at their peak
items.e: Days 2-4 correspond to peak inflammatory and immune activation, when a major operation acts as a second hit. Definitive surgery is usually done once physiology has recovered, around days 5-10.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: In Pape's criteria for the 'borderline' polytrauma patient, which of the following values places the patient in this category?
o: Mean pulmonary artery pressure over 24 mmHg
items.e: Borderline criteria include ISS over 40 (or over 20 with thoracic trauma), bilateral lung contusion, mean PAP over 24 mmHg and hypothermia under 35 °C. A lactate under 2.5 mmol/L is a feature of the stable patient.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: In Vallier's 'early appropriate care' protocol, definitive fixation of major pelvic, acetabular, spinal and femoral fractures within 36 hours is undertaken once the lactate falls below:
items.e: EAC uses resuscitation endpoints of lactate under 4.0 mmol/L, pH 7.25 or above or base excess -5.5 or better. The threshold of 2.5 mmol/L comes from Pape's definition of the stable patient.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: Under the Berlin definition of polytrauma, AIS 3 or more in at least two regions must be accompanied by a physiological risk factor. The age threshold counted as one such factor is:
items.e: The Berlin physiological variables are hypotension (systolic 90 or less), GCS 8 or less, base excess -6 or worse, coagulopathy (INR 1.4 or more / PTT 40 s or more) and age 70 or more.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: Permissive hypotension (systolic about 80-90 mmHg) during damage-control resuscitation is inappropriate in a patient who also has:
items.e: With traumatic brain injury, cerebral perfusion depends on adequate mean arterial pressure (about 80 mmHg or more), so permissive hypotension is avoided. Torso and limb haemorrhage are the very situations where it is used.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: In the military and prehospital modification of the primary survey, <C>ABCDE, the initial <C> stands for:
items.e: Exsanguinating limb haemorrhage kills faster than airway compromise in penetrating and blast injury, so tourniquets and haemostatic dressings come first. Cervical spine control remains part of the 'A' step.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: The 'lethal triad' of trauma (hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy) is extended to the 'lethal diamond' by adding:
items.e: Ionised hypocalcaemia, worsened by citrate in transfused blood, impairs coagulation and myocardial contractility and is the fourth corner of the lethal diamond.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: In the classic trimodal distribution of trauma deaths, the peak most amenable to rapid ATLS-based intervention is:
o: The first peak (seconds to minutes), from brainstem and great vessel injury
The third peak (days to weeks), from sepsis and multi-organ failure
The second peak (minutes to hours), from haemorrhage, airway compromise and tension pneumothorax
The first peak, from high cervical cord transection
items.e: The 'golden hour' deaths of the second peak are largely preventable with prompt resuscitation and haemorrhage control. Immediate deaths are best addressed by injury prevention.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: The final Gustilo-Anderson type of an open tibial fracture should be assigned:
o: In the emergency department from the wound size
At the time of definitive wound closure only
At 6 weeks once infection has been excluded
items.e: The true extent of soft-tissue damage, periosteal stripping and contamination is only evident after debridement. Grading from the skin wound in the emergency department often underestimates the injury.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: A farmer sustains an open tibial fracture in a cattle shed with a 1 cm wound heavily contaminated with soil and manure. After debridement the bone is well covered by viable soft tissue. The Gustilo-Anderson type is:
items.e: Farmyard contamination places the injury in type III regardless of wound length; adequate soft-tissue cover after debridement makes it IIIA. IIIB would need periosteal stripping with exposed bone requiring a flap.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: An open tibial fracture has a 5 cm laceration, moderate soft-tissue damage, little contamination and a simple transverse fracture. The Gustilo-Anderson type is:
items.e: Type II wounds are 1-10 cm with moderate soft-tissue damage and a non-comminuted, low-energy fracture. Type I wounds are under 1 cm, and type III implies high energy, heavy contamination or extensive soft-tissue injury.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: For an open fracture contaminated with soil in a farmyard, the antibiotic added to standard cephalosporin cover specifically to cover clostridia and other anaerobes is:
items.e: Soil and faecal contamination carries a risk of clostridial infection (gas gangrene), so penicillin is added. Gentamicin, not penicillin, is the addition for gram-negative cover in type III injuries.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: Following current open-fracture guidance, systemic prophylactic antibiotics are continued:
o: As a single dose before debridement only
For 6 weeks as treatment of presumed osteomyelitis
Until radiological union of the fracture
Until about 24 hours after definitive wound closure, and not beyond 72 hours
items.e: Prophylaxis continues until definitive soft-tissue closure and stops about 24 hours later, with a ceiling of about 72 hours. Longer courses do not reduce infection but select resistant organisms.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: According to BOAST open fracture standards, a high-energy open fracture without gross contamination should undergo debridement within:
items.e: BOAST sets 12 hours for high-energy open fractures, 24 hours for other low-energy open fractures, and immediate surgery for gross marine/agricultural/sewage contamination, vascular injury or compartment syndrome.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: The '4 Cs' used to judge muscle viability at open-fracture debridement are colour, consistency, contractility and:
o: Capillary refill time of the overlying skin
items.e: Viable muscle is pink, firm, contracts when stimulated and bleeds when cut; dead muscle is excised. Compartment pressure and serum CK do not assess individual muscle viability at surgery.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: The recommended wound care for an open fracture in the emergency department before theatre is:
o: Copious irrigation with several litres of saline in the department
Probing the wound to see whether bone is exposed
Photograph the wound and cover it with a saline-soaked dressing, without irrigation or probing
Wound swabs for culture before any antibiotic is given
items.e: A photograph avoids repeated dressing removal; the wound is covered, the limb realigned and splinted, and antibiotics given promptly. Irrigation and probing in the department add contamination without benefit, and pre-debridement swabs do not predict infecting organisms.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: In the FLOW trial of irrigation for open fractures, which irrigation solution was associated with a higher reoperation rate than normal saline?
items.e: FLOW compared castile soap with normal saline (and three pressures) and found more reoperations with soap. Saline at low pressure is therefore recommended.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: The WOLLF trial compared negative-pressure wound therapy with standard dressings after debridement of severe open lower-limb fractures. It found that NPWT:
o: Gave no difference in disability or deep infection at 12 months
Allowed definitive cover to be delayed safely to 3 weeks
Significantly improved disability scores at 12 months
items.e: WOLLF showed no significant benefit of NPWT over standard dressings in Disability Rating Index or deep infection. NPWT is only a temporary dressing until early definitive cover.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: From the LEAP study, how should absent plantar sensation at presentation in a severe open tibial fracture be interpreted?
o: It confirms tibial nerve transection and mandates primary amputation
It should not by itself be an indication for amputation, as about half of such feet regained sensation
It predicts worse 2-year function after salvage than after amputation
It is the strongest component of the MESS
items.e: In LEAP, about half of initially insensate feet regained sensation by 2 years and insensate salvaged limbs did as well as matched controls. Plantar sensation is not a component of the MESS.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: In the Mangled Extremity Severity Score, the limb ischaemia points are doubled when the ischaemia time exceeds:
items.e: MESS scores skeletal/soft-tissue energy, limb ischaemia (doubled beyond 6 hours), shock and age; 7 or more historically suggested amputation but has poor predictive value.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: As the Achilles tendon descends to the calcaneus its fibres rotate about 90 degrees. Where do the fibres derived from the soleus come to insert?
o: Medial part of the calcaneal footprint
Lateral part of the calcaneal footprint
Plantar fascia via a continuous sheet
Superior (proximal) margin of the footprint only
items.e: The tendon twists so that soleus fibres end up inserting medially and gastrocnemius fibres laterally/posteriorly; this torsion concentrates stress in the mid-portion.

items.q: Which artery is the main supply to the mid-portion (watershed region) of the Achilles tendon, through the paratenon?
items.e: The proximal and distal (insertional) parts are supplied by the posterior tibial artery, while the poorly perfused mid-portion depends on the peroneal artery.

items.q: Which statement best describes the gliding covering of the Achilles tendon?
o: It has a synovial sheath only in its distal 2 cm
It has neither a paratenon nor a sheath
It has a paratenon and no true synovial sheath
It has a true synovial sheath along its whole length
items.e: The Achilles is enveloped by a vascular paratenon rather than a synovial sheath; inflammation of this layer gives paratenonitis with crepitus.

items.q: A patient lies prone with both knees flexed to 90 degrees. The injured foot hangs in neutral while the opposite foot rests in slight plantarflexion. This is the:
o: Matles test, indicating Achilles tendon rupture
items.e: Loss of the normal resting plantarflexion tension with the knee flexed (Matles test) indicates loss of continuity of the Achilles tendon.

items.q: According to the AAOS clinical practice guideline, how can an acute Achilles tendon rupture be diagnosed?
o: Two or more positive clinical tests such as calf squeeze, palpable gap, decreased plantarflexion strength or increased passive dorsiflexion
A single positive calf squeeze test plus a plain radiograph
Ultrasound is required in every case to confirm the diagnosis
MRI is mandatory in every case before treatment
items.e: The AAOS guideline recommends a diagnosis based on two or more of the standard physical examination findings; imaging is reserved for equivocal cases.

items.q: About 20% of acute Achilles tendon ruptures are missed at first presentation. The main reason is that:
o: Active plantarflexion is preserved through FHL, FDL, tibialis posterior and the peronei
The calf squeeze test is normal in most ruptures
Pain is usually felt in the forefoot
items.e: Other plantarflexors allow weak active plantarflexion, so the patient may still walk and push off, misleading the examiner.

items.q: In the Copeland sphygmomanometer test for Achilles rupture, a cuff around the calf is inflated to about 100 mmHg with the foot plantarflexed. A ruptured tendon is indicated when passive dorsiflexion:
o: Produces a rise to about 140 mmHg
Produces little or no rise in cuff pressure
items.e: With an intact tendon, passive dorsiflexion tensions the triceps surae and raises the pressure (to about 140 mmHg); failure of the pressure to rise indicates rupture.

items.q: In the O'Brien needle test, a needle is inserted through the skin into the Achilles tendon about 10 cm above the insertion. Rupture distal to the needle is indicated when, on passive dorsiflexion and plantarflexion of the foot:
o: The patient feels pain at the needle site
The needle hub swivels in the opposite direction to the foot movement
The needle is expelled from the tendon
The needle hub does not swivel
items.e: If the tendon is in continuity distal to the needle, foot movement makes the hub swivel; no movement of the hub indicates rupture between the needle and the insertion.

items.q: On a lateral ankle radiograph after a suspected Achilles rupture, the triangular radiolucent fat pad between the Achilles tendon, FHL and the calcaneus is distorted. This fat pad is:
items.e: Kager's triangle is bounded by the Achilles posteriorly, FHL anteriorly and the calcaneus inferiorly; its distortion or obliteration suggests Achilles rupture.

items.q: Which plantarflexion position is typically used at the start of an accelerated functional non-operative protocol for acute Achilles rupture?
o: Full (maximal) equinus in an above-knee cast
About 20-30 degrees of plantarflexion in a boot with heel wedges
10 degrees of dorsiflexion in a night splint
Neutral (0 degrees) in a walking boot
items.e: Functional protocols begin with about 20-30 degrees of equinus using wedges, allow early protected weight bearing, and gradually reduce the equinus over 6-8 weeks.

items.q: During non-operative functional rehabilitation of an acute Achilles rupture, which activity should be avoided for about the first 12 weeks?
o: Active plantarflexion exercises within the boot range
Protected weight bearing in the boot
Passive dorsiflexion stretching of the ankle
items.e: Passive dorsiflexion stretching risks elongation of the healing tendon (weak push-off) or re-rupture, so it is avoided for about 12 weeks.

items.q: For an open repair of an acute Achilles tendon rupture, the skin incision is usually placed just medial to the tendon mainly to:
o: Gain access to the FHL for routine transfer
Allow direct repair of the plantaris
Avoid the sural nerve and lesser saphenous vein on the lateral side
items.e: A posteromedial incision avoids the sural nerve, which lies lateral to the tendon in the distal leg.

items.q: Compared with non-operative functional treatment of an acute Achilles rupture, the main disadvantage of open surgical repair is a higher rate of:
items.e: Surgery slightly reduces re-rupture but adds wound breakdown and infection risk (about 5-10% after open repair); elongation is more a feature of non-operative care.

items.q: The UKSTAR trial (2020) in adults with acute Achilles tendon rupture compared which two treatments?
o: Functional bracing versus plaster casting, both non-operative
items.e: UKSTAR randomised non-operatively treated patients to a functional brace or plaster cast and found no significant difference in the Achilles Tendon Rupture Score at 9 months.

items.q: Which patient-reported outcome measure is specific to Achilles tendon rupture and was the primary outcome of the UKSTAR trial?
items.e: ATRS is designed for Achilles rupture; VISA-A is used for Achilles tendinopathy.

items.q: Which questionnaire is the standard patient-reported measure of severity in Achilles tendinopathy?
o: VISA-A (Victorian Institute of Sport Assessment - Achilles)
items.e: VISA-A quantifies pain, function and activity in Achilles tendinopathy; Kujala and Lysholm are knee scores.

items.q: In the Kuwada classification of chronic Achilles ruptures, a defect larger than 6 cm after debridement (type IV) is usually treated with:
o: Tendon transfer combined with a free tendon graft or augmentation
items.e: Kuwada type IV defects (over 6 cm) need recession plus tendon transfer and free tendon graft or synthetic augmentation; end-to-end repair suits type II.

items.q: According to the Myerson approach to chronic Achilles rupture, a defect of 1-2 cm after debridement is best managed by:
items.e: Small defects (under 1-2 cm) can be closed end to end; 2-5 cm defects need V-Y advancement with or without FHL transfer, and over 5 cm FHL transfer with or without turndown or graft.

items.q: FHL is generally preferred to FDL or peroneus brevis for tendon transfer in chronic Achilles reconstruction mainly because:
o: Its harvest never affects hallux function
It is an antagonist of the triceps surae
It is strong, fires in phase with the gastrosoleus and its low-lying muscle belly brings a blood supply
It inserts directly on the calcaneus normally
items.e: FHL is the second strongest plantarflexor, is in phase with the gastrosoleus, lies adjacent to the Achilles, and its vascularised muscle belly improves the local blood supply.

items.q: In a short-harvest FHL transfer for chronic Achilles insufficiency, the FHL tendon is usually fixed to the calcaneus by:
o: A staple on the talar neck
An interference screw in a bone tunnel in the posterior calcaneal tuberosity
items.e: The harvested FHL is passed into a tunnel drilled in the calcaneal tuberosity, close to the Achilles insertion, and fixed (commonly with an interference screw).

items.q: A long FHL harvest through a second plantar midfoot incision divides the tendon distal to its crossing with FDL. This crossing point is known as the:
o: Master knot of the plantar fascia
items.e: At the knot of Henry in the plantar midfoot, FHL and FDL cross; a long harvest requires dissection here, with risk to the medial plantar nerve.

items.q: Which reconstruction for chronic Achilles rupture uses two strips of gastrocnemius aponeurosis that are twisted 180 degrees and turned down to bridge the gap?
items.e: Lindholm used medial and lateral aponeurotic flaps turned down over the repair; Bosworth used a single central strip; Strayer is a gastrocnemius recession; Hoke is a percutaneous lengthening.

items.q: A runner with chronic mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy has a thickened tendon and a palpable tender nodule that moves proximally and distally with ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion. This 'painful arc sign' indicates:
items.e: A tender swelling that moves with the tendon is within the tendon (tendinosis); in isolated paratenonitis the tender area stays fixed as the tendon glides.

items.q: A runner has acute diffuse swelling around the Achilles mid-portion with palpable crepitus, and the tender area does not move with ankle movement. The likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Paratenonitis (inflammation of the paratenon) gives crepitus and a fixed tender zone; intratendinous lesions move with the tendon.

items.q: In the Royal London Hospital test for mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy, the tender point found with the ankle slightly plantarflexed:
o: Becomes much less tender when the ankle is actively dorsiflexed
Becomes more tender when the ankle is dorsiflexed
Disappears when the knee is flexed
Is reproduced only by single-leg hopping
items.e: Tenderness that reduces markedly in dorsiflexion (tendon under tension) is a positive Royal London Hospital test for mid-portion tendinopathy.

items.q: The Alfredson eccentric protocol for mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy is done with the knee both straight and bent. The bent-knee exercises mainly load the:
items.e: Bending the knee slackens the gastrocnemius (which crosses the knee), so the bent-knee drops target the soleus component of the tendon.

items.q: A runner with mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy has neovessels entering the ventral tendon on colour Doppler. Which injected agent was introduced specifically to sclerose these neovessels?
items.e: Polidocanol sclerotherapy (Öhberg and Alfredson) targets the neovessels and accompanying nerves; corticosteroid injection into the tendon is avoided because of rupture risk.

items.q: High-volume image-guided injection for resistant mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy works by injecting a large volume of saline (with local anaesthetic) into which space?
o: Into the substance of the tendon at the area of tendinosis
Between the anterior (ventral) tendon and Kager's fat pad
items.e: The high volume is placed ventral to the tendon to strip the paratenon from the neovessels and nerves, which are thought to be pain generators.

items.q: A runner with chronic medial-sided mid-portion Achilles pain fails 6 months of loading. At surgery a tendon is found closely adherent to and compressing the medial Achilles. Which tendon is commonly released in this situation?
items.e: The plantaris runs along the medial Achilles and can contribute to medial mid-portion tendinopathy; its release (often with scraping of neovessels) is a recognised procedure.

items.q: Immediately after an acute Achilles rupture, a firm cord is palpable along the medial side of the gap and may mislead the examiner into thinking the tendon is intact. This is most likely the:
items.e: The plantaris often survives Achilles rupture and lies medially; its palpable cord can mask the gap.

items.q: In surgery for mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy, if more than about 50% of the tendon cross-section has to be debrided, the usual recommendation is to:
o: Close the paratenon only and immobilise
Inject corticosteroid into the remaining tendon
Augment the tendon with an FHL transfer
items.e: Debridement of over 50% leaves a weak tendon; augmentation with FHL transfer is advised to protect against rupture.

items.q: In insertional Achilles tendinopathy, how is the eccentric loading programme modified compared with the mid-portion protocol?
o: Eccentric loading is replaced by a steroid injection
Loading is done into maximal dorsiflexion off a step
Exercises are done only with the knee bent
Heel drops are done on flat ground without dropping into dorsiflexion
items.e: Dropping into dorsiflexion compresses the insertion against the posterosuperior calcaneus; floor-level eccentrics avoid this impingement.

items.q: For operative treatment of insertional Achilles tendinopathy with a Haglund prominence and calcification, a commonly used approach that gives access to the calcification, the bursa and the bony prominence is:
o: An anterolateral approach to the ankle
items.e: A midline tendon-splitting approach gives access for excision of calcification, retrocalcaneal bursa and Haglund deformity, followed by reattachment with suture anchors.

items.q: A dorsal closing-wedge osteotomy of the calcaneal tuberosity, used to reduce the prominence and change the Achilles lever in insertional tendinopathy, is known as the:
items.e: The Zadek (Keck and Kelly) dorsal closing-wedge osteotomy treats insertional tendinopathy/Haglund; Dwyer and Koutsogiannis are hindfoot alignment osteotomies and Evans is a lateral column lengthening.

items.q: On a lateral radiograph of a patient with Haglund deformity, Pavlov's parallel pitch lines are drawn. The deformity is considered significant when:
o: The calcaneal pitch angle is below 10 degrees
The posterosuperior calcaneal prominence rises above the upper parallel pitch line
items.e: A prominence projecting above the upper of the two parallel pitch lines is regarded as a positive (abnormal) finding for Haglund deformity.

items.q: Haglund syndrome consists of a posterosuperior calcaneal prominence together with:
o: Tarsal tunnel syndrome and pes planus
Retrocalcaneal bursitis and insertional Achilles tendinopathy
items.e: The prominence irritates the retrocalcaneal bursa and the insertion of the tendon; the triad is called Haglund syndrome.

items.q: The retrocalcaneal bursa lies:
o: Between the anterior surface of the distal Achilles tendon and the posterosuperior calcaneus
Between the skin and the posterior surface of the Achilles
items.e: The retrocalcaneal bursa is deep to the tendon against the calcaneus; the retro-Achilles (subcutaneous) bursa lies between the tendon and skin.

items.q: A 25-year-old man has bilateral insertional Achilles pain and heel swelling with inflammatory low back pain and morning stiffness. Which investigation is most relevant to the underlying cause?
o: Nerve conduction studies of the tibial nerve
HLA-B27 testing with sacroiliac joint imaging
items.e: Bilateral insertional Achilles enthesitis in a young man with inflammatory back pain suggests a seronegative spondyloarthropathy.

items.q: The risk of fluoroquinolone-associated Achilles tendon rupture is greatest in which patient?
items.e: Fluoroquinolone tendinopathy risk rises with age over 60, concurrent corticosteroid use and renal or transplant disease.

items.q: At the lateral wall of the calcaneus, the peroneal (trochlear) tubercle separates the two peroneal tendons. Which arrangement is correct?
o: Both tendons pass below it in one sheath
Both tendons pass above it in one sheath
Peroneus longus passes above it and peroneus brevis below it
Peroneus brevis passes above it and peroneus longus below it
items.e: Peroneus brevis runs superior to the peroneal tubercle towards the fifth metatarsal; peroneus longus runs inferior to it towards the cuboid groove.

items.q: Peroneus longus inserts into the:
o: Plantar-lateral base of the first metatarsal and the medial cuneiform
Plantar surface of the cuboid only
items.e: Peroneus longus crosses the sole in the cuboid tunnel to insert on the first metatarsal base and medial cuneiform, plantarflexing the first ray.

items.q: Behind the lateral malleolus, the relationship of the peroneal tendons within the retromalleolar groove is:
o: Peroneus longus lies anterior and peroneus brevis posterior
Peroneus brevis lies anterior (closer to the fibula) and peroneus longus posterior
They lie side by side in separate bony grooves
items.e: Brevis lies against the fibula in the groove and is compressed there by longus, which explains why brevis develops split tears.

items.q: A longitudinal split tear of peroneus brevis involves less than 50% of the usable tendon cross-section. The usual surgical treatment is:
o: Excision of the tendon with FHL transfer
Debridement and tubularisation of the tendon
items.e: Tears involving less than half the tendon are debrided and repaired (tubularised); if more than 50% is involved, tenodesis to peroneus longus is recommended.

items.q: Which anatomical variants predispose to peroneus brevis tears by crowding the retromalleolar groove?
o: A low-lying peroneus brevis muscle belly or an accessory peroneus quartus
items.e: Extra bulk in the fibro-osseous tunnel (low-lying brevis belly or peroneus quartus) increases pressure on the tendons.

items.q: In the Eckert-Davis classification of superior peroneal retinaculum injury in peroneal tendon dislocation, which grade is the most common?
o: Grade 1: the retinaculum is stripped from the fibula together with its periosteum
Grade 4 (Oden): the retinaculum is torn from its calcaneal attachment
Grade 2: the fibrocartilaginous rim is elevated with the retinaculum
Grade 3: a cortical fragment is avulsed from the fibula
items.e: Grade 1, a periosteal stripping of the SPR from the fibula creating a false pouch, is the commonest; grade 3 produces the radiographic fleck sign.

items.q: Which surgical procedure is commonly combined with SPR repair for chronic recurrent peroneal tendon dislocation, especially when the retromalleolar groove is shallow?
items.e: Chronic dislocation is treated by repairing or reconstructing the SPR and deepening the fibular groove to give the tendons a stable bed.
