items.e: CBVA is measured on a clinical photograph or radiograph with the patient standing with hips and knees extended; it quantifies horizontal gaze and guides the size of osteotomy in ankylosing spondylitis.

items.q: The Global Alignment and Proportion (GAP) score proposed by Yilgor differs from absolute SRS-Schwab targets because it:
o: Applies to children with idiopathic scoliosis only
Uses parameters proportioned to the individual's pelvic incidence to predict mechanical complications
Is calculated from CT bone density
items.e: GAP uses relative, PI-adjusted values (relative pelvic version, relative lumbar lordosis, lordosis distribution, relative spinopelvic alignment, age) and predicted mechanical failure such as PJK better than fixed absolute targets.

items.q: Age-adjusted alignment targets (Lafage) in adult spinal deformity imply that in a 78-year-old, aggressively correcting to the alignment of a young adult tends to:
o: Reduce the risk of proximal junctional kyphosis
Have no effect on mechanical complications
Increase the risk of proximal junctional kyphosis
items.e: Older patients normally have more positive alignment; over-correction beyond age-appropriate targets is a recognised risk factor for PJK and proximal junctional failure.

items.q: In the SRS-Schwab adult spinal deformity classification, curve type 'N' means:
o: No major coronal curve (under 30°), i.e. a primarily sagittal deformity
items.e: Type N denotes no coronal curve of 30° or more, so the deformity is mainly sagittal; T, L and D denote thoracic, thoracolumbar/lumbar and double curves.

items.q: In the SRS-Schwab classification, a patient with a 55° thoracic curve and a 22° lumbar curve is curve type:
items.e: Type T is a thoracic major curve with the lumbar curve under 30°; type D needs two curves each of 30° or more.

items.q: The most common of the Roussouly sagittal shape types in the normal population, with a sacral slope of 35-45° and a harmonious lordosis, is type:
items.e: Type 3 is the balanced, commonest shape; types 1 and 2 have SS under 35°, type 4 over 45°.

items.q: A 35-year-old with a flat back (Roussouly type 2, sacral slope under 35° with long hypolordosis) is particularly predisposed to:
o: Early disc degeneration and disc herniation
items.e: In flat type 2 spines the load is borne mainly by the discs, predisposing to early disc degeneration and herniation; high-lordosis type 4 overloads the posterior elements.

items.q: A Roussouly type 1 spine (sacral slope under 35°, short lordosis with a long thoracolumbar kyphosis) is associated with:
o: Disc degeneration at the thoracolumbar junction and posterior element impingement at L5-S1
items.e: Type 1 has a short hyperlordotic segment at L5-S1 below a long kyphosis, causing TL disc degeneration and posterior impingement at L5-S1.

items.q: In a Roussouly type 4 spine (sacral slope over 45°, long high lordosis), the characteristic degenerative pattern is:
o: Multilevel disc herniation from axial loading
Facet arthritis and posterior element overload, including spondylolysis
items.e: High lordosis shifts load to the posterior column, causing facet arthritis, spondylolysis and spinous process contact; flat spines overload the discs instead.

items.q: When sagittal malalignment develops, the pelvis compensates mainly by:
o: Retroversion around the femoral heads, increasing pelvic tilt
items.e: Pelvic retroversion (higher PT, lower SS) is the key compensatory mechanism; PI is fixed and cannot change.

items.q: A 70-year-old with lumbar flatback also has bilateral 25° hip flexion contractures from osteoarthritis. The contractures worsen her stooped posture mainly because they:
o: Limit the hip extension reserve needed for pelvic retroversion
items.e: Retroverting the pelvis requires hip extension; fixed hip flexion removes this reserve, so the patient cannot compensate and leans forward.

items.q: In a patient compensating for loss of lordosis, hyperextension of the remaining mobile lumbar segments above a fused segment typically leads to:
o: Retrolisthesis and facet overload at those levels
items.e: Compensatory hyperextension stresses the posterior elements of mobile segments, causing facet overload and retrolisthesis.

items.q: Which compensatory mechanism for sagittal imbalance is the last to be recruited and the most energy-expensive?
items.e: Knee flexion ('crouched' posture) is recruited after spinal and pelvic compensation are exhausted and demands constant quadriceps effort.

items.q: Classic iatrogenic flatback syndrome was most often caused by:
o: Harrington distraction rods extending into the lower lumbar spine
Anterior lumbar interbody fusion with lordotic cages
items.e: Distraction instrumentation across the lumbar spine flattened lordosis, producing forward-leaning posture, knee flexion and back pain.

items.q: The term 'hip-spine syndrome', describing coexisting hip and spine pathology that confuses diagnosis and treatment, was introduced by:
items.e: Offierski and MacNab (1983) described hip-spine syndrome, classifying it as simple, complex, secondary or misdiagnosed.

items.q: When a normal person moves from standing to sitting, the pelvis:
o: Does not move relative to the spine
Retroverts by about 20°, increasing functional acetabular anteversion
items.e: Sitting tilts the pelvis posteriorly (SS falls, PT rises), opening the acetabulum anteriorly; this protects against anterior impingement and posterior dislocation after THA.

items.q: A 66-year-old with a prior L2-S1 instrumented fusion needs a total hip arthroplasty. Compared with a patient with a mobile spine, she has:
o: Lower dislocation risk because the pelvis is stable
No difference if the cup is placed in the Lewinnek zone
Increased risk of anterior dislocation only when standing
Increased risk of dislocation and impingement, so a dual-mobility cup is often considered
items.e: A stiff fused spine prevents normal pelvic retroversion on sitting, so the hip flexes more and impinges, raising dislocation risk; adjusting cup position and using dual-mobility bearings reduce it.

items.q: In spinopelvic mobility assessment before THA, a 'stiff' spine is usually defined by a change in sacral slope between standing and sitting of less than about:
items.e: A standing-to-sitting change in sacral slope under about 10° indicates a stiff spinopelvic unit; normal is roughly 20° or more.

items.q: Which of the following is a recognised risk factor for proximal junctional kyphosis after adult deformity surgery?
o: Upper instrumented vertebra in the upper thoracic spine
Upper instrumented vertebra at the thoracolumbar junction
Under-correction of the sagittal vertical axis
items.e: Stopping the construct at the thoracolumbar junction places the UIV at a stress transition; older age, osteoporosis, large corrections and over-correction are also risk factors.

items.q: Which technique is used at the upper instrumented vertebra to reduce proximal junctional kyphosis and failure?
o: Bigger pedicle screws with more rigid rods
Releasing the interspinous ligament above the UIV
Vertebral cement augmentation of the UIV and the level above
Ending the fusion at the apex of thoracic kyphosis
items.e: Cement augmentation, transitional rods or hooks ('soft landing'), tethers and teriparatide are used; disrupting the posterior ligaments above the UIV increases PJK risk.

items.q: Proximal junctional failure, as opposed to radiographic proximal junctional kyphosis, implies:
o: Asymptomatic kyphosis seen on routine films
Fracture, instability, implant pull-out or neurological deficit at the junction, often needing revision
items.e: PJF is the structural failure end of the spectrum (fracture, ligament failure, screw pull-out, myelopathy) and commonly requires extension of the fusion.

items.q: A Smith-Petersen or Ponte osteotomy gives approximately how much sagittal correction per level?
o: About 10° (roughly 1° per mm of posterior bone resected)
items.e: Posterior column osteotomies give about 10° per level; PSO gives 30-35° at one level and VCR more than 40°.

items.q: The essential prerequisite for correction through a Ponte or Smith-Petersen osteotomy is:
o: A mobile anterior column with an open disc space
A coronal curve of more than 60°
items.e: These posterior-only osteotomies shorten the posterior column and hinge open the disc anteriorly, so the disc must be mobile; a fused anterior column needs a three-column osteotomy such as PSO.

items.q: Correction through a pedicle subtraction osteotomy is achieved by:
o: Opening the anterior column through the disc
Closing a posterior-based wedge through all three columns, hinging on the anterior vertebral cortex
Resecting the whole vertebral body and both adjacent discs
items.e: PSO removes a wedge of posterior elements, pedicles and vertebral body and closes it, so the anterior column is not lengthened; this avoids stretching the great vessels.

items.q: Lumbar pedicle subtraction osteotomy for fixed sagittal imbalance is most often performed at L3 because:
o: L3 has the largest pedicles in the spine
It preserves the L3 nerve root
It lies below the conus and near the apex of lumbar lordosis, giving large SVA correction
items.e: L3 is caudal to the conus, so cord manipulation is avoided, and a lower osteotomy moves C7 further posteriorly for the same angular correction.

items.q: In the Schwab anatomical classification of spinal osteotomies, a standard pedicle subtraction osteotomy is grade:
items.e: Grade 1 is partial facet resection, 2 is complete facet (Ponte) resection, 3 PSO, 4 extended PSO including disc, 5 VCR and 6 multilevel VCR.

items.q: Vertebral column resection, compared with other spinal osteotomies, is reserved for:
o: Rigid, severe angular or multiplanar deformities, at the highest neurological risk
items.e: VCR removes one or more entire vertebral segments to correct severe rigid deformity (e.g. congenital kyphoscoliosis, post-tubercular kyphosis) and carries the greatest risk of neurological injury.

items.q: For fixed cervical kyphosis in ankylosing spondylitis, the extension osteotomy is classically performed at C7-T1 because:
o: The C7 pedicles are the largest in the spine
C7 is above the brachial plexus
The vertebral artery usually enters the transverse foramen at C6 and the canal at C7 is relatively wide
items.e: At C7 the vertebral artery normally lies outside the foramen transversarium and the canal is roomy, and C8 root injury is less disabling than injury to higher roots.

items.q: In planning osteotomy for chin-on-chest deformity in ankylosing spondylitis, the target chin-brow vertical angle is approximately:
items.e: A small residual flexion of about 0-10° allows forward gaze and view of the ground; over-correction into extension impairs walking and seeing the floor.

items.q: For restoring segmental lordosis at L5-S1 in a degenerative fusion, which interbody technique typically gives the most lordosis?
items.e: ALIF allows a large lordotic cage after ALL and anterior annulus release; TLIF/PLIF cages placed posteriorly give less lordosis.

items.q: A lumbar fusion is performed with the patient positioned with hips flexed, and the segments are fused in relative kyphosis. The most likely long-term consequence is:
o: Pseudarthrosis at the fused level only
items.e: Fusing in hypolordosis creates PI-LL mismatch, forcing the adjacent segments to hyperextend and accelerating adjacent segment disease and flatback.

items.q: To maximise lumbar lordosis during prone posterior lumbar fusion, the patient is best positioned:
o: With hips and knees flexed on a Wilson frame
On an open frame with hips extended
items.e: Hip extension on an open Jackson-type frame anteverts the pelvis and increases lordosis; hip flexion positions flatten it.

items.q: A 14-year-old with isthmic spondylolisthesis is assessed for risk of slip progression. Which combination of radiographic features most strongly predicts progression?
o: Low pelvic incidence and low slip angle
Normal pelvic incidence with a pars defect at L4
Sacral slope under 35° with a flat back
High pelvic incidence and high slip angle
items.e: High PI and kyphotic lumbosacral angulation (high slip angle) increase shear and predict progression of paediatric isthmic slips.

items.q: The main neurological risk of reducing a high-grade L5-S1 spondylolisthesis is:
items.e: Reduction stretches the L5 root, which is the classic complication; most palsies are partial and recover.

items.q: In the Spinal Deformity Study Group classification of high-grade spondylolisthesis, an 'unbalanced' (retroverted) pelvis is characterised by:
o: High sacral slope and low pelvic tilt
Low sacral slope and high pelvic tilt
Normal pelvic incidence and normal tilt
items.e: In high-grade slips, a retroverted pelvis with high PT and low SS indicates an unbalanced sacropelvis and supports reduction to restore alignment.

items.q: A 62-year-old has an SVA of 3 cm, but pelvic tilt is 34° and pelvic incidence is 60° with lumbar lordosis 25°. The best interpretation is:
o: Sagittal malalignment masked by pelvic retroversion (compensated)
items.e: A normal-looking SVA can hide significant malalignment when the pelvis is maximally retroverted; the PI-LL mismatch of 35° and PT 34° reveal it.

items.q: To accurately assess sagittal alignment, standing full-length lateral radiographs should be taken with the arms positioned:
o: Holding a walking frame in front
With fists resting on the clavicles
items.e: The clavicle position keeps the arms off the spine without the posterior shift caused by arms held straight forward or overhead; arms at the sides obscure the upper spine.

items.q: In a patient with ankylosing spondylitis who has both a fixed lumbar kyphosis and severe bilateral hip flexion contractures from ankylosis, the usual sequence is:
o: Total hip arthroplasties before spinal osteotomy
Spinal osteotomy first, then hip replacement
items.e: Correcting fixed hip flexion first is commonly advised because it restores hip extension, may reduce the spinal correction needed and makes positioning and osteotomy planning more accurate.

items.q: A pedicle subtraction osteotomy has healed poorly with a rod fracture at the osteotomy level. A technique proven to reduce this complication is:
o: Using a single rod on each side of smaller diameter
items.e: Rod fracture and pseudarthrosis concentrate at the PSO; multi-rod constructs (satellite or accessory rods) and interbody support at adjacent levels reduce failure.

items.q: Long-term studies of conventional (non-cross-linked) polyethylene in THA showed that periprosthetic osteolysis became common once linear wear exceeded about:
items.e: Dumbleton's analysis identified an osteolysis threshold of about 0.1 mm/year linear wear for conventional polyethylene; below about 0.05 mm/year osteolysis was rare.

items.q: With conventional polyethylene, increasing the femoral head diameter from 22 mm to 32 mm while keeping the same liner material will typically:
o: Decrease both linear and volumetric wear
Decrease linear wear but increase volumetric wear
Increase linear wear but decrease volumetric wear
Increase both linear and volumetric wear
items.e: Volumetric wear rises with the square of head radius (V = πr²w), whereas linear penetration falls with larger heads; volumetric wear determines the particle load and hence osteolysis.

items.q: After irradiation cross-linking of UHMWPE, thermal 'annealing' below the melting point rather than remelting above it has the main disadvantage of:
o: Markedly reducing crystallinity and fatigue strength
Reversing the cross-links and restoring high wear rates
Making the liner radiolucent and impossible to assess for wear
Leaving residual free radicals that permit later in-vivo oxidation
items.e: Annealing preserves crystallinity and mechanical properties but does not eliminate all free radicals, so oxidation can occur in vivo; remelting removes free radicals at the cost of crystallinity, fatigue strength and toughness.

items.q: Vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol) is blended into or diffused into highly cross-linked polyethylene in order to:
o: Quench residual free radicals and resist oxidation without needing remelting
Act as a lubricant that converts the bearing to fluid-film lubrication
Make the polyethylene radio-opaque so liner wear can be measured
Increase the degree of cross-linking achieved for a given radiation dose
items.e: Vitamin E is an antioxidant that stabilises free radicals, giving oxidative resistance while preserving the mechanical properties that remelting would reduce.

items.q: A retrieved tibial insert that was gamma-irradiated in air and left on the shelf for several years before implantation shows a 'subsurface white band' and delamination. The underlying process is:
o: Ethylene oxide residue damaging the surface
Oxidative embrittlement caused by free radicals reacting with oxygen
Excessive cross-linking from a high radiation dose
Creep of the polyethylene under constant load
items.e: Gamma sterilisation in air creates free radicals that react with oxygen over time (shelf ageing), causing chain scission and a brittle subsurface band prone to fatigue delamination.

items.q: Which method of sterilising UHMWPE components neither cross-links the polymer nor generates free radicals?
o: Gamma irradiation in an inert atmosphere
items.e: Ethylene oxide and gas plasma sterilisation do not produce free radicals or cross-links; all forms of ionising radiation (gamma or electron beam) generate free radicals, even if packaged in inert gas.

items.q: To limit contact stress and delamination, the minimum polyethylene thickness generally recommended for a tibial insert in TKA is about:
items.e: Inserts thinner than about 6–8 mm develop high subsurface contact stresses that promote fatigue cracking and delamination, especially with low-conformity designs.

items.q: Compared with the acetabular liner in THA, the dominant polyethylene wear mechanism in a TKA tibial insert is:
o: Fatigue wear (pitting and delamination) from low conformity and rolling-sliding contact
Third-body wear from cement particles as the usual primary mechanism
Adhesive wear from a highly conforming ball-and-socket articulation
Corrosive wear from fretting of the insert against the femoral component
items.e: The relatively non-conforming knee surfaces with combined rolling and sliding generate high cyclic subsurface stresses, so pitting and delamination predominate; adhesive/abrasive wear dominates in the conforming hip.

items.q: The reported incidence of audible squeaking after modern ceramic-on-ceramic THA is approximately:
items.e: Squeaking occurs in roughly 1–3% of ceramic-on-ceramic hips and is associated with cup malposition, edge loading, stripe wear and impingement.

items.q: MHRA guidance for patients with metal-on-metal hips regards blood cobalt or chromium levels as of concern (warranting further imaging and review) above about:
items.e: A blood level above about 7 µg/L (ppb) of cobalt or chromium indicates potential soft-tissue reaction and calls for cross-sectional imaging and closer follow-up.

items.q: A 54-year-old woman with a metal-on-metal hip resurfacing has groin discomfort and a raised blood cobalt level. The best investigation to detect a pseudotumour and assess the abductors is:
o: MRI with metal artefact reduction sequences (MARS)
items.e: MARS MRI shows solid or cystic pseudotumours and abductor muscle damage; ultrasound is an alternative. Bone scans and radiographs cannot characterise soft-tissue masses.

items.q: Compared with revision of a metal-on-polyethylene THA for simple wear, revision of a metal-on-metal hip for an adverse local tissue reaction with abductor necrosis has:
o: Higher rates of complications such as dislocation and re-revision
Lower complication rates because the bone stock is always preserved
Fewer infections because metal ions are bactericidal
items.e: Revision for ALTR has worse outcomes than revision for other aseptic causes, largely because soft-tissue and abductor destruction lead to instability and further revision.

items.q: In hip simulator studies, which bearing couple shows the lowest volumetric wear rate?
items.e: Ceramic-on-ceramic has the lowest wear of all bearings, with inert particles, because of its hardness, smoothness and excellent wettability.

items.q: A patient with a painful TKA and positive nickel patch testing has a negative infection work-up. Regarding metal hypersensitivity as a cause of TKA failure, current evidence suggests it is:
o: An absolute indication for revision to a ceramic-coated implant
The commonest cause of early revision of TKA
A rare, debated cause that should be a diagnosis of exclusion
Reliably confirmed by a positive skin patch test alone
items.e: True metal hypersensitivity causing TKA failure is rare and controversial; infection, instability, malalignment and loosening must be excluded first, and patch testing correlates poorly with implant outcome.

items.q: In a brachial plexus injury, paralysis of the rhomboids and levator scapulae indicates a lesion involving the nerve that arises directly from the:
items.e: The dorsal scapular nerve arises from the C5 root close to the foramen, so its paralysis places the lesion very proximally (root level, often preganglionic).

items.q: A motorcyclist with a brachial plexus injury has winging of the scapula due to serratus anterior paralysis. This localises the lesion to:
o: The roots, proximal to formation of the trunks
The terminal branches in the axilla
items.e: The long thoracic nerve arises from the C5–C7 roots; serratus paralysis therefore implies a very proximal root-level (often preganglionic) injury.

items.q: The suprascapular nerve, supplying supraspinatus and infraspinatus, arises from which part of the brachial plexus?
items.e: The suprascapular nerve (C5–6) and nerve to subclavius are branches of the upper trunk; testing the spinati therefore helps distinguish a trunk-level from a cord-level lesion.

items.q: Which component of the brachial plexus gives off no named branches?
items.e: The anterior and posterior divisions lie behind the clavicle and give no branches; roots, trunks and cords all have named branches.

items.q: The cords of the brachial plexus are named according to their relationship with the:
o: Coracoid process at the level of the glenoid
Subclavian vein at the first rib
Second part of the axillary artery, deep to pectoralis minor
items.e: The lateral, medial and posterior cords are named by their position around the second part of the axillary artery behind pectoralis minor.

items.q: After an infraclavicular injury, a patient cannot contract latissimus dorsi. The nerve involved arises from the:
items.e: The thoracodorsal nerve (C6–8) to latissimus dorsi is a branch of the posterior cord, along with the subscapular, axillary and radial nerves.

items.q: Paralysis of the clavicular head of pectoralis major with a normal sternal head, together with weak biceps, best localises a plexus lesion to the:
items.e: The lateral pectoral nerve (clavicular head) and musculocutaneous nerve both arise from the lateral cord; the sternal head is supplied mainly by the medial pectoral nerve from the medial cord.

items.q: The medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm is a branch of the:
items.e: The medial cord (C8–T1) gives the medial pectoral nerve, the medial cutaneous nerves of the arm and forearm, the ulnar nerve and the medial root of the median nerve.

items.q: A 'prefixed' brachial plexus is one in which the plexus receives its main contribution from roots:
items.e: A prefixed plexus shifts one level cranially (C4–C8), whereas a postfixed plexus receives C6–T2.

items.q: In traction injuries of the brachial plexus, the C5 and C6 roots are more often ruptured distal to the dorsal root ganglion, whereas C8 and T1 are more often avulsed, mainly because the upper roots:
o: Are anchored by strong transverse radicular ligaments in the gutters of the transverse processes
Are shorter and lie deeper within the spinal canal
Receive a better blood supply from the vertebral artery
items.e: Strong ligamentous attachment of C5–C6 to the transverse processes protects them from avulsion, so they tend to rupture postganglionically; the lower roots lack this support and avulse.

items.q: Six weeks after a closed brachial plexus injury, percussion in the supraclavicular fossa produces tingling radiating down the arm. This suggests:
o: Complete recovery is already under way and no further follow-up is needed
A postganglionic rupture with a proximal stump available for grafting
Injury limited to the terminal branches in the axilla
Root avulsion from the spinal cord
items.e: A positive Tinel sign in the neck indicates viable axons in continuity with the cord at that level, i.e. a postganglionic lesion; it is absent in preganglionic avulsions.

items.q: MRI of the cervical spine after a high-energy brachial plexus injury shows a CSF-filled outpouching at the C8 foramen with absent rootlets. This indicates:
o: Compression of the C8 root by a disc herniation
Postganglionic rupture of the lower trunk
Preganglionic avulsion of the C8 root
items.e: A traumatic pseudomeningocele with absent rootlets indicates root avulsion (preganglionic), which cannot recover spontaneously or be repaired directly.

items.q: Which radiographic finding after trauma most suggests a preganglionic (root avulsion) brachial plexus injury?
o: Fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus
Fracture of the cervical transverse processes
items.e: Transverse process and first rib fractures indicate violent traction on the roots and are associated with avulsion; clavicle and proximal humerus fractures are associated with postganglionic or infraclavicular lesions.

items.q: A chest radiograph of a polytrauma patient with a flail, pulseless arm shows the scapula displaced laterally compared with the opposite side. The diagnosis and its usual prognosis are:
o: Scapulothoracic dissociation, with a poor prognosis for arm function
Scapular body fracture, with excellent recovery
Posterior shoulder dislocation, with full recovery after reduction
Isolated acromioclavicular dislocation, with a good prognosis
items.e: Lateral scapular displacement signifies scapulothoracic dissociation, usually with plexus avulsion and subclavian/axillary vascular injury, and a poor functional outcome.

items.q: In adult traumatic brachial plexus injury, the most common pattern of involvement is:
items.e: Pan-plexus injury accounts for about half to three-quarters of adult traction injuries; isolated lower plexus lesions are rare in adults.

items.q: A worker's arm is caught in a machine and violently pulled upward above his head. Which part of the brachial plexus is most likely to be injured?
items.e: Forced hyperabduction of the arm stretches the lower roots (Klumpke pattern), whereas forcing the head away from a depressed shoulder injures the upper roots.

items.q: After a closed brachial plexus injury, electrodiagnostic studies are usually deferred until about 3–4 weeks because:
o: Sensory nerve action potentials cannot be recorded until reinnervation
Surgery is always performed before 3 weeks, so the study is only for documentation
Nerve conduction studies are dangerous in the first month
Wallerian degeneration must be complete before fibrillations and loss of distal conduction appear
items.e: Distal axons continue to conduct for days after transection and denervation potentials take 2–4 weeks to develop, so studies done too early can be falsely reassuring.

items.q: On EMG after a brachial plexus injury, denervation of the cervical paraspinal muscles indicates:
o: A preganglionic lesion, because the posterior primary rami arise very proximally
An injury of the divisions behind the clavicle
items.e: The paraspinals are supplied by posterior primary rami that branch at the foramen, so their denervation means the injury is at or proximal to the root (avulsion).

items.q: A 28-year-old has a stab wound in the posterior triangle of the neck with complete loss of shoulder abduction and elbow flexion. The recommended management is:
o: Free functioning muscle transfer at 6 months
items.e: Sharp open plexus injuries are explored and repaired immediately (or within days), as the nerve ends are clean and retraction has not occurred.

items.q: A closed traction injury of the upper plexus with a Tinel sign in the neck and no signs of avulsion is being observed. If there is no clinical or EMG recovery, exploration should ideally be performed by:
items.e: Closed postganglionic lesions are observed for about 3 months; without recovery they are explored, ideally before 6 months, as results deteriorate thereafter.

items.q: Nerve transfers to restore biceps function are generally futile when performed 18–24 months after injury because:
o: Wallerian degeneration has not yet occurred
The dorsal root ganglion has died
The motor end plates of denervated muscle have degenerated irreversibly
items.e: Denervated muscle undergoes irreversible fibrosis and loss of motor end plates by about 12–18 months, so late cases need free functioning muscle or tendon transfers.

items.q: In reconstruction of a complete (pan-plexus) brachial plexus injury, the function given highest priority is usually:
items.e: The accepted order is elbow flexion first, then shoulder stability/abduction, then hand sensation, and finally wrist and finger function.

items.q: In the double fascicular (Mackinnon) transfer for elbow flexion, an ulnar fascicle is coapted to the biceps branch and a fascicle of which nerve is transferred to the brachialis branch?
items.e: The double fascicular transfer uses redundant fascicles of the ulnar nerve (to biceps) and median nerve (to brachialis) for stronger elbow flexion than a single transfer.

items.q: In a pan-plexus avulsion with no intraplexal donor available, which extraplexal donor is commonly transferred to the musculocutaneous nerve to restore elbow flexion?
items.e: When all roots are avulsed, extraplexal donors such as intercostal nerves (3rd–5th), the spinal accessory nerve or the phrenic nerve are used; the other options are plexus-derived and unavailable.

items.q: In a complete brachial plexus avulsion, the contralateral C7 root may be used as a donor. The main advantage of this transfer is that it:
o: Is performed through a single short incision in the axilla
Provides a large number of motor axons with minimal lasting deficit in the normal limb
items.e: Contralateral C7 offers abundant axons and its sacrifice usually causes only transient deficits in the normal arm, but it usually needs a long graft and recovery is slow.

items.q: Shoulder arthrodesis for a flail shoulder after brachial plexus injury requires which muscles to be functioning?
items.e: After fusion, shoulder movement occurs through the scapulothoracic articulation, which depends on functioning trapezius and serratus anterior.

items.q: The recommended position for shoulder arthrodesis in a brachial plexus palsy is approximately:
o: 20–30° abduction, 20–30° flexion and about 40° internal rotation
items.e: This position allows the hand to reach the mouth and midline while sitting comfortably at the side; excessive abduction causes scapular winging and pain.

items.q: The Steindler flexorplasty for weak elbow flexion involves:
o: Transfer of latissimus dorsi to the biceps tendon
Transfer of triceps to the biceps tendon
Proximal advancement of the common flexor-pronator origin on the humerus
Free gracilis transfer neurotised by intercostal nerves
items.e: Moving the flexor-pronator origin about 5 cm proximally on the humerus increases its moment arm as an elbow flexor; it needs good forearm flexor strength.

items.q: A patient with a flail, anaesthetic arm and severe deafferentation pain after root avulsions asks for an above-elbow amputation to relieve the pain. The patient should be advised that amputation:
o: Relieves pain only if combined with shoulder fusion
Is the treatment of choice for pain within the first 3 months
items.e: Deafferentation pain arises centrally from avulsed dorsal horn neurons, so amputation does not relieve it; DREZ lesioning is considered for intractable cases.

items.q: During brachial plexus exploration, intraoperative frozen section of a root shows dorsal root ganglion cells within the resected specimen. This indicates:
o: The root has been avulsed, so the DRG lies distal to the injury
A postganglionic rupture suitable for grafting
items.e: Ganglion cells in the stump mean the DRG has been pulled out with the root, i.e. the lesion is preganglionic and the stump cannot be used as a graft source.

items.q: In Horner syndrome after a brachial plexus injury, the sign arises because the T1 root carries:
o: Parasympathetic fibres to the ciliary ganglion
Preganglionic sympathetic fibres destined for the stellate (cervicothoracic) ganglion
Motor fibres to levator palpebrae superioris
items.e: Preganglionic sympathetic outflow to the head leaves via T1 to the stellate ganglion; avulsion of T1 interrupts it, producing ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis and enophthalmos.

items.q: A young motorcyclist lands on his shoulder with his head forced to the opposite side. He has lost shoulder abduction and elbow flexion with normal hand function. The injured roots are:
items.e: Forcing the head away from a depressed shoulder stretches the upper roots, causing an Erb (C5–C6) pattern with loss of abduction, external rotation and elbow flexion.

items.q: A patient with a brachial plexus injury after a motorcycle crash has an absent radial pulse and an expanding supraclavicular haematoma. The immediate priority is:
o: Observation with serial pulse checks for 3 weeks
MRI of the cervical spine to assess for root avulsion
Nerve conduction studies to grade the plexus injury
Emergency vascular repair, with plexus exploration at the same time or later
items.e: Associated subclavian/axillary arterial injury is a limb-threatening emergency requiring urgent repair; the plexus can be explored at the same sitting or later.

items.q: The contractile cell responsible for nodule formation and contracture in Dupuytren disease, identified by alpha-smooth muscle actin staining, is the:
items.e: Dupuytren tissue is driven by myofibroblasts expressing alpha-smooth muscle actin, which contract and lay down collagen. Fibrocytes predominate only in the late, acellular residual stage.

items.q: Which digital fascial structure, lying dorsal to the neurovascular bundle, is characteristically NOT involved in Dupuytren disease?
items.e: Cleland ligaments lie dorsal to the bundle and are spared; Grayson ligaments lie volar to it and contribute to the spiral cord.

items.q: A 62-year-old man with Dupuytren disease cannot spread his ring and little fingers apart; there is a taut transverse band across the distal web. Which cord is responsible?
items.e: The natatory ligament in the distal web becomes the natatory cord, producing a web-space (adduction) contracture.

items.q: After an otherwise complete fasciectomy, a patient has a persistent DIP joint flexion contracture. The cord most likely left behind, lying dorsal to the neurovascular bundle, is the:
items.e: The retrovascular band of Thomine lies dorsal to the bundle and, when diseased, causes DIP contracture that often persists after fasciectomy.

items.q: Which Dupuytren cord produces an isolated MCP joint flexion contracture?
items.e: The pretendinous band in the palm becomes the pretendinous cord, which crosses only the MCP joint and flexes it.

items.q: A PIP joint contracture of the little finger caused by a cord arising from the ulnar side of the hypothenar muscles, inserting on the ulnar base of the middle phalanx, is typically due to the:
items.e: The abductor digiti minimi cord runs along the ulnar border of the little finger to cause PIP contracture and can displace the ulnar neurovascular bundle.

items.q: Which Dupuytren cord has no recognisable normal fascial precursor and arises as a distal continuation of the pretendinous cord into the finger?
items.e: The central cord develops in the midline of the finger as an extension of the pretendinous cord without a normal anatomical band to precede it; it causes PIP contracture.

items.q: The Hueston tabletop test in Dupuytren disease is considered positive when the patient:
o: Feels pain on pressing the palmar nodule
Has tingling on tapping the cord
Cannot place the palm and fingers flat on a table
items.e: Inability to lay the hand flat on a table indicates significant contracture and is a practical indication to offer treatment.

items.q: A ring finger has Dupuytren contractures of 40° at the MCP joint and 60° at the PIP joint, with a normal DIP joint. Its Tubiana stage is:
items.e: Tubiana stages total flexion deformity per ray: stage 1 0-45°, 2 45-90°, 3 90-135°, 4 over 135°. A total of 100° is stage 3.

items.q: MCP joint contractures in Dupuytren disease are usually fully correctable after cord release, unlike PIP contractures, mainly because the MCP joint:
o: Has collateral ligaments that are taut in flexion and so do not shorten
Is not crossed by any diseased cord
items.e: MCP collateral ligaments are tight in flexion, so a flexed MCP joint does not develop secondary capsuloligamentous contracture; the PIP joint develops volar plate, check-rein and collateral contracture.

items.q: The commonest significant adverse event during finger manipulation after collagenase Clostridium histolyticum injection for Dupuytren disease is:
items.e: Skin tears occur in a notable proportion of manipulations and usually heal with dressings; tendon rupture is rare.

items.q: After a collagenase Clostridium histolyticum injection into a Dupuytren cord, finger manipulation to rupture the cord is performed:
items.e: Manipulation under local anaesthesia is done 1-3 days after injection, once the collagen has been enzymatically weakened.

items.q: Flexor tendon rupture after collagenase injection for Dupuytren disease is most associated with injecting a cord at the:
o: PIP level of the little finger
Distal palmar crease over the index finger
items.e: Tendon ruptures have mainly followed PIP-level injections in the ring and little fingers, where the cord lies close to the flexor tendons; injections there must be shallow.

items.q: An 80-year-old man with a 50° MCP contracture of the ring finger from a discrete palmar pretendinous cord wants a quick office procedure with minimal downtime. The best option is:
items.e: Needle fasciotomy suits well-defined palmar cords causing MCP contracture, is office-based under local anaesthesia and allows rapid recovery, accepting higher recurrence.

items.q: Which treatment for Dupuytren contracture has the highest recurrence rate at 5 years?
items.e: Needle fasciotomy recurs in about half or more of patients at 5 years, versus roughly 20-40% after limited fasciectomy and least after dermofasciectomy.

items.q: The UK DISC randomised trial in Dupuytren contracture compared:
items.e: DISC compared collagenase with limited fasciectomy and found surgery slightly better clinically, while collagenase gave faster recovery.

items.q: In Dupuytren surgery, leaving a transverse palmar incision open to heal by secondary intention to reduce haematoma and pain is known as the technique of:
items.e: The McCash open-palm technique leaves the palmar wound open, lowering haematoma, swelling and stiffness, which is helpful in elderly patients.

items.q: At the end of a fasciectomy for a 90° PIP Dupuytren contracture, the finger stays white after the tourniquet is released. The first step is to:
o: Immediately explore and graft both digital arteries
Flex the finger to relieve tension on the digital arteries and warm it
Pin the PIP joint in full extension
items.e: Vasospasm or stretch of chronically shortened digital arteries is common after correcting severe PIP contracture; relax the finger into flexion, warm it and use topical vasodilators before considering microvascular repair.

items.q: The finger most commonly affected by Dupuytren disease is the:
items.e: Frequency is ring > little > middle > thumb > index; index involvement is least common.

items.q: Dupuytren disease in patients with diabetes mellitus typically:
o: Mainly affects the thumb and index finger
Presents with severe PIP contractures of the little finger
Is aggressive with frequent ectopic lesions
Is milder, with nodules affecting the middle and ring fingers
items.e: Diabetic Dupuytren disease tends to be mild, nodular and to involve the middle and ring fingers rather than producing severe contractures.

items.q: Which group of drugs is classically associated with Dupuytren disease?
o: Anticonvulsants such as phenytoin and phenobarbital
items.e: Epilepsy and its treatment with anticonvulsants (phenytoin, phenobarbital) are recognised associations. Fluoroquinolones are associated with tendinopathy rather than Dupuytren disease.

items.q: The growth factor considered central to myofibroblast differentiation and collagen production in Dupuytren disease is:
items.e: TGF-beta drives fibroblast-to-myofibroblast differentiation; PDGF and basic FGF also contribute.

items.q: In Luck's classification, the residual stage of Dupuytren disease is characterised by:
o: Myofibroblasts aligning along lines of tension
Highly cellular nodules of proliferating myofibroblasts
Relatively acellular, tendon-like cords with fibrocytes and mainly type I collagen
items.e: Luck stages are proliferative (cellular nodules), involutional (myofibroblasts align along tension lines) and residual (acellular, tendon-like cords).

items.q: After a ring finger fasciectomy, Dupuytren disease appears 3 years later in the previously untouched little finger. This is best termed:
items.e: Recurrence is new disease within the operated field; disease outside that field is extension.

items.q: A severe, long-standing 100° PIP contracture of the little finger is to be treated by continuous gradual soft-tissue elongation before or instead of fasciectomy. The device used is:
o: A dynamic external fixator (such as TEC or Digit Widget)
A Kirschner wire across the PIP joint
items.e: Continuous elongation with a dynamic external fixator gradually stretches the skin, cord and joint capsule in severe PIP contractures.

items.q: After excision of all Dupuytren cords, a 30° PIP contracture persists. The structures released next are usually the:
items.e: Residual PIP contracture is due to secondary joint contracture; releasing the check-rein ligaments, volar plate and accessory collaterals improves extension while protecting the central slip.

items.q: In caput ulnae syndrome of the rheumatoid wrist, the extensor carpi ulnaris tendon typically:
o: Remains in its groove and stabilises the DRUJ
Subluxes volarly and acts as a wrist flexor
Displaces dorsally over the ulnar head
items.e: Destruction of the ECU subsheath lets the tendon slip volar to the wrist axis, so it flexes the wrist and fails to resist carpal supination and radial deviation.

items.q: In a rheumatoid wrist, pressing down on the prominent dorsal ulnar head makes it depress and spring back up. This sign indicates:
o: Distal radioulnar joint instability with dorsal ulnar head subluxation
items.e: The 'piano key' sign reflects DRUJ and TFCC destruction with dorsal subluxation of the ulnar head in caput ulnae syndrome.

items.q: In the rheumatoid 'zig-zag' deformity of the wrist and hand, the wrist typically deviates:
o: Radially, while the fingers drift ulnarly at the MCP joints
Ulnarly, while the fingers drift radially
items.e: Radial deviation of the metacarpals at the wrist is balanced by ulnar drift of the digits; this wrist deviation must be corrected for MCP procedures to last.

items.q: A woman with rheumatoid arthritis cannot actively extend her middle finger MCP joint, but once the examiner passively extends it she can hold it there. The likely cause is:
o: Volar dislocation of the MCP joint
Ulnar subluxation of the extensor tendon into the gutter between metacarpal heads
Extensor tendon rupture at the wrist
items.e: Sagittal band attenuation allows the tendon to slip off the knuckle; once the joint is put in extension the recentred tendon can hold it. A ruptured tendon or nerve palsy could not maintain extension.

items.q: A rheumatoid patient cannot extend the index MCP joint either actively or passively; radiographs show volar displacement of the proximal phalanx. The cause of extension loss is:
o: Extensor tendon subluxation into the ulnar gutter
MCP joint volar subluxation or dislocation
items.e: Inability to extend even passively points to a joint problem; tendon ruptures, subluxations and nerve palsies leave passive extension intact.

items.q: A rheumatoid patient has attrition rupture of the extensor tendons to the little and ring fingers (EDM and EDC ring/little) only. A common reconstruction is:
o: Free tendon grafts to each finger from palmaris longus
Transfer of FCU to all ruptured tendons
Side-to-side suture of the ring stump to the middle EDC plus EIP transfer to the little finger
items.e: For two ruptured tendons, the ring is sutured to the adjacent intact EDC and EIP is transferred to the little finger; the prominent ulnar head must also be dealt with.

items.q: A rheumatoid patient has ruptured extensor tendons to the middle, ring and little fingers. Adjacent intact tendons are insufficient. A recognised reconstruction uses:
o: Transfer of flexor digitorum superficialis (ring or middle) through the interosseous membrane or around the forearm
Side-to-side suture to the index EDC alone
items.e: When three or more extensors are ruptured, FDS transfers or intercalated grafts are needed because side-to-side suture and EIP alone cannot power the fingers.

items.q: A woman with rheumatoid arthritis suddenly cannot lift her thumb off the table (retropulsion), with no wrist extension loss. The usual tendon transfer is:
o: Extensor indicis proprius to extensor pollicis longus
items.e: EPL rupture at Lister's tubercle is common in RA; EIP-to-EPL transfer is the standard reconstruction.

items.q: During dorsal wrist tenosynovectomy in rheumatoid arthritis, the extensor retinaculum is commonly:
o: Repaired superficial to the tendons under tension
Transposed deep to the extensor tendons to cover the dorsal wrist capsule
Used as a free graft for the EPL
items.e: Placing part of the retinaculum beneath the tendons interposes a smooth layer between tendons and the eroded bone or ulnar head, protecting against attrition rupture; part may be kept superficial to prevent bowstringing.

items.q: For DRUJ destruction in a 40-year-old with rheumatoid arthritis and early ulnar translocation of the carpus, the Sauvé-Kapandji procedure is preferred over Darrach because it:
o: Restores full pronation-supination without a pseudarthrosis
Avoids any osteotomy of the ulna
Preserves the ulnar head as a support for the carpus, preventing ulnar translocation
items.e: Sauvé-Kapandji fuses the DRUJ and creates a proximal ulnar pseudarthrosis, maintaining ulnar-sided carpal support; Darrach excision removes it and suits low-demand elderly patients.

items.q: A recognised problem after Darrach excision of the distal ulna is:
o: Instability and radioulnar convergence of the ulnar stump
items.e: Removing the distal ulna can leave an unstable stump that impinges against the radius (convergence), especially in younger, active patients.

items.q: In rheumatoid arthritis with radiocarpal destruction but a preserved midcarpal joint, which partial arthrodesis prevents progressive ulnar translocation while keeping some wrist motion?
items.e: Radiolunate (Chamay) fusion stabilises the carpus on the radius and stops ulnar translocation, while motion continues through the midcarpal joint.

items.q: A rheumatoid patient needs bilateral total wrist arthrodesis. To help perineal hygiene, a common recommendation is to:
o: Fuse both wrists in marked ulnar deviation
Fuse one wrist in slight flexion (or replace one wrist)
Fuse one wrist in full supination
items.e: With bilateral fusions, one wrist is placed in slight flexion or an arthroplasty is done on one side so that hygiene tasks remain possible.

items.q: The Larsen system is used in rheumatoid arthritis to grade:
o: Disease activity by joint counts and ESR
items.e: Larsen grading describes radiographic damage (0 normal to 5 mutilating destruction); disease activity is measured by scores such as DAS28.

items.q: A silicone (Swanson) MCP joint implant in rheumatoid arthritis functions mainly as a:
o: Flexible spacer stabilised by a fibrous capsule that forms around it
Uncemented surface replacement relying on bone ingrowth
items.e: The one-piece silicone implant is not fixed to bone; it pistons within the canals and is stabilised by encapsulation, so soft-tissue rebalancing is essential.

items.q: In early rheumatoid ulnar drift without joint destruction, a cross-intrinsic transfer involves:
o: Transferring FDS to the central slip
Moving the ulnar intrinsic tendon of one finger to the radial lateral band of the adjacent ulnar finger
Transferring the radial intrinsic to the flexor sheath
Suturing EDC of the index to EIP
items.e: The deforming ulnar intrinsic is released and rerouted to the radial side of the neighbouring finger, converting a deforming force into a corrective one.

items.q: Ulnar subluxation of the extensor tendon at the MCP joint in rheumatoid ulnar drift results mainly from attenuation of the:
items.e: Synovitis stretches the radial sagittal band, letting the extensor slide ulnarly into the intermetacarpal valley, where it becomes an ulnar deviator.

items.q: A rheumatoid swan-neck deformity of the ring finger has a stiff PIP joint with destroyed articular surfaces on radiographs (Nalebuff type IV). Preferred treatment for this finger is:
items.e: Type IV needs a salvage procedure: arthroplasty is favoured in the ring and little fingers for grip, whereas arthrodesis is preferred in the index and middle fingers for stable lateral pinch.

items.q: A rheumatoid swan-neck finger is stiff in all MCP positions, but the PIP joint surfaces are preserved on radiographs (Nalebuff type III). Treatment typically involves:
o: PIP manipulation with lateral band mobilisation and dorsal skin release
items.e: In type III the joint is intact but stiff, so the PIP is gently manipulated, the lateral bands freed to slide volarly, and a dorsal skin release may be needed.

items.q: Intrinsic tightness is confirmed (Bunnell-Littler test) when passive PIP flexion is:
o: The same in all MCP positions
Reduced with the MCP joint extended compared with the MCP joint flexed
Reduced with the MCP joint flexed compared with extended
Increased when the wrist is flexed
items.e: Extending the MCP joint tightens the intrinsics over it, limiting PIP flexion; flexing the MCP relaxes them and PIP flexion improves.

items.q: A rheumatoid PIP joint has a passively correctable boutonniere with about a 35° extension lag and a preserved joint surface (moderate stage). The usual operation is:
o: Central slip reconstruction with dorsal relocation of the lateral bands
items.e: Moderate, correctable boutonniere needs repair of the extensor mechanism; tenotomy suits mild stages and arthrodesis or arthroplasty the fixed, destroyed joint.

items.q: A rheumatoid thumb with CMC joint subluxation, adduction contracture, MCP hyperextension and IP flexion (Nalebuff type III) is usually treated with:
o: Trapeziectomy-based CMC arthroplasty with MCP fusion or volar capsulodesis
items.e: The swan-neck thumb starts at the CMC joint, so CMC arthroplasty with correction of MCP hyperextension (and first web release if needed) is required.

items.q: Early boutonniere (Nalebuff type I) deformity of the rheumatoid thumb, with a passively correctable MCP joint and no joint destruction, can be treated by:
o: MCP synovectomy with EPL rerouting to the base of the proximal phalanx
items.e: Synovitis stretches EPB and the dorsal capsule while EPL slips ulnarly; synovectomy and rerouting EPL to act on the proximal phalanx restores MCP extension. Fixed or destroyed joints need MCP fusion.

items.q: In arthritis mutilans of the thumb (Nalebuff type VI) with bone resorption and 'telescoping', the usual treatment is:
o: Arthrodesis with bone grafting to restore length
items.e: Bone loss leaves no stable joints to replace; fusion with bone graft restores length and stability.

items.q: A radiograph of a psoriatic hand shows a DIP joint with a sharpened distal end of the middle phalanx sitting in a widened, cupped base of the distal phalanx. This appearance is called:
items.e: Pencil-in-cup DIP changes are typical of psoriatic arthritis; gull-wing appearance is erosive OA and rat-bite erosions are gouty.

items.q: Systemic sclerosis typically produces which finger deformity, often with dorsal skin ulceration over the joint?
o: MCP ulnar drift with volar subluxation
items.e: Scleroderma causes PIP flexion contractures with dorsal skin breakdown; PIP arthrodesis with bone shortening is a common treatment.

items.q: Radiographs of the hand in chronic tophaceous gout typically show:
o: Punched-out juxta-articular erosions with overhanging edges
Chondrocalcinosis of the TFCC as the main finding
Symmetric periarticular osteopenia with marginal erosions only
items.e: Well-defined 'rat-bite' erosions with sclerotic overhanging edges and preserved joint space are classic for gout.

items.q: Prophylactic dorsal tenosynovectomy in rheumatoid arthritis is generally advised when:
o: Tenosynovitis persists for about 4-6 months despite adequate medical treatment
items.e: Persistent tenosynovitis despite optimal medical treatment over several months carries a high risk of tendon rupture, so synovectomy is offered before rupture.

items.q: A patient cannot hold the hand at the mouth without abducting the shoulder (the arm must be lifted sideways to bring the hand to the mouth). This positive hornblower's sign indicates loss of function of:
items.e: The hornblower's sign reflects loss of external rotation in abduction, which is provided mainly by teres minor (axillary nerve). Supraspinatus loss causes weakness of abduction initiation, not a hornblower's sign.

items.q: Teres minor, the main external rotator with the arm abducted, is supplied by the:
items.e: Teres minor is supplied by the posterior branch of the axillary nerve (C5-C6). The lower subscapular nerve supplies subscapularis and teres major, and the suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus.

items.q: A patient with a painful shoulder cannot bring the hand behind the back, so the lift-off test cannot be done. Which test is the best alternative to assess subscapularis?
items.e: The belly-press test assesses subscapularis with the hand on the abdomen and needs little internal rotation; a deficient subscapularis lets the elbow drop back behind the trunk. Lift-off requires enough internal rotation to place the hand behind the back.

items.q: In the Jobe (empty can) test for supraspinatus, the arm is held in:
o: 90 degrees of elevation in the scapular plane with full internal rotation (thumb pointing down)
90 degrees of abduction in the coronal plane with full external rotation
Full forward flexion with the elbow extended and palm up
20 degrees of abduction with the elbow flexed at 90 degrees
items.e: The Jobe test applies downward resistance to the arm elevated 90 degrees in the scapular plane with the thumb down, isolating supraspinatus. The arm at 20 degrees abduction with the elbow flexed is the position for the external rotation lag sign.

items.q: Anatomical studies of the supraspinatus footprint on the greater tuberosity report a mean medial-to-lateral width of approximately:
items.e: The supraspinatus footprint is about 12-13 mm wide medial to lateral, which is the basis for restoring footprint coverage with double-row or suture-bridge repairs. Partial tears involving over 6 mm of thickness (about half the tendon) are Ellman grade 3.

items.q: Codman's 'critical zone', a relatively hypovascular area where degenerative supraspinatus tears often begin, is located:
o: At the musculotendinous junction near the glenoid
On the bursal surface over the coracoid
About 1 cm proximal to the insertion on the greater tuberosity
At the rotator interval next to the biceps pulley
items.e: Codman described a hypovascular critical zone about 1 cm proximal to the supraspinatus insertion, although the concept of hypovascularity is debated. It is not at the musculotendinous junction, which is the site of Cho type 2 re-tears after double-row repair.

items.q: In the coronal plane, the rotator cuff stabilises the glenohumeral joint by forming a force couple in which the deltoid is balanced by:
o: The inferior cuff muscles (subscapularis, infraspinatus and teres minor)
items.e: The coronal force couple pits the upward pull of the deltoid against the depressing action of the inferior cuff (subscapularis, infraspinatus, teres minor), keeping the humeral head centred. Trapezius and serratus form the scapular rotation couple, not the glenohumeral one.

items.q: In the transverse (axial) plane, the rotator cuff force couple that keeps the humeral head centred is formed by:
o: Subscapularis anteriorly against infraspinatus and teres minor posteriorly
Long head of biceps against triceps
items.e: In the axial plane, subscapularis anteriorly balances infraspinatus and teres minor posteriorly. A tear that unbalances this couple, such as a posterosuperior tear extending into infraspinatus and teres minor, can cause pseudoparalysis.

items.q: Ultrasound studies of asymptomatic volunteers show that the prevalence of full-thickness rotator cuff tears in people over 80 years old is roughly:
items.e: Asymptomatic full-thickness tears become more common with age, reaching about 25% in people over 60 and about 50% in people over 80. A tear found on imaging in an older patient may therefore not be the cause of the symptoms.

items.q: A low critical shoulder angle (below about 30 degrees) on a true AP radiograph is associated with:
items.e: A small CSA (under about 30 degrees) is associated with primary glenohumeral osteoarthritis, whereas a large CSA (over about 35 degrees) is associated with degenerative cuff tears because of a greater superior shear force.

items.q: In Bigliani's original study of cadaveric acromial shapes, the commonest acromial morphology was:
items.e: Type II (curved) was the commonest shape in Bigliani's series, while type III (hooked) was most strongly associated with full-thickness cuff tears. Type IV was a later addition by other authors.

items.q: In the Ellman classification, a partial-thickness tear on the subacromial side of the supraspinatus is classified as type:
items.e: Ellman types are A (articular), B (bursal) and C (interstitial). Bursal-sided tears are linked to extrinsic subacromial impingement, whereas articular-sided tears such as the PASTA lesion are commoner overall.

items.q: An articular-sided partial supraspinatus tear measures 4 mm deep on MRI. Its Ellman grade is:
items.e: Ellman grade 1 is under 3 mm, grade 2 is 3-6 mm and grade 3 is over 6 mm (more than half the tendon thickness). A grade 2 tear is usually treated non-operatively or by debridement rather than repair.

items.q: According to Gerber's definition, a rotator cuff tear is 'massive' when there is:
o: A tear over 1 cm in any dimension
A complete tear of at least two tendons
Retraction to the humeral head on coronal MRI
items.e: Gerber defined a massive tear as a complete tear of two or more tendons; DeOrio and Cofield instead use a size over 5 cm. Retraction to the humeral head is Patte stage 2, not a definition of a massive tear.

items.q: At arthroscopy, a crescent-shaped supraspinatus tear has a short medial-to-lateral dimension and its edge reaches the footprint easily. The appropriate repair is:
o: Direct repair of the tendon edge to the bone footprint
items.e: Crescent tears are mobile from medial to lateral and are repaired directly to bone. Margin convergence is used first for U-shaped tears, whose apex lies far medially.

items.q: On coronal MRI, a supraspinatus tendon stump has retracted to lie over the humeral head but not as far as the glenoid. Its Patte stage is:
items.e: Patte stage 1 lies close to the insertion, stage 2 at the level of the humeral head and stage 3 at the glenoid. Greater retraction is linked to lower reparability and a higher re-tear rate.

items.q: In the Goutallier classification, a supraspinatus muscle that still contains more muscle than fat (but more than just some fatty streaks) is grade:
items.e: Goutallier grade 1 has some fatty streaks, grade 2 has more muscle than fat, grade 3 equal fat and muscle and grade 4 more fat than muscle. Grades 3-4 predict poor healing and a high re-tear rate.

items.q: The Goutallier classification of rotator cuff fatty infiltration was originally described using:
items.e: Goutallier described fatty degeneration on CT in 1994; Fuchs later adapted the grading to MRI, which is now used in practice.

items.q: On a sagittal oblique MRI at the most lateral image where the scapular spine joins the scapular body, a line is drawn between the superior borders of the coracoid and the scapular spine. The supraspinatus belly lies wholly below this line. This 'positive tangent sign' indicates:
items.e: A positive tangent sign (supraspinatus not crossing the line) indicates muscle atrophy and predicts a poorer chance of successful repair. It does not identify partial tears or calcific deposits.

items.q: In Lafosse's classification of subscapularis tears, type V is:
o: A complete tear with eccentric (anterosuperior) humeral head position and fatty degeneration
A partial tear of the upper third
A complete tear of the upper third
A complete tear of the whole tendon with a centred humeral head
items.e: Lafosse type IV is a complete tear with the head still centred, while type V has eccentric head position (subluxation) and fatty degeneration, signalling a usually irreparable tear.

items.q: A painful arc on active abduction caused by subacromial impingement or a supraspinatus lesion is typically felt between:
o: 30 and 45 degrees only in external rotation
items.e: Subacromial pain typically occurs between about 60 and 120 degrees of abduction, when the greater tuberosity passes under the coracoacromial arch. Pain in the last 30 degrees (above about 150 degrees) suggests an acromioclavicular joint source.

items.q: A patient's pain on passive forward flexion with the arm internally rotated is abolished after 10 mL of lidocaine is injected into the subacromial space. This positive result is called the:
items.e: The Neer sign is pain on passive forward flexion with internal rotation; relief of that pain after subacromial local anaesthetic is the Neer test, confirming a subacromial source.

items.q: On a true AP radiograph, an acromiohumeral interval of 4 mm in a patient with a chronic cuff tear most strongly suggests:
o: A massive, probably irreparable cuff tear
items.e: An acromiohumeral interval under 7 mm suggests a cuff tear, and under 5 mm suggests a massive, often irreparable tear with superior migration of the head. Frozen shoulder gives normal radiographs.

items.q: For detecting a small articular-sided partial-thickness rotator cuff tear, the most sensitive imaging investigation is:
items.e: Intra-articular contrast in MR arthrography fills articular-sided defects and increases sensitivity for partial articular tears. Plain radiographs and CT do not show tendon tears.

items.q: For diagnosing a full-thickness rotator cuff tear, ultrasound performed by an experienced operator compared with MRI has:
o: Much lower accuracy and should not be used
Higher accuracy for muscle fatty infiltration
Similar accuracy, with the advantage of dynamic assessment
No ability to measure tear size
items.e: In experienced hands ultrasound has similar accuracy to MRI for full-thickness tears and allows dynamic testing at low cost, but it is operator-dependent and less good for fatty infiltration and labral pathology.

items.q: The FIMPACT trial (Paavola et al., BMJ 2018) of patients with subacromial pain found that arthroscopic subacromial decompression compared with diagnostic arthroscopy alone:
o: Gave much better pain relief at 2 years
Reduced the rate of later rotator cuff tears
Was superior only in patients with a hooked acromion
Gave no clinically important difference in outcomes
items.e: FIMPACT, like CSAW, found subacromial decompression no better than diagnostic arthroscopy (a placebo surgery), so the routine role of acromioplasty for subacromial pain is limited.

items.q: A 50-year-old has a symptomatic articular-sided partial supraspinatus tear involving about 30% of the tendon thickness, not improved by 6 months of physiotherapy. The usual surgical treatment is:
o: Arthroscopic debridement with or without acromioplasty
Completion of the tear and double-row repair
items.e: Partial tears under about 50% of the thickness are usually debrided (with or without acromioplasty), whereas tears over 50% (Ellman grade 3) are repaired by transtendon repair or completion and repair.

items.q: A 45-year-old labourer falls on an outstretched arm and has an acute traumatic full-thickness supraspinatus tear with marked weakness. The recommended timing of repair is:
o: After at least 6 months of physiotherapy
Only once fatty infiltration reaches Goutallier grade 2
items.e: Acute traumatic tears in active patients are repaired early, ideally within about 3-6 weeks, before the tendon retracts and the muscle develops atrophy and fatty infiltration. A trial of physiotherapy is reserved for chronic degenerative tears.

items.q: In the MOON prospective cohort (Kuhn et al., 2013) of patients with atraumatic full-thickness rotator cuff tears treated with a structured physiotherapy programme, approximately what proportion avoided surgery at 2 years?
items.e: About three-quarters of MOON patients with atraumatic full-thickness tears improved with physiotherapy and did not choose surgery at 2 years, so a trial of rehabilitation is reasonable for chronic degenerative tears.

items.q: An untreated degenerative full-thickness supraspinatus tear is more likely to enlarge over time if it:
o: Involves the anterior rotator cable and is symptomatic
items.e: About half of full-thickness tears enlarge over several years; progression is commoner with symptomatic tears, larger tears and tears that disrupt the anterior attachment of the rotator cable.

items.q: After double-row rotator cuff repair, a re-tear at the musculotendinous junction medial to the medial row, with tendon tissue left attached at the footprint, is classified as:
items.e: Cho type 2 re-tears occur medial to the medial row at the musculotendinous junction and are characteristic of double-row or suture-bridge repairs. Cho type 1 re-tears occur at the footprint and are commoner after single-row repair.

items.q: Compared with patients whose rotator cuff repair has healed on MRI, patients with an MRI-confirmed re-tear typically have:
o: Severe pain and worse outcomes than before surgery
Often good pain relief but lower strength
Identical strength and function in every study
items.e: Many patients with a re-tear still have good pain relief and satisfaction, but healed repairs have better strength and functional scores. Re-tear does not usually make the patient worse than before surgery.

items.q: Randomised trials comparing early with delayed passive motion after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair have shown:
o: Early motion greatly reduces re-tear rates in large tears
Delayed motion leads to permanent stiffness in most patients
Broadly similar outcomes, with a possible higher re-tear risk from early motion in larger tears
items.e: Outcomes are broadly similar whether passive motion starts early or is delayed; early motion may raise re-tear risk in larger tears while giving slightly faster return of range. Most protocols use a sling for about 4-6 weeks.

items.q: After a biceps tenotomy performed during rotator cuff repair in a 70-year-old, the most common cosmetic consequence is:
items.e: Tenotomy lets the long head of biceps retract distally, causing a Popeye deformity and sometimes cramping. Tenodesis is preferred in younger or cosmetically concerned patients to avoid this.

items.q: During arthroscopic debridement of a massive irreparable rotator cuff tear in an elderly patient, the surgeon avoids acromioplasty and coracoacromial ligament release mainly to prevent:
o: Anterosuperior escape of the humeral head
items.e: With a deficient cuff, the coracoacromial arch is the last restraint to superior migration; releasing it can cause anterosuperior escape of the humeral head, which is very hard to salvage.

items.q: In Mihata's original technique of superior capsular reconstruction for an irreparable supraspinatus tear, the graft used was:
o: Fascia lata autograft about 6-8 mm thick
items.e: Mihata used a thick fascia lata autograft (about 6-8 mm) fixed from the superior glenoid to the greater tuberosity to restore superior stability. Acellular dermal allograft is a common alternative, but it is thinner.

items.q: The START:REACTS randomised trial (Metcalfe et al., Lancet 2022) compared arthroscopic debridement plus a subacromial balloon spacer with debridement alone for irreparable cuff tears. It found:
o: The balloon spacer gave much better function at 12 months
The balloon spacer reduced the need for reverse arthroplasty
No benefit from the balloon; function was slightly worse with it
The balloon was superior only in patients with pseudoparalysis
items.e: START:REACTS found no benefit of the InSpace balloon over debridement alone, with outcomes slightly favouring debridement alone, so the balloon is not recommended routinely.

items.q: Latissimus dorsi transfer to the greater tuberosity for an irreparable posterosuperior cuff tear gives poor results and is relatively contraindicated when there is:
o: A positive external rotation lag sign
items.e: Latissimus dorsi transfer needs an intact or repairable subscapularis to balance the transverse force couple; subscapularis deficiency predicts failure. An ER lag sign and infraspinatus fatty degeneration are the usual indications, not contraindications.

items.q: Compared with latissimus dorsi transfer, the advantage of lower trapezius transfer (Elhassan) for an irreparable posterosuperior cuff tear is that it:
o: Has a line of pull closer to infraspinatus and contracts in phase with external rotation
Can be done without any incision
items.e: The lower trapezius has a vector similar to infraspinatus and is in phase with external rotation, which makes retraining easier. It usually needs an Achilles tendon allograft (or other graft) to reach the greater tuberosity.

items.q: During pectoralis major transfer for an irreparable subscapularis tear, passing the transferred tendon behind (deep to) the conjoint tendon gives a more anatomical vector but puts which nerve at particular risk?
items.e: The musculocutaneous nerve enters coracobrachialis a few centimetres below the coracoid, so routing the pectoralis major tendon deep to the conjoint tendon can compress or stretch it.

items.q: A 76-year-old has a massive cuff tear with pseudoparalysis and early cuff tear arthropathy (superior migration with acetabularisation of the acromion). The most predictable treatment to restore elevation is:
items.e: Reverse total shoulder arthroplasty restores elevation in elderly patients with pseudoparalysis and cuff tear arthropathy by medialising and lowering the centre of rotation to tension the deltoid. Anatomical TSA fails without a functioning cuff.

items.q: Pseudoparalysis of the shoulder in a massive rotator cuff tear is defined as:
o: Full active and passive motion with weakness only
Loss of both active and passive external rotation
Pain-free elevation but positive hornblower's sign
Active forward elevation less than 90 degrees despite full passive range
items.e: Pseudoparalysis is active elevation under 90 degrees with full passive range and no neurological cause. Loss of both active and passive external rotation instead suggests frozen shoulder or arthritis.

items.q: Calcific tendinitis of the rotator cuff is caused by deposition of:
items.e: Calcific tendinitis results from cell-mediated deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite, mostly in supraspinatus of women aged 30-50, and is not a degenerative process. Calcium pyrophosphate deposition causes chondrocalcinosis and pseudogout.

items.q: A 42-year-old woman has chronic shoulder pain from a 15 mm calcific deposit in supraspinatus that has not settled with physiotherapy. Which treatment has the best evidence before surgery?
items.e: Ultrasound-guided barbotage has the strongest evidence among minimally invasive options for chronic calcific tendinitis; ESWT is an alternative, and arthroscopic excision is reserved for failures.

items.q: In the Gärtner radiographic classification of calcific tendinitis, a cloudy, translucent deposit with ill-defined edges (type III) indicates that the deposit is most likely in the:
items.e: Gärtner type III deposits are fluffy and translucent, typical of the resorptive phase, which is the most acutely painful and often resolves on its own. Type I deposits are dense and well-defined (formative).

items.q: A 52-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes has 4 months of shoulder pain and stiffness. Radiographs are normal. The clinical hallmark that distinguishes frozen shoulder from a rotator cuff tear is:
o: A painful arc with full range
Loss of passive external rotation with the arm at the side
items.e: Adhesive capsulitis causes loss of both active and passive motion, especially passive external rotation at the side, with normal radiographs. A cuff tear causes weakness with preserved passive motion.

items.q: An alert, sober 30-year-old driver is brought in after a rear-end collision. He has no midline cervical tenderness and no neurological deficit, but has a painful closed femoral shaft fracture. Under the NEXUS criteria, cervical spine imaging is:
o: Not required, because there is no midline tenderness
Required, because a painful distracting injury is present
Required only if he is older than 65 years
Not required if he can actively rotate his neck 45 degrees each way
items.e: A painful distracting injury is one of the five NEXUS criteria, so its presence alone mandates imaging. Neck rotation testing belongs to the Canadian C-spine rule, not NEXUS.

items.q: Under the Canadian C-spine rule, which single factor places an alert trauma patient in the high-risk group that mandates imaging regardless of other findings?
o: Having been ambulatory at any time at the scene
Sitting position in the emergency department
items.e: High-risk factors are age 65 or more, a dangerous mechanism and limb paraesthesia. The other options are low-risk factors that allow safe assessment of neck range of motion.

items.q: In a patient classified as low risk by the Canadian C-spine rule, cervical imaging can be omitted if the patient is able to actively rotate the neck:
o: 30 degrees to the left and right
45 degrees to the left and right
60 degrees to the left and right
90 degrees to the left and right
items.e: The final step of the Canadian C-spine rule is active rotation of 45 degrees to each side; if achieved, no imaging is needed.

items.q: A 45-year-old is alert after a high-speed car crash and has midline cervical tenderness. The initial imaging investigation of choice is:
o: Multidetector CT of the cervical spine
items.e: CT is the first-line imaging in adult cervical trauma because radiographs miss many injuries, especially at the craniocervical and cervicothoracic junctions. Flexion-extension views are unsafe and unhelpful acutely.

items.q: On a lateral cervical radiograph or CT, a Powers ratio (basion-posterior arch distance divided by opisthion-anterior arch distance) greater than 1 indicates:
items.e: A Powers ratio over 1 means the occiput has shifted forward on the atlas, i.e. anterior atlanto-occipital dislocation. The ratio is insensitive to purely longitudinal or posterior dissociation.

items.q: According to Harris's 'rule of 12', atlanto-occipital dissociation is suggested when the basion-dens interval exceeds:
items.e: Both the basion-dens interval and the basion-axial interval should be under 12 mm on a lateral radiograph; values above this suggest craniocervical dissociation.

items.q: Atlanto-occipital dissociation is relatively more common (and more often survived) in children than in adults mainly because children have:
o: An unossified dens that cannot resist translation
A relatively large head and small, horizontally oriented occipital condyles
A transverse ligament that is ossified and brittle
items.e: The disproportionately large head and flat, horizontal occipital condyles of young children make the craniocervical junction vulnerable to dissociation.

items.q: CT in a child after a high-speed crash shows atlanto-occipital dissociation. Which initial measure must be avoided?
items.e: Traction distracts an already dissociated craniocervical junction and can cause catastrophic neurological deterioration. Definitive treatment is occipitocervical fusion.

items.q: In the Traynelis classification of atlanto-occipital dislocation, type II refers to:
o: Anterior displacement of the occiput on the atlas
Posterior displacement of the occiput on the atlas
Rotatory displacement of the occiput with an intact tectorial membrane
Longitudinal (vertical) distraction of the occiput from the atlas
items.e: Traynelis type I is anterior, type II is longitudinal (distraction) and type III is posterior displacement of the occiput relative to the atlas.

items.q: A young man dives into a shallow pool and strikes the vertex of his head on the bottom. CT shows fractures of both the anterior and posterior arches of C1 with lateral spread of the lateral masses. The mechanism is:
items.e: The Jefferson burst fracture is caused by axial load driving the occipital condyles into the lateral masses, splitting the ring at both arches.

items.q: Neurological injury is uncommon after an isolated Jefferson fracture of the atlas because:
o: The spinal cord at C1 has no blood supply that can be injured
The fragments displace outwards, enlarging the spinal canal
The dens always protects the cord from displacement
items.e: In a burst of the C1 ring the lateral masses spread centrifugally, widening rather than narrowing the canal.

items.q: MRI after a C1 ring fracture shows a midsubstance tear of the transverse atlantal ligament (Dickman type I). The recommended treatment is:
items.e: Midsubstance TAL ruptures do not heal with immobilisation and leave atlantoaxial instability, so C1-C2 fusion is advised. Dickman type II (bony avulsion) injuries often heal with external immobilisation.

items.q: MRI and CT show that the transverse atlantal ligament has avulsed a fragment of bone from the medial tubercle of the C1 lateral mass (Dickman type II). The appropriate initial management is:
o: No immobilisation, since the injury is always stable
items.e: Bony avulsion injuries of the TAL heal in about three-quarters of cases with rigid orthosis or halo; fusion is reserved for persistent instability.

items.q: A 50-year-old has an isolated fracture of the posterior arch of C1 after a fall, with an intact transverse ligament on MRI. Management is:
items.e: Stable C1 fractures with an intact TAL heal reliably with external immobilisation.
