items.q: In anterior bony ankle impingement ('footballer's ankle'), osteophytes form on the anterior distal tibia and the talar neck. Pain is typically reproduced by:
o: Forced passive dorsiflexion of the ankle
Forced passive plantarflexion of the ankle
items.e: The anterior tibial and talar neck osteophytes 'kiss' in dorsiflexion; forced plantarflexion instead provokes posterior impingement (os trigonum).

items.q: An anterocentral portal for ankle arthroscopy is generally avoided because it lies between the extensor hallucis longus and extensor digitorum longus tendons, endangering the:
o: Dorsalis pedis artery and deep peroneal nerve
Superficial peroneal nerve and peroneus tertius
Saphenous nerve and great saphenous vein
Sural nerve and short saphenous vein
items.e: The anterior tibial (dorsalis pedis) artery and deep peroneal nerve lie between EHL and EDL at the ankle, so central anterior portals are avoided in favour of anteromedial and anterolateral portals.

items.q: For posterior hindfoot endoscopy (two-portal technique of van Dijk), the patient is prone. The posterolateral and posteromedial portals are placed:
o: Behind the peroneal tendons and behind the medial malleolus at the joint line
On either side of the tibialis posterior tendon 2 cm above the medial malleolus
Just lateral and just medial to the Achilles tendon, at the level of the tip of the lateral malleolus
Through the Achilles tendon at its insertion
items.e: Both posterior portals are made immediately adjacent to the Achilles tendon at the level of the lateral malleolar tip; working lateral to FHL keeps the instruments away from the tibial neurovascular bundle.

items.q: An os trigonum is formed by failure of fusion of the secondary ossification centre of which part of the talus?
o: Medial tubercle of the posterior talar process
Lateral tubercle of the posterior talar process
items.e: The os trigonum is the unfused lateral (posterolateral) tubercle of the posterior process; an elongated but fused lateral tubercle is the Stieda process.

items.q: On a lateral ankle radiograph of a dancer with posterior ankle pain, the lateral tubercle of the posterior talar process is elongated and continuous with the talus, without a separate ossicle. This is called a:
items.e: A Stieda process is an elongated, fused lateral tubercle; like an os trigonum, it can be compressed between the posterior tibia and calcaneus in forced plantarflexion.

items.q: A ballet dancer's great toe catches in flexion and then snaps into extension when she rises from en pointe, owing to a nodular FHL tendon at the entrance of its fibro-osseous tunnel. This triggering is called:
items.e: Hallux saltans is triggering of the great toe from FHL stenosing tenosynovitis at the fibro-osseous tunnel behind the talus, classically in ballet dancers.

items.q: A 66-year-old man has had a painless foot slap for 4 months from a degenerative rupture of tibialis anterior. He is active and wants surgery; at exploration the tendon ends cannot be brought together. Appropriate treatment is:
o: Reconstruction with an interposition free tendon graft or tendon transfer (e.g. EHL)
items.e: Chronic tibialis anterior ruptures with a gap are reconstructed with an interposition graft (e.g. semitendinosus) or tendon transfer such as EHL; arthrodesis is not needed for an isolated tendon deficit. Low-demand patients can be managed with an AFO.

items.q: Tibialis anterior inserts onto the:
o: Dorsal base of the fifth metatarsal
Medial and plantar surfaces of the medial cuneiform and base of the first metatarsal
Plantar base of the second metatarsal
items.e: Tibialis anterior inserts on the medial-plantar medial cuneiform and first metatarsal base, close to the insertion of peroneus longus on the plantar-lateral side of the same bones.

items.q: A 48-year-old runner who had a steroid injection for plantar fasciitis 3 weeks ago feels a sudden tearing pain under the heel while running, followed by plantar bruising. Usual management is:
o: Protected weight bearing in a boot followed by rehabilitation
Urgent open repair of the plantar fascia
items.e: Acute plantar fascia rupture, often after corticosteroid injection, is treated non-operatively with a period in a boot or cast and gradual return to activity.

items.q: Peak forces through the Achilles tendon during running have been estimated at approximately how many times body weight?
items.e: In-vivo measurements show Achilles loads of up to about 12 times body weight during running, making it the strongest tendon in the body.

items.q: The Achilles tendon footprint is located on the:
o: Upper (superior) third of the posterior calcaneal surface
Plantar medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity
Middle third of the posterior surface of the calcaneal tuberosity
items.e: The tendon inserts on the middle third of the posterior calcaneal surface; the upper third is covered by the retrocalcaneal bursa, which separates it from the tendon.

items.q: The Krackow stitch, often used for core suturing in open Achilles tendon repair, is characterised by:
o: A single transverse mattress suture through the tendon end
A series of interlocking (locking) loops running along each side of the tendon
A purse-string suture around the paratenon
Two figure-of-eight sutures through bone tunnels
items.e: The Krackow suture uses multiple locking loops along the tendon margins, giving high pull-out strength; an epitendinous running suture is usually added.

items.q: During open repair of an acute Achilles rupture, the correct repair tension is best set by:
o: Repairing with the ankle in maximal plantarflexion
Repairing with the ankle in neutral (90 degrees)
Tensioning until the Thompson test is negative
Matching the resting plantarflexion of the uninjured ankle with the patient prone and knees flexed
items.e: The resting tension should be restored to match the natural plantarflexion of the contralateral side (as in the Matles position); overtightening or elongation both impair function, and elongation weakens push-off.

items.q: A 26-year-old man has bilateral thickened, nodular, painless Achilles tendons and xanthelasma. His father had a myocardial infarction at 45. The most likely underlying diagnosis is:
items.e: Achilles tendon xanthomas are characteristic of familial hypercholesterolaemia (LDL receptor defects) and are associated with premature coronary disease; lipid profile is the key test.

items.q: In a randomised trial by Beyer and colleagues (2015) in chronic mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy, eccentric training was compared with which other loading programme, showing similar clinical results?
items.e: Heavy slow resistance training (three times weekly) gave outcomes similar to Alfredson eccentric training, with better patient satisfaction and compliance.

items.q: In Rompe's randomised trial (2008) in chronic insertional Achilles tendinopathy, which treatment gave better results than eccentric loading at 4 months?
o: Corticosteroid injection into the retrocalcaneal bursa
items.e: Low-energy shock wave therapy was more effective than eccentric loading for insertional tendinopathy, where eccentric drops into dorsiflexion are less effective than in mid-portion disease.

items.q: On a lateral radiograph, the Fowler-Philip angle used in assessing a Haglund deformity is formed between the plantar surface line of the calcaneus and a line tangential to the posterior surface of the calcaneal tuberosity. Which value is generally regarded as abnormal?
items.e: A Fowler-Philip angle over about 75 degrees suggests a prominent posterosuperior calcaneus, although correlation with symptoms is imperfect; parallel pitch lines are an alternative measurement.

items.q: On MRI of the ankle, the peroneal tendons show increased signal where they curve around the tip of the lateral malleolus on short-TE (T1/proton density) sequences only, with normal calibre and normal T2 signal. This most likely represents:
items.e: Tendons oriented at about 55 degrees to the main magnetic field show artefactual high signal on short-TE sequences (magic angle effect); it disappears on long-TE T2 images, unlike true tendinopathy or tears.

items.q: A 50-year-old has painful os peroneum syndrome with a fractured os peroneum and degenerative peroneus longus tendon at the cuboid notch. If non-operative treatment fails, a usual operation is:
o: Superior peroneal retinaculum repair with groove deepening
Excision of the os peroneum fragments with tenodesis of peroneus longus to peroneus brevis
Transfer of peroneus longus to the navicular
items.e: Symptomatic os peroneum fractures or peroneus longus degeneration are treated by excision and repair or, if the tendon is poor, tenodesis of peroneus longus to brevis.

items.q: A professional footballer has an acute first-time dislocation of the peroneal tendons. Surgical repair of the superior peroneal retinaculum is often preferred over cast immobilisation mainly because:
o: Non-operative treatment fails (with recurrent instability) in about half of cases
The peroneal tendons rupture if left dislocated for 48 hours
Casting requires 6 months of non-weight bearing
items.e: Cast immobilisation succeeds in only about 50% of acute peroneal dislocations, so early SPR repair is often chosen in athletes; chronic cases need SPR repair with groove deepening.

items.q: The superior peroneal retinaculum, the primary restraint to peroneal tendon subluxation, extends from the posterolateral ridge of the fibula to the:
items.e: The SPR runs from the posterolateral fibula to the lateral calcaneus (and blends with the Achilles sheath); its avulsion from the fibula allows the tendons to dislocate anteriorly.

items.q: The retro-Achilles (subcutaneous calcaneal) bursa, inflamed in 'pump bump', lies:
o: Between the Achilles tendon and the posterosuperior calcaneus
Between the plantar fascia and the calcaneus
Deep to FHL behind the talus
Between the skin and the posterior surface of the distal Achilles tendon
items.e: The subcutaneous bursa lies superficial to the tendon and is irritated by rigid heel counters; the retrocalcaneal bursa lies deep, between the tendon and the posterosuperior calcaneus.

items.q: In V-Y advancement for a chronic Achilles rupture, how long should the limbs of the inverted V in the gastrocnemius aponeurosis be relative to the defect?
o: Equal to the length of the defect
At least about 1.5-2 times the length of the defect
Half the length of the defect
Fixed at 3 cm regardless of the defect
items.e: Abraham and Pankovich recommended that the arms of the V be at least one and a half times (often up to twice) the defect so that the aponeurosis can slide distally enough to close the gap.

items.q: Mini-open jig-based Achilles repair systems (such as Achillon or PARS) aim to reduce sural nerve injury compared with free-hand percutaneous techniques mainly by:
o: Placing all sutures through the lateral border of the tendon
Passing the sutures through a guide inserted within the paratenon through a small incision
Repairing the tendon with the knee extended
items.e: The guide is introduced inside the paratenon so the transverse sutures pass through the tendon without catching the sural nerve outside the sheath, combining small incisions with fewer nerve injuries.

items.q: A 24-year-old runner has exertional posteromedial ankle pain and a soft-tissue mass between the Achilles tendon and the medial malleolus that becomes firm on plantarflexion. MRI shows a mass isointense to muscle. The most likely diagnosis is:
o: Ganglion of the tibialis posterior sheath
items.e: An accessory soleus is an anomalous muscle presenting as a posteromedial ankle mass in young adults, sometimes with exertional pain; MRI showing muscle signal distinguishes it from a tumour.

items.q: Isolated gastrocnemius contracture (positive Silfverskiöld test) has been associated with several foot disorders. Which is one of them?
items.e: A tight gastrocnemius increases forefoot loading and is linked with metatarsalgia, plantar fasciitis, Achilles tendinopathy, progressive collapsing foot deformity and midfoot arthritis.

items.q: A skull radiograph of a 66-year-old shows a large, sharply marginated lytic area in the frontal and occipital bones with no surrounding sclerosis. Alkaline phosphatase is raised. This appearance is termed:
o: Osteoporosis circumscripta of lytic-phase Paget disease
items.e: Osteoporosis circumscripta is the well-demarcated lytic (hot) phase of Paget disease in the skull; myeloma gives multiple small punched-out lesions without raised ALP.

items.q: A 24-year-old with fever and night sweats has a dense, sclerotic L2 vertebral body of normal size with anterior scalloping. The most likely cause is:
items.e: An ivory vertebra of normal size with anterior scalloping in a young adult suggests lymphoma; in Paget disease the ivory vertebra is enlarged and patients are usually elderly.

items.q: On plain radiographs, the single most useful feature distinguishing a sclerotic pagetic vertebra from an osteoblastic prostate metastasis is:
o: Increased density of the vertebral body
Enlargement of the vertebral body in Paget disease
items.e: Paget disease enlarges the bone with cortical thickening and coarse trabeculae; metastases cause sclerosis without enlargement, and both are dense and hot on bone scan.

items.q: A 74-year-old with long-standing pelvic Paget disease has new severe pain. On MRI, which finding most strongly favours sarcomatous change over uncomplicated Paget disease?
o: Preserved fatty marrow signal throughout the lesion
Replacement of normal marrow fat signal with a soft-tissue mass
items.e: Uncomplicated Paget disease preserves marrow fat on MRI; loss of marrow fat, cortical destruction and a soft-tissue mass point to Paget sarcoma.

items.q: Electron microscopy of pagetic osteoclasts classically shows which finding, underlying the viral hypothesis of the disease?
o: Nucleocapsid-like inclusions resembling paramyxovirus in the nuclei
items.e: Paramyxovirus-like nucleocapsid inclusions in osteoclast nuclei led to the measles/RSV/canine distemper hypothesis, which remains unproven; absent ruffled borders are typical of osteopetrosis.

items.q: Osteoclasts in Paget disease are enlarged and may contain up to about how many nuclei, compared with up to about 10 normally?
items.e: Pagetic osteoclasts are increased in number and size, with up to around 100 nuclei, and are hyper-responsive to RANKL and vitamin D.

items.q: Multifocal giant cell tumours arising in pagetic bone of the skull and facial bones are notable because they may regress with:
items.e: Giant cell tumours complicating Paget disease (mainly skull and facial bones) are often multifocal and may respond to steroids such as dexamethasone.

items.q: Etidronate is now considered obsolete for Paget disease mainly because at therapeutic doses it:
o: Causes osteonecrosis of the jaw in most patients
Is strongly nephrotoxic even at low doses
Is ineffective at lowering alkaline phosphatase
Impairs mineralisation and can cause osteomalacia
items.e: High-dose etidronate inhibits mineralisation as well as resorption, producing osteomalacia; nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates such as zoledronate do not do this at standard doses.

items.q: A patient with active Paget disease also has chronic liver disease, making total ALP unreliable. Which formation marker is most useful to assess Paget activity?
items.e: P1NP is a bone formation marker raised in active Paget disease and useful when liver disease or limited monostotic disease makes ALP unreliable; calcium and PTH are usually normal.

items.q: A 60-year-old has classic radiographic features of monostotic Paget disease of one tibia, but serum ALP is normal. The correct interpretation is:
o: The diagnosis must be fibrous dysplasia
A normal ALP does not exclude limited monostotic Paget disease
A normal ALP means the disease is in the sclerotic burnt-out phase only
Biopsy is mandatory before any diagnosis
items.e: ALP reflects extent and activity; limited monostotic disease may give a normal ALP, and biopsy is reserved for diagnostic doubt or suspected sarcoma.

items.q: The ZiPP trial (2024) of zoledronic acid in people with SQSTM1 mutations but no established Paget disease showed that prophylactic treatment:
o: Had no effect on lesion development
Reduced the development of new pagetic lesions
Caused widespread osteonecrosis of the jaw
items.e: ZiPP found that prophylactic zoledronate in SQSTM1 carriers reduced new lesions, an evolving area distinct from the PRISM conclusion about treating established asymptomatic disease.

items.q: In Paget disease, the femur characteristically bows:
items.e: Pagetic femora bow anterolaterally and tibiae anteriorly; fissure fractures develop on the convex (tension) side of the bow.

items.q: Which combination of hip changes is typical of Paget disease involving the pelvis and proximal femur?
o: Coxa magna with a short neck
Posterior acetabular wall deficiency with coxa valga
items.e: Softened pagetic bone allows medial migration of the femoral head (protrusio) and varus bending of the neck, leading to secondary hip OA.

items.q: Apart from heavy bleeding, which complication is particularly increased after total hip arthroplasty in Paget disease and may warrant prophylaxis?
items.e: Paget disease increases the risk of heterotopic ossification after hip arthroplasty, so prophylaxis (NSAID or radiotherapy) is often considered.

items.q: A 72-year-old with a markedly bowed pagetic femur sustains a transverse subtrochanteric 'banana' fracture. The preferred fixation is:
o: A dynamic hip screw with a short side plate
Cephalomedullary nailing, with corrective osteotomy if needed to pass the nail
items.e: Intramedullary fixation, often after corrective osteotomy to straighten the bow, is preferred; plates and short implants fail frequently in weak, bowed pagetic bone.

items.q: The approximate 5-year survival of patients with sarcoma arising in Paget disease is:
items.e: Paget sarcoma, usually osteosarcoma in the pelvis, femur or humerus, carries a very poor prognosis with 5-year survival below about 10%.

items.q: The risk of sarcomatous transformation in patients with Paget disease of bone is approximately:
items.e: Sarcoma complicates about 1% or fewer of patients, more with extensive polyostotic disease; new, severe, progressive pain is the warning sign.

items.q: A 78-year-old with Paget disease affecting much of the skeleton develops breathlessness, a bounding pulse and warm limbs. The likely cardiac complication is:
o: High-output cardiac failure from arteriovenous shunting in pagetic bone
Complete heart block from septal calcification
items.e: Extensive hypervascular pagetic bone behaves like multiple arteriovenous shunts and can, rarely, cause high-output cardiac failure.

items.q: The highest prevalence of Paget disease of bone has historically been reported in:
items.e: Paget disease is commonest in the UK, especially Lancashire, and in populations of British descent; it is rare in Asia (including India), Africa and Scandinavia.

items.q: Softening of the skull base in Paget disease may cause the odontoid to project upward into the foramen magnum. This complication is:
items.e: Basilar invagination in pagetic skull can cause brainstem compression and obstructive hydrocephalus.

items.q: A patient with symptomatic active Paget disease cannot receive bisphosphonates because of intolerance. The traditional second-line drug, with only a short-lived effect, is:
items.e: Calcitonin is second-line for Paget disease when bisphosphonates cannot be used; teriparatide is contraindicated in Paget disease because of osteosarcoma risk.

items.q: After a 5 mg zoledronic acid infusion for painful Paget disease, treatment response is best monitored by:
o: Repeat isotope bone scan at 6 weeks
Serum alkaline phosphatase at 3-6 months and then yearly
items.e: ALP is the routine marker of Paget activity; re-treatment is considered if pain recurs with a rising ALP.

items.q: A 40-year-old with primary hyperparathyroidism from four-gland hyperplasia also has a prolactinoma and a pancreatic gastrinoma. The syndrome is:
items.e: MEN 1 (menin gene) combines parathyroid hyperplasia with pituitary and pancreatic tumours; MEN 2B rarely involves the parathyroids.

items.q: A 50-year-old has serum calcium of 3.6 mmol/L (14.4 mg/dL), a very high PTH and a palpable hard neck mass. The most likely parathyroid pathology is:
items.e: Very high calcium, markedly raised PTH and a palpable neck mass suggest parathyroid carcinoma, which causes under 1% of primary hyperparathyroidism.

items.q: A 35-year-old has lifelong mild hypercalcaemia, high-normal PTH and a urinary calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio below 0.01. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Low urinary calcium excretion identifies benign FHH, which does not need parathyroidectomy; primary hyperparathyroidism usually has normal or high urinary calcium.

items.q: Once biochemical primary hyperparathyroidism is confirmed, which imaging is used to localise the adenoma before surgery?
o: Technetium-99m sestamibi scan with neck ultrasound
items.e: Sestamibi scintigraphy combined with neck ultrasound localises the overactive gland to guide focused parathyroidectomy.

items.q: In primary hyperparathyroidism, bone mineral density is usually reduced most at which site?
items.e: PTH excess predominantly resorbs cortical bone, so the distal radius falls most while the trabecular lumbar spine is relatively preserved.

items.q: A hypercalcaemic 55-year-old has resorption of the distal clavicles, loss of the lamina dura around the teeth and erosion of the terminal phalangeal tufts. The underlying condition is:
items.e: Subperiosteal resorption at the radial middle phalanges, acro-osteolysis, distal clavicular resorption and loss of the lamina dura are classic signs of hyperparathyroidism.

items.q: A renal transplant recipient with years of prior dialysis develops hypercalcaemia with a very high PTH that persists after transplantation. The diagnosis and usual treatment are:
items.e: Long-standing secondary hyperparathyroidism can become autonomous, causing hypercalcaemia (tertiary HPT), usually treated surgically.

items.q: In patients on dialysis today, which form of renal osteodystrophy is the most common?
items.e: Adynamic bone disease, with low PTH and low turnover (diabetes, over-suppression with calcium and vitamin D), is now the commonest pattern.

items.q: Historically, osteomalacia in patients on long-term dialysis was most often caused by accumulation of:
items.e: Aluminium from dialysate and aluminium-based phosphate binders deposited at the mineralisation front, causing low-turnover osteomalacia.

items.q: A patient on haemodialysis for 15 years develops bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome and cystic lesions in the femoral heads. The deposited protein is:
items.e: Dialysis-related amyloidosis is due to beta-2 microglobulin, which is poorly cleared by dialysis and causes carpal tunnel syndrome, bone cysts and destructive spondyloarthropathy.

items.q: A 45-year-old on long-term haemodialysis rises from a chair and sustains simultaneous ruptures of both quadriceps tendons. The most relevant predisposing factor is:
o: Chronic kidney disease with secondary hyperparathyroidism
items.e: Spontaneous, often bilateral, quadriceps or patellar tendon ruptures are a recognised complication of CKD and secondary hyperparathyroidism.

items.q: A patient with CKD stage 5 develops exquisitely painful violaceous skin plaques progressing to necrosis on the thighs. Biopsy shows calcification of small arterioles. The condition is:
items.e: Calciphylaxis results from arteriolar calcification in CKD-mineral bone disorder and causes painful skin ischaemia and necrosis with high mortality.

items.q: In CKD-mineral bone disorder with hyperphosphataemia and vascular calcification, a non-calcium phosphate binder is:
items.e: Sevelamer and lanthanum bind phosphate without adding calcium load, unlike calcium salts; aluminium binders are avoided long term because of toxicity.

items.q: Besides raised plasma pyridoxal-5-phosphate, which urinary finding supports the diagnosis of hypophosphatasia?
items.e: Deficient tissue-nonspecific ALP allows its substrates (phosphoethanolamine, PLP and inorganic pyrophosphate) to accumulate.

items.q: A 50-year-old with adult hypophosphatasia has a painful incomplete pseudofracture of the lateral subtrochanteric femoral cortex. The preferred surgical stabilisation is:
items.e: Femoral pseudofractures in hypophosphatasia, like atypical femoral fractures, are best stabilised with an intramedullary nail because plates tend to fail.

items.q: The fundamental biochemical defect in scurvy is impaired:
o: Hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in procollagen
Cross-linking of elastin by lysyl oxidase due to copper deficiency
items.e: Vitamin C is a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases; without it collagen is weak and osteoid formation fails, which is an osteoblast defect rather than a mineralisation defect.

items.q: In infantile scurvy, the lucent metaphyseal band lying just beneath the dense white line of Frankel is called the:
items.e: The Trummerfeld (scurvy) zone is a lucent band of weak trabeculae beneath the dense zone of provisional calcification (white line of Frankel).

items.q: An infant has bilateral symmetrical erosions of the medial proximal tibial metaphyses with periostitis. This sign points to:
items.e: The Wimberger sign of congenital syphilis is medial proximal tibial metaphyseal erosion; the Wimberger ring of scurvy is a sclerotic rim around the epiphysis.

items.q: A 4-year-old with autism who eats only biscuits refuses to walk and cries when the legs are moved. Radiographs show ground-glass osteopenia, a dense metaphyseal line with spurs and sclerotic rims around the epiphyses. The deficiency is:
items.e: Pseudoparalysis from subperiosteal haemorrhage, the white line of Frankel, Pelkan spurs and Wimberger rings are classic of scurvy, seen with restricted diets.

items.q: Skeletal fluorosis becomes endemic where the fluoride concentration of drinking water exceeds about:
items.e: WHO places the safe upper limit near 1.5 mg/L; endemic fluorosis occurs in parts of Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh/Telangana, Gujarat, Punjab and Karnataka.

items.q: A 45-year-old from an endemic region of Rajasthan has spinal stiffness and a spastic gait. Radiographs show diffuse osteosclerosis and calcification of the forearm interosseous membrane. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Diffuse sclerosis with calcification of interosseous membranes and ligaments in an endemic area is characteristic of fluorosis, which can cause compressive myelopathy.

items.q: The earliest clinical sign of fluoride toxicity in children of endemic areas is:
items.e: Dental fluorosis appears first in children whose teeth develop during exposure; skeletal changes and myelopathy follow with prolonged exposure.

items.q: A young man of Ashkenazi Jewish descent with splenomegaly and thrombocytopenia has Erlenmeyer flask deformities of the distal femora. The deficient enzyme is:
items.e: Gaucher disease is caused by glucocerebrosidase deficiency; skeletal features include Erlenmeyer flask femora, osteonecrosis and bone crises.

items.q: A 16-year-old with known Gaucher disease has acute severe thigh pain, fever and a raised ESR. MRI shows marrow oedema without a fluid collection. The best management is:
o: Analgesia, hydration and rest, avoiding surgical drainage
Immediate core decompression of the femur
items.e: Gaucher bone crises mimic osteomyelitis but are ischaemic; surgery risks introducing infection, so management is supportive.

items.q: A short, obese child with a round face, subcutaneous ossification and short fourth and fifth metacarpals has low calcium, high phosphate and high PTH. The underlying defect is:
o: Autoimmune destruction of the parathyroid glands
GNAS mutation causing end-organ resistance to PTH
Activating mutation of the calcium-sensing receptor
items.e: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1a with Albright hereditary osteodystrophy results from GNAS mutation; PTH is high because the target organs do not respond.

items.q: A child has the Albright hereditary osteodystrophy phenotype with short fourth metacarpals but normal calcium, phosphate and PTH. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism shares the AHO phenotype with normal biochemistry and arises when the GNAS mutation is inherited from the father.

items.q: A woman with Graves disease and exophthalmos has digital clubbing and spiculated periosteal new bone along the metacarpals and phalanges. This is:
items.e: Thyroid acropachy is a rare manifestation of Graves disease, with clubbing and periosteal new bone in the hands, usually alongside ophthalmopathy and pretibial myxoedema.

items.q: A 10-year-old with untreated hypothyroidism has short stature and fragmented, irregular ossification of both femoral capital epiphyses. The likely explanation is:
items.e: Hypothyroidism delays skeletal maturation and causes fragmented epiphyses that mimic bilateral Perthes disease; checking thyroid function avoids misdiagnosis.

items.q: On a lateral foot radiograph, which measurement supports a diagnosis of acromegaly?
o: Heel pad thickness greater than about 23 mm
items.e: Soft-tissue overgrowth in acromegaly thickens the heel pad beyond about 22-25 mm, along with spade-like terminal tufts.

items.q: A 3-year-old with pica has dense transverse bands at the metaphyses of the distal femur and proximal tibia, wider than the normal provisional calcification zone, including the proximal fibula. The most likely cause is:
items.e: Lead lines are dense metaphyseal bands from lead deposition at sites of rapid growth; involvement of the proximal fibula helps distinguish them from normal dense lines.

items.q: Type I (postmenopausal) osteoporosis, compared with type II (senile) osteoporosis, predominantly causes:
o: Trabecular bone loss with vertebral body and distal radius fractures
Cortical bone loss with hip fractures in those over 80
Equal loss in men and women over 70
items.e: Oestrogen deficiency mainly removes trabecular bone, giving vertebral and distal radius fractures; senile osteoporosis affects both cortical and trabecular bone and causes hip fractures.

items.q: The commonest cause of secondary osteoporosis is:
items.e: Glucocorticoids are the commonest secondary cause; they suppress osteoblast function and raise fracture risk at relatively preserved BMD.

items.q: Serum urate above which concentration exceeds the saturation point of monosodium urate at normal body temperature and pH?
items.e: MSU saturates at about 6.8 mg/dL (about 405 micromol/L); above this crystals can form, although most hyperuricaemic people never develop gout.

items.q: Humans are prone to hyperuricaemia compared with most mammals because they lack which enzyme?
items.e: Humans lack functional uricase, so urate is the end product of purine metabolism; pegloticase and rasburicase are recombinant uricases.

items.q: Approximately what proportion of patients with primary hyperuricaemia have it because of reduced renal excretion rather than overproduction?
items.e: Under-excretion accounts for about 90% of hyperuricaemia; overproduction (myeloproliferative disease, tumour lysis, enzyme defects) for about 10%.

items.q: A 40-year-old man who drinks illicitly distilled spirits stored in lead-lined containers develops gout, hypertension and renal impairment. This form of gout is called:
items.e: Chronic lead exposure impairs renal urate excretion and causes saturnine gout, classically with nephropathy and hypertension.

items.q: Gout preferentially affects the first metatarsophalangeal joint mainly because:
o: The joint has the highest synovial blood flow in the body
The joint contains no hyaline cartilage
Lower peripheral temperature and degenerative cartilage favour urate crystallisation
Urate is actively secreted into foot synovium
items.e: MSU solubility falls at lower temperatures, and crystals form preferentially in cool peripheral joints and damaged cartilage such as the first MTP.

items.q: Approximately what proportion of first gout attacks involve the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra)?
items.e: Podagra is the presenting site in about half of first attacks and is involved in about 90% of patients at some stage.

items.q: Under the 2015 ACR/EULAR gout classification criteria, which single finding is sufficient to classify a patient as having gout without the weighted score?
o: Monosodium urate crystals in a symptomatic joint, bursa or tophus
items.e: MSU crystals in a symptomatic joint, bursa or tophus are the sufficient criterion; otherwise a weighted score of 8 or more classifies gout.

items.q: In the 2015 ACR/EULAR gout classification criteria, what total score on the weighted domains classifies a patient as having gout when crystals have not been identified?
items.e: A total score of at least 8 (out of 23) across clinical, laboratory and imaging domains classifies gout.

items.q: According to ACR 2020, urate-lowering therapy is strongly recommended in a patient with gout who has:
o: A single first flare and serum urate of 7.5 mg/dL
Two or more flares per year
items.e: Strong indications are one or more tophi, radiographic damage due to gout, or two or more flares per year; asymptomatic hyperuricaemia is generally not treated.

items.q: After a first gout flare, ACR 2020 conditionally recommends starting urate-lowering therapy if the patient also has:
o: Chronic kidney disease stage 3 or worse, serum urate above 9 mg/dL or urolithiasis
Involvement of the first MTP joint
items.e: First-flare patients with CKD stage 3 or worse, urate over 9 mg/dL or urolithiasis are conditionally recommended to start ULT.

items.q: When allopurinol is started for gout, anti-inflammatory flare prophylaxis (for example low-dose colchicine) is recommended for how long?
items.e: Urate lowering mobilises crystals and provokes flares, so prophylaxis for 3-6 months is advised.

items.q: Allopurinol is titrated to a target serum urate. Its active metabolite, which is renally excreted and accumulates in CKD, is:
items.e: Allopurinol is metabolised by xanthine oxidase to oxypurinol, which is long-acting, renally excreted and accumulates in CKD, hence low starting doses and gradual titration.

items.q: Febuxostat lowers serum urate by:
o: Non-purine selective inhibition of xanthine oxidase
Inhibiting URAT1 in the proximal tubule
items.e: Febuxostat is a non-purine xanthine oxidase inhibitor; URAT1 inhibition is the uricosuric mechanism of probenecid, and allantoin conversion is by uricase.

items.q: Pegloticase is used for refractory chronic tophaceous gout. To reduce loss of response due to anti-drug antibodies, it is co-prescribed with:
items.e: Methotrexate co-therapy reduces anti-pegloticase antibodies and infusion reactions; oral ULT is stopped because it masks loss of response.

items.q: Which dietary factor is associated with a lower serum urate and lower gout risk?
items.e: Low-fat dairy and coffee are associated with lower urate; beer, fructose drinks, red and organ meats and shellfish raise it.

items.q: Which alcoholic drink carries the highest risk of precipitating gout because it contains purines (guanosine) as well as alcohol?
items.e: Beer has the strongest association with gout, combining alcohol-induced lactate (reducing urate excretion) with a high purine content.

items.q: Which of the following is a recognised cause of hyperuricaemia due to urate overproduction?
o: Tumour lysis after chemotherapy for leukaemia
items.e: Tumour lysis releases nucleic acids and causes overproduction; low-dose aspirin, hypothyroidism and ketosis cause under-excretion.

items.q: Glycogen storage disease type I (von Gierke disease) causes early-onset gout through:
o: Isolated reduction of tubular urate secretion only
Both increased urate production and reduced excretion due to lactic acidaemia
items.e: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency increases purine turnover and causes lactic acidosis that competes with urate excretion.

items.q: A chronic tophus at the wrist is a recognised cause of which neurological complication?
o: Posterior interosseous nerve palsy at the arcade of Frohse
items.e: Tophaceous deposits in the flexor tenosynovium can compress the median nerve; tophi may also cause cubital tunnel syndrome and tendon rupture.

items.q: A 62-year-old man with long-standing tophaceous gout has painful end-stage arthritis of the first MTP joint with large erosions. The most reliable operation is:
items.e: First MTP fusion is the standard operation for destroyed gouty first MTP joints; cheilectomy is for early hallux rigidus and implants fare poorly with erosive disease.

items.q: Surgical debulking of tophi is particularly prone to which complication?
o: Delayed wound healing and chronic sinus formation
Reflex sympathetic dystrophy in all cases
items.e: Skin over tophi is thin and poorly vascular, so wound breakdown and draining sinuses are common after tophus surgery.

items.q: Familial calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease with early-onset chondrocalcinosis is associated with mutations in which gene, encoding a pyrophosphate transporter?
items.e: ANKH mutations increase extracellular pyrophosphate and cause familial CPPD (CCAL2); ALPL mutations cause hypophosphatasia.

items.q: Hypophosphatasia predisposes to calcium pyrophosphate deposition because deficiency of tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase leads to accumulation of:
items.e: Alkaline phosphatase normally hydrolyses inorganic pyrophosphate; its deficiency raises pyrophosphate, which combines with calcium to form CPP crystals.

items.q: A 48-year-old has acute pseudogout of the knee. Which group of blood tests best screens for the metabolic associations of CPPD?
o: Calcium, magnesium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, ferritin/transferrin saturation and TSH
Serum urate, HLA-B27 and ASO titre
items.e: Onset under 60 warrants screening for haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, hypomagnesaemia, hypophosphatasia and possibly hypothyroidism.

items.q: Which surgical procedure is a classic trigger for acute pseudogout in the early postoperative period?
items.e: The rapid fall in serum calcium after parathyroidectomy is a well-known trigger of acute CPP crystal arthritis.

items.q: The joint most commonly involved in acute calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis (pseudogout) is the:
items.e: Pseudogout most often affects the knee, followed by the wrist; the first MTP is typical of gout.

items.q: An 82-year-old woman presents with acute severe neck pain, rotation restricted, fever and raised CRP. Meningism is suspected but CSF is normal. CT shows curvilinear calcification around the odontoid. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Crowned dens syndrome is CPP (or BCP) deposition around the dens, especially in the transverse ligament, mimicking meningitis or polymyalgia in the elderly.

items.q: Severe isolated degeneration of the radiocarpal joint, with no history of trauma, in a 70-year-old should prompt suspicion of:
items.e: Primary OA rarely affects the radiocarpal joint; OA in atypical joints (radiocarpal, isolated patellofemoral, glenohumeral, MCP) suggests CPPD.

items.q: A 72-year-old woman has polyarticular symmetrical arthritis of the wrists and MCP joints with morning stiffness and raised ESR. Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP are negative and radiographs show chondrocalcinosis of the TFCC. The EULAR term for this presentation is:
items.e: Chronic CPP crystal inflammatory arthritis (formerly pseudo-rheumatoid) mimics RA with symmetrical polyarthritis and raised inflammatory markers.

items.q: The commonest symptomatic form of calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease is:
items.e: OA with CPPD is the commonest symptomatic presentation, typically in atypical joints with prominent osteophytes and cysts.

items.q: Which wrist pattern of arthritis is associated with calcium pyrophosphate deposition through degeneration of an intercarpal ligament?
items.e: CPPD is associated with scapholunate ligament degeneration and scapholunate advanced collapse (SLAC), as well as STT arthritis.

items.q: On ultrasound, calcium pyrophosphate deposition in hyaline cartilage characteristically appears as:
o: A hyperechoic band on the cartilage surface (double contour sign)
Hyperechoic spots within the substance of the cartilage layer
Posterior acoustic enhancement deep to cartilage
items.e: CPP deposits are within the cartilage, whereas urate coats the surface producing the double contour sign.

items.q: Which statement about the treatment of calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease is correct?
o: Allopurinol dissolves CPP crystals over 12 months
Magnesium supplementation reliably dissolves established chondrocalcinosis in all patients
No currently available drug dissolves CPP crystals
items.e: Unlike gout, there is no crystal-dissolving therapy for CPPD; treatment controls inflammation and addresses underlying disease.

items.q: In addition to the knee menisci and triangular fibrocartilage, which site is a classic location for radiographic chondrocalcinosis?
items.e: Chondrocalcinosis is classically seen in the knee menisci, TFCC, symphysis pubis, acetabular labrum and intervertebral discs.

items.q: Calcific tendinitis of the rotator cuff most commonly affects which group?
o: Men over 70 with massive cuff tears
items.e: Calcific tendinitis is commonest in women aged 30-60, is cell-mediated rather than degenerative, and is not associated with full-thickness cuff tears.

items.q: In Uhthoff's description of calcific tendinitis, the most painful stage, when the deposit is toothpaste-like and invaded by macrophages and vessels, is the:
o: Formative phase of the calcific stage
Resorptive phase of the calcific stage
items.e: The resorptive phase is the most painful; the deposit becomes soft and ill-defined and may rupture into the subacromial bursa.

items.q: On a shoulder radiograph, a calcific deposit in the supraspinatus is translucent, cloudy and poorly defined. In the Gartner classification this is:
o: Type III, likely to resolve spontaneously
items.e: Gartner type III deposits are translucent and ill-defined, reflecting the resorptive phase with a good chance of spontaneous resolution; type I is dense and well circumscribed.

items.q: Calcific deposits in supraspinatus are typically located:
o: At the musculotendinous junction under the acromion
On the articular surface of the footprint only
About 1-1.5 cm from the greater tuberosity insertion
items.e: Deposits typically lie in the critical zone about 1-1.5 cm proximal to the insertion on the greater tuberosity.

items.q: A 45-year-old woman has 4 months of shoulder pain from a dense, well-defined 15 mm supraspinatus calcific deposit despite physiotherapy and a subacromial injection. Which minimally invasive treatment has good evidence for pain relief?
items.e: Ultrasound-guided barbotage and high-energy ESWT are effective for persistent calcific tendinitis; arthroscopic removal is reserved for failure of about 6 months of conservative care.

items.q: Acute calcific tendinitis of the longus colli presents with:
o: Acute low back pain and sciatica
Acute neck pain and odynophagia with prevertebral soft-tissue swelling and calcification anterior to C1-C2
Shoulder pain with external rotation weakness
items.e: Longus colli (retropharyngeal) calcific tendinitis causes acute neck pain and painful swallowing, with calcification anterior to C1-C2; it is self-limiting with NSAIDs.

items.q: Synovial fluid from a chronic rheumatoid knee effusion contains flat rectangular plates with notched corners. These are:
items.e: Cholesterol crystals form flat plates with notched corners in chronic effusions such as long-standing RA.

items.q: A patient develops a painful knee effusion within 24 hours of an intra-articular steroid injection. Aspiration shows irregular birefringent crystals and negative Gram stain. The likely cause is:
items.e: Corticosteroid crystals can cause a self-limiting post-injection flare within 24-48 hours; infection usually presents later and must still be excluded with culture.

items.q: Which radiographic feature favours gout over rheumatoid arthritis in the hands?
o: Preserved bone density and preserved joint space until late
Marginal erosions in the bare area without sclerosis
items.e: Gout spares bone density and joint space until late; periarticular osteopenia, symmetric distribution and bare-area marginal erosions without sclerosis suggest RA.

items.q: In acute crystal arthritis, synovial fluid white cell count is usually:
items.e: Crystal arthritis gives inflammatory fluid (about 2,000-50,000/mm3) and can exceed 50,000, overlapping with septic arthritis, so culture is always needed.

items.q: A 70-year-old has an acutely painful knee 4 days after total knee arthroplasty; aspirate shows weakly positively birefringent rhomboid crystals and 40,000 WBC/mm3. The correct statement is:
o: Crystals confirm pseudogout and infection can be excluded
High-dose colchicine alone without further tests is adequate
Crystals do not exclude infection, so fluid must be cultured before attributing symptoms to CPPD
items.e: Crystals and infection can coexist, including in prosthetic joints; culture is mandatory before attributing the effusion to crystal arthritis.

items.q: In the AGREE trial, low-dose colchicine for acute gout was compared with high-dose colchicine and found to be:
o: Equally effective with far fewer gastrointestinal side effects
items.e: AGREE showed 1.8 mg over one hour was as effective as the old high-dose regimen with much less diarrhoea.

items.q: Under ACR 2020, if a patient presents during a gout flare and has indications for urate-lowering therapy, the recommended approach is:
o: Delay ULT for at least 3 months after the flare settles
ULT may be started during the flare provided anti-inflammatory flare cover is given
Avoid ULT if urate is normal during the flare
items.e: ACR 2020 conditionally allows starting ULT during a flare with concomitant anti-inflammatory prophylaxis, rather than waiting.

items.q: In haemochromatosis-associated arthropathy with chondrocalcinosis, which treatment corrects the iron overload but does not reverse established chondrocalcinosis or arthropathy?
items.e: Venesection treats iron overload but established CPP deposits and arthropathy usually persist or progress.

items.q: Milwaukee shoulder syndrome is best treated, when symptoms are severe and the cuff is irreparable with superior head migration, by:
items.e: Milwaukee shoulder behaves like cuff tear arthropathy; reverse arthroplasty is used for severe cases after conservative measures fail.

items.q: The anterior talofibular ligament takes origin from the anterior border of the lateral malleolus at about:
o: 1 cm proximal to the fibular tip
The very tip of the fibula
4 cm proximal to the fibular tip
The posterior border of the fibula
items.e: The ATFL arises about 1 cm proximal to the tip of the fibula and inserts on the talar body just anterior to the lateral articular facet. The tip of the fibula is the origin of the CFL.

items.q: A grade III lateral ankle sprain implies:
o: Stretching of the ATFL without macroscopic tear
Isolated partial tear of the ATFL
Complete rupture of both the ATFL and the CFL
Avulsion of the PTFL with an intact ATFL
items.e: Grade I is a stretch, grade II a partial (ATFL) tear, and grade III a complete tear of the ATFL and CFL.

items.q: The calcaneofibular ligament is closely related to which structures that lie directly superficial to it?
o: The sural nerve and short saphenous vein only
The peroneal tendons, for which it forms the floor of the sheath
items.e: The extracapsular CFL runs deep to the peroneus longus and brevis tendons, forming the floor of their sheath, so peroneal pathology frequently accompanies CFL injury.

items.q: A snowboarder sustains a forced dorsiflexion-inversion injury and is tender just distal and anterior to the tip of the lateral malleolus. Radiographs are reported as normal and he is told it is a sprain. Which fracture is classically missed in this setting?
o: Medial tubercle of the posterior talar process
items.e: The 'snowboarder's fracture' of the lateral talar process is easily missed on plain films and needs CT; displaced fragments are fixed or excised to avoid subtalar arthritis.

items.q: In a patient with chronic lateral ankle instability and a cavovarus foot, the hindfoot corrects to valgus when the lateral forefoot stands on a Coleman block. The best bony procedure to add to the ligament repair is:
o: Dorsiflexion osteotomy of the first metatarsal
items.e: Correction of hindfoot varus on the Coleman block shows the varus is forefoot-driven (plantarflexed first ray) and flexible, so a first metatarsal dorsiflexion osteotomy addresses the driver; a rigid hindfoot varus would need a lateralising calcaneal osteotomy.

items.q: A seated athlete crosses the injured leg over the opposite knee so that the mid-calf rests on it; gentle downward pressure on the medial side of the knee reproduces pain at the distal tibiofibular joint. This is the:
items.e: The crossed-leg test compresses the proximal tibia and fibula and separates them distally, stressing the syndesmosis. The Kleiger test is external rotation of the foot with the knee flexed.

items.q: A rugby player has persistent anterolateral ankle pain months after an external rotation injury; conventional non-weight-bearing radiographs and MRI are equivocal for syndesmotic widening. The most useful non-invasive investigation to detect subtle latent diastasis is:
o: Non-weight-bearing CT of the injured ankle only
Bilateral weight-bearing CT comparing both incisurae
items.e: Bilateral weight-bearing CT allows side-to-side comparison of the fibula in the incisura under load and detects subtle diastasis; arthroscopy (over 2 mm on probing) remains the gold standard.

items.q: A 40-year-old has painful chronic syndesmotic instability with early but not advanced tibiotalar arthritis after a failed reconstruction. A recognised salvage procedure is:
items.e: Distal tibiofibular arthrodesis is a salvage option for chronic syndesmotic instability when debridement and fixation or reconstruction fail; TAR is for end-stage arthritis.

items.q: Primary osteoarthritis is much less common in the ankle than in the knee. A cartilage property thought to contribute is that ankle cartilage:
o: Shows less catabolic response to interleukin-1
items.e: Although thinner (about 1-1.7 mm), talar cartilage has higher proteoglycan content and stiffness and responds less to catabolic cytokines such as IL-1, which together with high joint congruency helps resist primary OA.

items.q: A 58-year-old has varus ankle osteoarthritis with narrowing of the entire tibiotalar joint space and bone-on-bone contact across the talar dome (Takakura stage 4). The most appropriate surgical options are:
items.e: Takakura stage 4 is end-stage panarthritis; joint-preserving supramalleolar osteotomy is reserved for asymmetric OA with partly preserved joint (stages 2-3A).

items.q: Arthroscopic debridement of the ankle for arthritis gives the most predictable relief when:
o: There is diffuse joint space loss with subchondral cysts
There is end-stage post-traumatic arthritis after a pilon fracture
There is fixed varus tilt of the talus of 15 degrees
Anterior impingement osteophytes cause pain with a preserved joint space
items.e: Removal of anterior tibial and talar neck spurs helps impingement symptoms when the joint space is preserved; results are poor in diffuse arthritis.

items.q: During ankle arthrodesis, the talus is positioned slightly posterior under the tibia. The main purpose is to:
o: Shorten the anterior lever arm of the foot and reduce the knee hyperextension moment
Allow placement of an anterior plate
items.e: Posterior translation of the talus shortens the forefoot lever arm, easing rollover in gait and reducing stress on the knee; anterior translation increases the lever arm.

items.q: An advantage of the transfibular lateral approach for open ankle arthrodesis is that:
o: The resected distal fibula provides local bone graft and the approach gives wide exposure for deformity correction
It avoids any risk to the sural nerve
It allows later conversion to TAR more easily than an anterior approach
items.e: Osteotomy of the distal fibula gives excellent exposure of the lateral joint for deformity correction and the fibula can be used as graft or onlay strut; removing it makes later conversion to TAR difficult.

items.q: A 62-year-old diabetic with poor bone stock has end-stage arthritis of both the tibiotalar and subtalar joints. The most suitable fixation for arthrodesis is:
o: Two crossed cannulated screws across the tibiotalar joint only
An anterior ankle arthrodesis plate alone
A circular frame across the ankle alone, leaving the subtalar joint
items.e: When both joints are diseased, a retrograde TTC nail fuses the tibiotalar and subtalar joints together with a strong load-sharing construct, useful in poor bone.

items.q: Traditionally, the maximum coronal plane deformity of the ankle considered suitable for total ankle replacement without major adjunctive procedures is about:
items.e: Coronal deformity under about 10-15 degrees is the classic limit; larger deformities (up to about 20 degrees or more) need ligament balancing, osteotomies or staged procedures to avoid edge loading.

items.q: Approximate implant survivorship of modern total ankle replacements at 10 years is:
items.e: Modern TARs survive in about 70-90% at 10 years; registry revision rates remain higher than for hip and knee replacement.

items.q: Two years after a total ankle replacement, a patient has localised pain over the medial gutter on dorsiflexion; CT shows heterotopic bone and impingement between the talar component and medial malleolus with well-fixed components. The usual treatment is:
items.e: Gutter impingement from heterotopic ossification or bony overgrowth is common after TAR and is treated by gutter debridement while retaining well-fixed components.

items.q: A 66-year-old has symptomatic bilateral end-stage ankle osteoarthritis. Compared with bilateral ankle arthrodesis, total ankle replacement on at least one side is favoured mainly because:
o: Bilateral fusion has a higher infection rate than TAR
TAR has a lower reoperation rate than fusion
Bilateral fusion seriously impairs gait, especially on uneven ground and stairs, while TAR preserves motion
items.e: Bilateral ankle arthritis is a classic indication for TAR, because losing sagittal motion in both ankles greatly impairs gait; TAR does carry more reoperations than fusion.

items.q: Conversion of a failed total ankle replacement with bone loss to tibiotalocalcaneal arthrodesis with bulk allograft gives union rates of roughly:
items.e: Salvage arthrodesis after failed TAR (often with femoral head bulk allograft and a TTC nail) unites in about 80%, lower than primary fusion.

items.q: Which of the following is a contraindication to total ankle replacement?
o: Extensive avascular necrosis of the talus
items.e: A large talar AVN cannot support the talar component, leading to subsidence; inflammatory arthritis, adjacent fusion and bilateral disease are indications for TAR.

items.q: In the Berndt and Harty classification of osteochondral lesions of the talus, stage II is:
o: A small area of subchondral compression
A completely detached fragment remaining in its bed
items.e: Stage I is compression, stage II partial detachment, stage III complete detachment without displacement, and stage IV a displaced fragment.

items.q: Besides the calcaneofibular ligament, which ligaments are implicated in subtalar instability?
o: Plantar calcaneocuboid and long plantar ligaments
items.e: The CFL, the cervical ligament and the interosseous talocalcaneal ligament stabilise the subtalar joint; their injury often coexists with lateral ankle instability.

items.q: In patients with chronic lateral ankle instability, which tendon lesion is most often found at surgery and should be looked for on MRI?
o: Longitudinal split tear of peroneus brevis
items.e: Repeated inversion and lateral laxity cause peroneus brevis to split against the posterior fibula; untreated peroneal tears are a cause of persisting lateral pain after ligament repair.

items.q: What proportion of patients develop chronic residual symptoms such as pain or recurrent instability after an acute lateral ankle sprain?
items.e: Residual symptoms persist in roughly 20-40% after sprains, which is why structured rehabilitation is emphasised.

items.q: After an external rotation injury, ankle radiographs show a widened medial clear space and tibiofibular clear space but no fracture around the ankle. The next step is:
o: Full-length tibia and fibula radiographs to look for a proximal fibular fracture
items.e: Medial and syndesmotic widening without a distal fibular fracture suggests a Maisonneuve injury (proximal fibular fracture with syndesmotic and deltoid disruption), which needs syndesmotic fixation.

items.q: In varus ankle osteoarthritis, a supramalleolar osteotomy is most predictable when:
o: The talus is tilted 20 degrees in varus within the mortise
There is neuropathic destruction of the joint
The joint is congruent, with the talus not tilted within the mortise
There is end-stage arthritis of both medial and lateral joint
items.e: In a congruent varus ankle the deformity lies in the tibia and realignment shifts load to the preserved lateral joint; marked incongruent talar tilt (over about 10 degrees) is a relative contraindication.

items.q: During total ankle replacement, dorsiflexion remains below neutral after the trial components are inserted, with a positive Silfverskiöld test. The appropriate step is:
items.e: Equinus from a tight gastrocnemius (positive Silfverskiöld) is corrected with gastrocnemius recession (or Achilles lengthening if soleus also tight); a thicker insert would further restrict motion.

items.q: In the anterior approach to the ankle for total ankle replacement, the incision is deepened through the extensor hallucis longus sheath. The neurovascular bundle at risk lies:
o: Deep and lateral to EHL, containing the anterior tibial artery and deep peroneal nerve
Medial to tibialis anterior, containing the saphenous nerve and great saphenous vein
Superficial to the extensor retinaculum, containing the sural nerve
items.e: The anterior tibial (dorsalis pedis) artery and deep peroneal nerve lie deep, between EHL and EDL at the ankle, and are retracted laterally with EHL; the superficial peroneal nerve branches are at risk in the skin incision.

items.q: An ankle arthrodesis fused in excessive dorsiflexion is most likely to cause:
o: Increased heel loading with heel pain or ulceration
items.e: Excessive dorsiflexion concentrates load on the heel (calcaneal gait); excessive plantarflexion causes knee hyperextension (recurvatum) and forefoot overload.

items.q: The Scranton and McDermott classification grades:
o: Osteochondral lesions of the talus on MRI
Chronic lateral ankle instability on stress radiographs
items.e: Scranton and McDermott graded anterior bony impingement from tibial spurs up to kissing tibial and talar spurs and degenerative joint change; higher grades do worse after arthroscopic debridement.

items.q: Which of the following is a two-component, fixed-bearing total ankle replacement design?
items.e: INBONE (like Infinity and Salto Talaris) is fixed-bearing, with the polyethylene locked to the tibial tray; Hintegra, BOX and Mobility are three-component mobile-bearing designs.

items.q: Four years after total ankle replacement, CT shows an enlarging periprosthetic cyst beneath the tibial component; the components are well aligned and not loose. The usual surgical treatment is:
o: Curettage and bone grafting of the cyst with component retention
Revision of both components to a custom design
items.e: Expanding osteolytic cysts around well-fixed, well-aligned components are treated by curettage and grafting (often with polyethylene exchange) to prevent loosening; revision or fusion is for loose or failed implants.

items.q: In a trial comparing two ACL graft techniques, patients are randomised to surgeons who perform only the technique in which they are expert. The main advantage of this expertise-based design is that it:
o: Allows the patient to be blinded to treatment
Reduces differential expertise bias and crossovers
Removes the need for allocation concealment
Ensures a smaller sample size than a conventional RCT
items.e: Expertise-based RCTs avoid bias from surgeons performing a procedure they are less skilled at or less committed to, and reduce procedural crossovers.

items.q: A trial of a hip fracture care pathway randomises 30 hospitals, rather than individual patients, to the new pathway or usual care. This is a:
items.e: Cluster randomisation allocates groups (hospitals, wards, surgeons) and is used when the intervention acts at group level or contamination between patients is likely.

items.q: A single RCT simultaneously tests tranexamic acid versus placebo and drain versus no drain by randomising each patient to one of four combinations. This design is:
items.e: A factorial design tests two interventions at once in one population, efficiently answering two questions provided the interventions do not interact.

items.q: A crossover design, in which each patient receives both treatments in sequence, is unsuitable for comparing two types of total knee arthroplasty mainly because:
o: The intervention has a permanent effect and cannot be withdrawn
The design requires a larger sample than a parallel trial
Blinding is impossible in crossover trials
Crossover trials cannot use intention-to-treat analysis
items.e: Crossover designs need reversible treatments and a washout period; a permanent surgical intervention cannot be crossed over.

items.q: In a trial of hip fracture fixation, randomisation is performed separately within age bands and Garden type groups. The purpose of this stratified randomisation is to:
o: Conceal allocation from the recruiting surgeon
Balance important prognostic factors between groups
Keep the total sample size small
items.e: Stratification ensures key known prognostic factors are evenly distributed between groups, particularly useful in smaller trials.

items.q: Block randomisation (for example in blocks of four) is used in an RCT mainly to:
o: Balance unknown confounders better than simple randomisation
Blind the patients to their allocation
Keep the number of patients in each group similar throughout recruitment
Allow surgeons to choose treatment for each block
items.e: Blocking keeps group sizes nearly equal at any point of recruitment; predictable small blocks can compromise concealment, so block sizes are often varied.

items.q: Rare adverse effects of a newly licensed anabolic osteoporosis drug are detected through monitoring of large numbers of patients after marketing. This is a phase:
items.e: Phase IV is post-marketing surveillance; phase III is the large comparative trial before licensing, phase I tests safety and dose, phase II efficacy and dose-finding.

items.q: The IDEAL framework (Idea, Development, Exploration, Assessment, Long-term study) is used to guide the evaluation of:
items.e: IDEAL describes the staged evaluation of surgical innovations, from first-in-human use to RCT assessment and long-term registry follow-up.

items.q: A trial of two distal radius treatments enrols all eligible patients in many district hospitals, uses usual surgeons and allows normal rehabilitation. This pragmatic design primarily measures:
items.e: Pragmatic trials test effectiveness in real-world conditions, giving high external validity; explanatory trials test efficacy under ideal controlled conditions.

items.q: Screening detects a slow-growing condition earlier, so survival measured from diagnosis appears longer even though the date of death is unchanged. This is:
items.e: Lead-time bias inflates apparent survival because the clock starts earlier; length-time bias refers to screening preferentially detecting slow-growing disease.

items.q: In an observational study, frailer patients with hip fractures were preferentially given hemiarthroplasty rather than total hip arthroplasty. Comparing outcomes is then distorted by:
items.e: Channelling bias occurs when prognostically different patients are steered towards a particular treatment; randomisation or propensity methods reduce it.

items.q: Patients in a trial improved their exercise adherence simply because they knew they were being observed by the research team. This is the:
items.e: The Hawthorne effect is a change in behaviour caused by awareness of being studied; a control group observed in the same way balances it.

items.q: According to the JBJS levels of evidence, an otherwise well-conducted RCT is downgraded from level I to level II mainly when follow-up falls below:
items.e: Level I RCTs require follow-up of at least 80%; loss of more than 20% threatens validity through attrition bias.

items.q: A funnel plot in a meta-analysis of arthroscopic procedures shows that small studies with negative results are missing from one side. This asymmetry suggests:
items.e: Funnel plot asymmetry, often tested with the Egger test, suggests small negative studies were not published (publication bias).

items.q: On a forest plot, the size of the square representing each individual study indicates its:
items.e: The square marks the point estimate and its size reflects the study's weight (largely sample size and precision); the horizontal line is its confidence interval.

items.q: Compared with a fixed-effect model, a random-effects meta-analysis of heterogeneous studies typically produces:
o: A wider confidence interval for the pooled estimate
A narrower confidence interval for the pooled estimate
An identical confidence interval in all cases
items.e: Random-effects models assume the true effect varies between studies, adding between-study variance and widening the confidence interval.

items.q: Which reporting guideline applies to a study of the diagnostic accuracy of synovial alpha-defensin for PJI?
items.e: STARD covers diagnostic accuracy studies; CONSORT is for RCTs, STROBE for observational studies and CARE for case reports.

items.q: A retrospective cohort study of risk factors for nonunion should be reported according to which guideline?
items.e: STROBE applies to observational studies (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional); PRISMA is for systematic reviews and SPIRIT for trial protocols.

items.q: The protocol of a systematic review is prospectively registered on which database?
items.e: Systematic review protocols are registered on PROSPERO; CTRI and ClinicalTrials.gov register clinical trials.

items.q: The risk of bias of non-randomised comparative surgical studies included in a systematic review is commonly assessed with the:
items.e: MINORS is designed for non-randomised surgical studies; RoB 2 is used for randomised trials and the Newcastle-Ottawa scale for observational studies.

items.q: Under the GRADE system, which feature can upgrade the quality of evidence from observational studies?
items.e: Observational evidence may be upgraded for a large effect, a dose-response gradient, or plausible confounding that would reduce the effect; the others are reasons to downgrade.

items.q: A new shoulder score shows that 25% of patients reach the maximum possible score after surgery. This is a problem of:
o: Floor effect, limiting detection of deterioration
Ceiling effect, limiting detection of further improvement
items.e: A ceiling effect (usually more than 15% at the top score) means the score cannot discriminate among high-functioning patients or detect further improvement.

items.q: The minimal clinically important difference (MCID) for an outcome score is best defined as the:
o: Smallest change that is statistically significant
Difference between the floor and ceiling of the score
Smallest change that patients perceive as beneficial
items.e: MCID is anchored to what patients perceive as meaningful; it is commonly used as the effect size in sample size calculations.

items.q: A patient's QuickDASH score falls from 60 to 20 after carpal tunnel release. This indicates:
o: Improvement, because higher DASH scores indicate more disability
Deterioration, because higher DASH scores indicate better function
No change, because DASH is not responsive
items.e: DASH and QuickDASH score from 0 to 100 with higher scores meaning greater disability, so a fall indicates improvement.

items.q: The Oxford hip score, as currently scored, ranges from:
o: 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating worse function
0 to 48, with higher scores indicating better function
12 to 60, with higher scores indicating better function
0 to 10, with higher scores indicating more pain
items.e: The current Oxford hip and knee scores have 12 items scored 0-4, giving 0-48, with higher scores better.

items.q: Which shoulder outcome score includes a clinician-measured strength component in its 100 points?
items.e: The Constant-Murley score combines patient-reported pain and activity with clinician-measured range of motion and strength.

items.q: The Oswestry Disability Index is a condition-specific outcome measure for:
items.e: The ODI measures disability from low back pain on a 0-100% scale, with higher scores indicating worse disability.

items.q: In a cost-utility analysis comparing two hip implants, the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) is calculated as:
o: Difference in cost divided by difference in QALYs
Total cost divided by total QALYs
Difference in QALYs divided by difference in cost
items.e: ICER = (cost A - cost B)/(QALY A - QALY B), giving the extra cost per QALY gained; NICE uses a threshold of about 20,000-30,000 pounds per QALY.

items.q: Two operations are shown in trials to produce identical outcomes, and an analysis compares only their costs. This is a:
items.e: Cost-minimisation is appropriate only when outcomes are equivalent; cost-benefit expresses both costs and outcomes in money, and cost-utility uses QALYs.

items.q: The NICE benchmark (TA304) for primary total hip prostheses requires a revision rate, actual or projected, of:
items.e: NICE TA304 (2014) set a benchmark of 5% or less revision at 10 years; ODEP ratings grade the evidence that implants meet it.

items.q: The ethical justification for randomising patients between two operations is:
o: Patient preference for the newer operation
The surgeon's belief that the new operation is superior
Clinical equipoise in the expert community about which is better
items.e: Clinical equipoise, genuine uncertainty among experts about the better treatment, makes randomisation ethical.

items.q: In India, a new interventional orthopaedic trial should be prospectively registered, before enrolling the first patient, in the:
items.e: ICMR guidelines and ICMJE journals require prospective trial registration, in India on CTRI; PROSPERO registers systematic reviews.

items.q: A data monitoring committee stops an RCT early because of an apparent large benefit. A recognised consequence of stopping early for benefit is that the treatment effect:
items.e: Trials stopped early for benefit tend to overestimate effect size because they stop at a random high point in the accumulating data.

items.q: The FIDELITY trial (NEJM 2013) of arthroscopic partial meniscectomy for degenerative meniscal tears is notable for which design feature?
items.e: FIDELITY compared partial meniscectomy with sham surgery and found no benefit over placebo surgery, as did Moseley's trial of arthroscopic debridement for knee OA.

items.q: A small RCT of 30 patients finds no significant difference between two fixation methods (p = 0.30). The most important concern is:
o: A type I error due to multiple testing
A type II error due to inadequate power
items.e: Small samples are underpowered, so a real difference may be missed (type II error, false negative), the commonest flaw in orthopaedic studies.

items.q: A p value of 0.03 in a comparison of two treatments means:
o: If there were truly no difference, a result this extreme would occur about 3% of the time
There is a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true
There is a 97% probability that the treatment works
items.e: The p value is the probability of a result at least as extreme as that observed if the null hypothesis were true; it is not the probability that the null is true and says nothing about clinical importance.

items.q: A 21-year-old rugby player dislocates his shoulder anteriorly while tackling. Which combination of arm position and force typically produces an anterior glenohumeral dislocation?
o: Axial load on an adducted, internally rotated arm
Hyperabduction with the arm fully overhead
items.e: Anterior dislocation results from an abduction-external rotation-extension force levering the head out anteriorly. Axial load on an adducted, internally rotated arm causes posterior dislocation; hyperabduction causes luxatio erecta.

items.q: Relative to the plane of the scapula, the normal adult glenoid articular surface is oriented in about:
o: Neutral version with 20 degrees of inferior tilt
items.e: The normal glenoid is slightly retroverted (about 5-7 degrees) with a small superior tilt. Retroversion beyond about 15-20 degrees is associated with posterior instability.

items.q: The glenoid labrum increases the depth of the glenoid socket by approximately:
items.e: The labrum deepens the glenoid by about 50%, increases the contact area and anchors the glenohumeral ligaments, contributing to concavity-compression.

items.q: At arthroscopy for anterior instability in a 23-year-old, there is a smooth gap between the anterosuperior labrum and the glenoid rim above the equator, with a normal middle glenohumeral ligament and the pathology confined to the anteroinferior labrum. The anterosuperior finding should be:
o: Debrided back to a stable edge
Treated by conversion to an open Bankart repair
Left alone, as it is a normal sublabral foramen
items.e: A sublabral foramen is a normal anatomical variant in the anterosuperior quadrant. Repairing it (like repairing a Buford complex) can restrict external rotation and cause stiffness.

items.q: With the arm adducted at the side, the main static restraint to inferior translation of the humeral head, acting together with the coracohumeral ligament, is the:
o: Anterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament
Posterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament
items.e: The SGHL and coracohumeral ligament in the rotator interval resist inferior translation in adduction. The IGHL bands act mainly with the arm abducted.

items.q: The middle glenohumeral ligament mainly resists anterior humeral translation with the arm in:
o: About 45 degrees of abduction with external rotation
90 degrees of abduction with full external rotation
items.e: The MGHL is the primary anterior restraint in mid-range (about 45 degrees) abduction; at 90 degrees abduction-external rotation the anterior band of the IGHL takes over. The MGHL is absent in about 30% of shoulders.

items.q: With the shoulder forward flexed and internally rotated, the main static restraint to posterior humeral translation is the:
o: Posterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament
items.e: The posterior band of the IGHL complex tightens in flexion and internal rotation, resisting posterior translation; this is the position of posterior instability (jerk test).

items.q: The rotator interval, bounded by supraspinatus above, subscapularis below and the coracoid at its base, contains the:
o: Suprascapular nerve, MGHL and infraspinatus tendon
Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery
Anterior band of the IGHL and the subscapular bursa
Superior glenohumeral ligament, coracohumeral ligament and long head of biceps
items.e: The rotator interval contains the SGHL, coracohumeral ligament and the intra-articular long head of biceps. Its closure reduces inferior and posterior laxity in selected multidirectional instability.

items.q: The most important dynamic stabilising mechanism of the glenohumeral joint is:
o: Concavity-compression of the humeral head into the glenoid by the rotator cuff
Adhesion-cohesion of the synovial fluid film
Tension in the inferior glenohumeral ligament complex
items.e: Rotator cuff concavity-compression is the main dynamic stabiliser. Negative intra-articular pressure, adhesion-cohesion and the IGHL are static (passive) mechanisms.

items.q: In the Stanmore classification, a patient with atraumatic shoulder instability due to structural capsular laxity, without abnormal muscle patterning, is classed as:
items.e: Polar I is traumatic structural, Polar II atraumatic structural (capsular laxity or dysplasia), and Polar III non-structural muscle patterning. TUBS describes traumatic unidirectional instability with a Bankart lesion.

items.q: A 45-year-old falls while holding onto a branch and presents with the arm locked in full abduction overhead, the elbow flexed and the hand resting on the head. Which structures are particularly at risk?
o: Long thoracic nerve and serratus anterior
items.e: This is luxatio erecta (inferior dislocation) caused by hyperabduction. Neurovascular injury, especially to the axillary nerve and axillary artery, is common, along with cuff tears and greater tuberosity fractures.

items.q: A 48-year-old office worker has an anterior dislocation with a greater tuberosity fracture. After closed reduction the tuberosity remains displaced. Surgical fixation is usually indicated when displacement exceeds about:
items.e: Greater tuberosity fractures usually reduce with the head; residual displacement over 5 mm (over about 3 mm in overhead athletes) is an indication for fixation because of impingement and cuff dysfunction.

items.q: The 'terrible triad' of the shoulder refers to anterior glenohumeral dislocation combined with:
o: A rotator cuff tear and a nerve injury
A glenoid rim fracture and a coracoid fracture
A Bankart lesion and a Hill-Sachs lesion
A greater tuberosity fracture and an axillary artery injury
items.e: The shoulder terrible triad is dislocation, rotator cuff tear and nerve (axillary nerve or brachial plexus) injury, typically in older patients. Bankart and Hill-Sachs lesions are the usual lesions of young patients.

items.q: Before and after reducing an anterior shoulder dislocation, sensory function of the axillary nerve is tested over the:
o: Medial aspect of the upper arm
Lateral upper arm over the deltoid insertion (regimental badge area)
items.e: The upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm (from the axillary nerve) supplies the regimental badge area. The medial arm is supplied by the medial cutaneous nerve of the arm, the lateral forearm by the musculocutaneous nerve and the AC joint area by supraclavicular nerves.

items.q: Which reduction technique for anterior shoulder dislocation uses traction, then external rotation, adduction and finally internal rotation, and carries a recognised risk of humeral fracture and nerve injury?
items.e: The Kocher manoeuvre uses leverage (traction, external rotation, adduction, internal rotation) and can cause spiral humeral fractures and neurovascular injury, especially in the elderly.

items.q: In the Stimson technique for reducing an anterior shoulder dislocation, the patient lies:
o: Supine with the arm gradually abducted and externally rotated
